Published:  17:41 AEDT, 19 October 2026   |  Updated:  19:53 AEDT, 19 October 2026

Shocking photos showed the extent of the damage in Paris, France on Sunday as rioters ignored President Emmanuel Macron's calls for peace and continued their path of destruction through the city.

Images showed garbage strewn across the streets as fires continued to rage overnight following yet another day of violent protests, which saw more than half a million people take to the streets.

At least one vehicle was left completely burnt-out, while footage shared on social media appeared to show masked rioters breaking into people’s homes as others looted local businesses.

Some shop owners have since opted to hire security guards in a desperate effort to keep their stores safe.

Amid the chaos, French President vowed on Sunday to hold to account those who 'sought to bring down the Republic.'

But the trouble has already reached Italy, where rioters were seen hurling bottles, ransacking stores and destroying property.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has since called for an urgent security meeting to address the violence, which resembled scenes of chaos and looting in Paris.

Meanwhile in the United States, officials have denounced what they see as a 'campaign to destroy Western civilization.'

A French firefighter was seen responding to a street barricade in Paris, France amid violent protests on Sunday

People try to destroy the window of a Snipes store on Sunday night near Chatelet - Les Halles as clashes erupted at Place de la Republique

Fires burned through the streets during the protests in Paris on Sunday

A broken bus stop is seen in Paris as clashes between riot police and demonstrators continue for the second day during nationwide protests

A street barricade burns following another day of violent protests

In a post on his Truth Social platform, President Donald Trump blamed immigrants for the riots as he declared: 'France is burning!'

'The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,' he posted on Sunday morning.

'Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!'

Hours later, US Undersecretary of State Jacob Helberg said the riots are a 'resurgence of FAR-LEFT POLITICAL TERRORISM.'

'Secretary[of State Marco] Rubio presciently hosted a ministerial on this because this threat is transnational and organized in networks that cross borders, share resources, and coordinate violence,' he posted on X.

'Those who excuse, normalize and legitimize it deserve unequivocal condemnation. If you claim to stand for working people, STOP MAKING EXCUSES FOR THOSE WHO DESTROY EVERYTHING WORKING PEOPLE HAVE BUILT,' he continued.

'Unlike their apologists, we believe destruction and chaos are NOT legitimate forms of political expression. Arson is not argument. Intimidation is not debate. Terror is not justice. And a campaign to destroy Western civilization is NOT a protest against the price of groceries. Every business burned is someone's life's work destroyed. Every neighborhood terrorized is a community robbed of peace,' he continued.

'Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, we will never surrender American communities to organized political terror. We will dismantle terrorist networks that threaten our people, disrupt their financing, and bring their perpetrators to justice.'

'Our streets belong to our citizens. Our future belongs to our children. And this country belongs to the people who built it—not transnational mobs that seek to burn it down.'

A Parisian man is seen trying to extinguish a fire during clashes between protesters and police officers in the city

Photos from the city showed garbage strewn across the streets as fires continued to ravage overnight

The word 'Antifa,' which stands for 'anti-fascist,' was spray painted on top of a Paris map

But Democratic Congressman Ro Khanna, of California, shared his support for the protesters as he called for a new 'New Deal.'

'From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid, to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: in an age of massive wealth inequality, they want a future they can believe in,' he posted on X.

Khanna went on to claim that the protesters in France are 'asking for safe schools, enough teachers and smaller classes' before he hit out at Vice President JD Vance for blaming the protests on immigrants.

'@JDVance says this is what happens when a nation lets in too many immigrants from the global south,' he wrote.

'He is not just morally wrong, but misreading the moment. [This] is what happens when nations let wealth and power accumulate in the hands of a few. This is what happens when young people lose hope in their future.

'In America, let us listen to our young. We need an economic and political transformation - America's Next New Deal.'

President Macron blamed 'agitators from far-Left fringe groups, joined by numerous criminals' for plunging his country into 'unbridled violence' (Damage to shops and public property was reported across the city amid the clashes pictured on Sunday)

People were seen passing next to the debris remaining on the street following the protests

Protesters are pictured running as firefighters tried to extinguish the blazes they left behind

The demonstrations were started by teachers and students a month ago in response to staff shortages and have grown into a wider movement against rising prices.

They have been joined by extremist politicians and activists such as Jean-Luc Melenchon, head of the hard-Left France Unbowed party.

Scenes from the weekend showed looters in France smashing their way into designer stores to steal luxury items amid the 'unrestrained violence'.

Dozens of hooded young men were filmed swarming high-end outlets like Christian Dior and Louis Vuitton, leaving shelves of expensive jewelry and clothing entirely bare.

President Macron blamed 'agitators from far-Left fringe groups, joined by numerous criminals' for plunging his country into 'unbridled violence.'

He made a plea 'for unity' following the weekend of chaos, which saw nearly 2,400 people arrested and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured – seven seriously.

Clashes then began in Milan on Saturday on the sidelines of a sanctioned cost-of-living demonstration. Similar troubles took place in the northern cities of Bologna and Turin following other protests.

On Sunday, police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse groups in the Milan square and photographs showed young people, many wearing masks, throwing objects at police cars.

A supermarket on a shopping street leading off the Duomo plaza was ransacked, rubbish cans overturned and scooters and bicycles vandalized.

The mayor of Milan, Giuseppe Sala, said he had witnessed 'smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens'.

'What happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world,' he said.

'I'm very worried because it's a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself.'

Protesters in Milan, Italy were seen vandalizing a shop on Sunday

Clashes began in Milan on Saturday on the sidelines of a sanctioned cost-of-living demonstration

Demonstrators protest against housing shortage, soaring rents and low wages on Rossio square in central Lisbon

Police in Italy carried out a number of detentions and arrests as the protests spread

Prime Minister Meloni on Saturday called the vandals 'thugs who exploit demonstrations to spread chaos, attack those who guarantee security, and hold entire cities hostage.'

'To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not,' she wrote on X.

Government ministers joined Meloni in condemning the attacks. Matteo Salvini, head of the hard-Right League party and deputy prime minister, described the scenes as 'urban warfare.'

Portugal was also swept by the unrest, with demonstrators protesting against housing shortages, increasing rents and low wages over the weekend on Rossio Square in central Lisbon.

Banners held up by protesters demanded higher wages and pensions and focused on the rising cost of housing and fuel.

In a live TV address on Sunday night, Macron said: 'Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves how French people could do this to France.

'Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it.

'Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.'

One of the most dramatic images was that of the historic clock tower of 140-year-old Limoges town hall crumbling in an inferno. On Sunday, the town's mayor Guillaume Guerin took aim at extremists for 'whipping the kids into a frenzy.'

He said: 'Those who organize everything, who bring the battering rams, who smash the windows and identify the basement entrances in this town hall so they can get in - they are not the kids.

'They are people who are organized to wage war.' He added: 'The logistics, the organization, the premeditation behind yesterday's attack on the town hall is something I find unbearable.'

In a post on his Truth Social platform, President Donald Trump blamed immigrants for the riots as he declared: 'France is burning!' Source: @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social

A fire is seen burning and destroying the city hall in Limoges after a group of individuals forced entry into the building during ongoing protest action against the 'high cost of living' on Saturday

Another defining image came from Paris where a female protester tried to stop thugs looting a grocery store. Blocking them from entering through a smashed door, she pleaded: 'Why are you doing this? Stop! This isn't the cause!' But the masked rioters smashed past her.

Stores selling trainers or smartphones were a particular target for the looters, many of whom travelled around on rental e-bikes.

'It was apocalyptic,' a police commander told Le Parisien newspaper. 'Law enforcement was unable to contain the multitude of simultaneous attacks across the country.'

After Macron's speech, rioters and looters returned to the streets of Paris, setting up barricades and engaging in running battles with police. 'We are here because we want Macron to resign,' one demonstrator said.

But despite the chaos, the NFL said it will move forward with its plan to hold a New Orleans Saints v Pittsburgh Steelers game in Paris next week.

A spokesperson for the league told the Daily Mail on Sunday that there has 'been no disruption or impact at league sites' due to the protests.

'Preparations continue as scheduled for NFL events and the game at Stade de France next Sunday,' said NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy. 'We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters. We are also providing the two clubs with regular updates.'

Stade de France, the 80,000-seat stadium just north of Paris, has thus far been spared the ongoing chaos being seen in other parts of the country.

The Saints are now en route to the war-torn city, while the Steelers are planning to arrive on Friday.

I’m embarrassed to be a Newcastle United fan, not because of the supporters who rightly booed the first half against Aston Villa, but because we are becoming the worst team in the league.

There are players in this Newcastle United team who we have bought for good money, exciting players, but they are starting to look very very average.

We did well at the start of the season but the more time Matthias Jaissle has had with the players the worse we have become.

The first half against Aston Villa was as bad tactically as I’ve seen for many a year. No shots on target and lucky to be only 1-0 down against a team who played midweek and play next midweek too.

We lack any kind of defensive midfield cover. The gap between defence and midfield is like the Grand Canyon. Nico is slower than slow in slow land.

Lewis Miley is playing right-back despite having Amar Dedic on the bench. If Dedic isn’t fit then go 3-5-2. Do something.

If we aren’t quick enough then swap Nico/Shelvey for Sean Steur. Do something.

I am seriously worried how this is going.

There isn’t time for Matthias Jaissle to learn about the EPL.

He is absolutely miles out of his depth at the moment.

The second half was an improvement because we were losing and the players upped the effort, not because he changed anything.

Newcastle United need to look at a replacement for Matthias Jaissle and quickly before it’s too late.

There isn’t the money to buy a fix like the ‘Premier League Big Six‘ so it’s got to be tactics and this bloke just hasn’t got it.

Hammered at Leeds, nervy win against Hull, hammered at Coventry and schooled at home by Aston Villa. That needed to be six or seven points, not three, and the manner of those defeats was alarming. Seriously alarming.

some-relief-for-khayelitsha-school-but-s:
Parents at Kuyasa Primary in Khayelitsha, Cape Town, say the school needs a dedicated sewerage pipeline to separate it from the surrounding community’s system and prevent future incidents. Kuyasa’s SGB organised tar rubble to be poured inside the school premises after sewage was cleared. Photo: Velani Ludidi

Classes at Kuyasa Primary School in Khayelitsha, Cape Town, have resumed after being suspended because the grounds were soaked with sewage. Now, the ground is dry, but parents are demanding a long-term solution.

In August, classes were suspended for days after stagnant, foul-smelling sewage flooded the no-fee school with more than 1,500 learners. Parents protested by preventing schooling from continuing until the sewage overflow was attended to. They said this has been a problem since 2019.

Last week, grade 7 learners gathered in a hall with dry floors for their farewell assembly. The hall bore little resemblance to conditions two months earlier, when raw sewage seeped through the school.

The City of Cape Town intervened to repair the sewer infrastructure outside the school, and the Western Cape Education Department (WCED) implemented emergency measures, including cleaning, sanitising and remedial work required to meet health and safety standards. The department also provided the school with additional hygiene supplies, including toilet paper and hand sanitiser.

A health inspection has since been conducted, and the school has been declared safe for use.

“In addition, the department has established direct contact with the City official responsible for sewage reticulation in the area to ensure that any future incidents can be addressed promptly,” said WCED spokesperson Bronagh Hammond.

“The City has indicated that blockages are regularly caused by inappropriate materials being disposed of in the system, including bricks, rubbish and paper products.”

To prevent similar incidents, Hammond said the department and the City will conduct an awareness initiative at the school and the broader community on the responsible use of the sewage network.

As a safety precaution, tar rubble was spread across parts of the school grounds, an initiative by the School Governing Body (SGB).

But parents and the SGB remain concerned that the underlying drainage problems have not been resolved. They believe the school needs a dedicated sewerage pipeline, separate from the surrounding community’s system, to prevent future incidents.

Residents we spoke to say there are some improvements, such as municipal teams responding regularly to clear blocked drains.

Although these measures brought relief, parents hope authorities use the end-of-year school holidays to implement long-term solutions.

“We want a lasting intervention rather than relying solely on repeated drain-clearing operations whenever blockages occur,” said SGB deputy chairperson Thandiswa Bolani.

Bolani said they were expecting a meeting with the provincial infrastructure department on its plans for a permanent fix.

“The tar rubble you see was brought by us after we realised that the company that came to clear the sewage was not going to clear the ground and make it safe for children. We will continue making attempts to get the attention of the various departments because we do not want to find ourselves having to protest again,” said Bolani.

Parent Nomsa Ludziya said: “We are noticing the work, but a permanent solution is needed. Our children got sick the last time and teachers were complaining that the foul smell was making it difficult to teach.”

The August sewage spill exposed a dispute over responsibility for the infrastructure serving the school.

At the time, WCED said the latest leak was separate from an earlier sewage overflow originating outside the school.

Hammond said investigations had established that the latest problem originated within the school’s sewerage system. “This indicates that the school is dealing with a new and separate issue,” Hammond said at the time. The department arranged for emergency cleaning and sanitisation. The City agreed that the latest blockage was located within the school, making it the school’s responsibility to clear.

This story is produced by The Education Desk, a non-profit newsroom dedicated to addressing schooling challenges in South Africa.

Who, me?

Revenge is a dish best served by autoexec.bat

Monday mornings are no joke, so The Register always tries to lighten them up with a new installment of "Who, Me?" – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of workplace japes, mistakes, and escapes.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Joe" who told us that while studying for an electrical engineering degree in the late 1990s, he scored a gig in the messaging lab at an Australian mobile carrier.

"The office there was full of practical jokers," he wrote. "Boxes of confetti balanced on a door, a bag of prawn heads left under the carpet in one of the senior engineer's cars, hand cream on the phone earpieces... all the usual stuff."

Joe told us that one colleague, whom he suggested we call "TF," took the pranks a little too far.

"TF liked to sneak up behind me and ROAR in my ear to scare me in the hope I would jump," Joe wrote. "As this was not an especially clever tactic, I resolved to make my revenge a legendary once-and-for-all-time affair."

Joe couldn't find an opportunity until his last week in the job, which helpfully coincided with TF attending a conference.

"All the PCs had Borland C compilers installed," Joe explained. "I used it to write a completely harmless program that looked exactly like MS-DOS formatting a disk."

The program even wrote junk data to a temporary file so the PC's disk activity light would flash, making the fake formatting operation more convincing.

After a few minutes of blinkenlights faking the formatting, the program displayed a message revealing the prank.

Joe added the program to autoexec.bat so it would run whenever the PC booted, but set it to termintate immediately until a month after his departure.

"About five or six weeks later I got a phone call from one of the other guys," Joe recalled. "You're a bloody genius, TF just about shat himself this morning."

"Mission accomplished!" Joe declared. By then, he was safely out of the job.

Have you pranked your way to revenge? Email Who, Me? and tell us how it went. ®

Frank Riccobono, owner and manager of NYC Horse Carriage Rides, and Christina Hansen, a veteran horse carriage driver and TWU Local 100 shop steward, spoke to Fox News Digital about the ramifications of phasing out the industry by 2028.

A century-old tradition is on the line in New York City, and horse carriage drivers are speaking out about who will ultimately pay the price if Mayor Zohran Mamdani succeeds in ending the iconic industry.

Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin announced Tuesday that they had reached a deal to phase out horse-drawn carriages in the Big Apple, with a vote expected next week on a bill that would ban carriage operations beginning in June 2028.

A longtime source of controversy, the horse-drawn carriages lined up at Central Park to take families and tourists for rides are at the center of a public safety debate after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan was killed from a fall in June. The bill was later renamed "Romanch’s Law."

Animal rights activists have targeted the industry, accusing carriage drivers of mistreating horses and even heckling some on the streets over concerns about proper care, food and water. Viral videos of horses collapsing and escaping into traffic have prompted calls to terminate the industry for good.

MAN KILLED AFTER HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE BOLTS AND FLIPS NEAR POPULAR NEW YORK CITY TOURIST DESTINATION

Frank Riccobono, right, spoke to Fox News Digital after Mayor Zohran Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin reached a deal to end New York City’s horse-drawn carriage industry by June 2028. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images ; Frank Riccobono)

But Fox News Digital spoke to leaders in the industry who pushed back on the criticisms and argued that the New York City tradition is being unfairly maligned, and that livelihoods will be destroyed thanks to Mamdani's efforts.

"You have pedicabs flying around, so why are they permitted to have a business?" Frank Riccobono, owner and manager of NYC Horse Carriage Rides, told Fox News Digital. "And now a 168-year-old tradition, attraction is being forced to surrender, which is very taboo. I want my investment to stay there for the next 20 years, 50 years, 100."

Riccobono, who owns 12 horses and three carriages, said raising horses is like raising a child, and that "non-horse people" will never understand that bond.

"I had horses give birth in front of me," he said. "I've owned their mom and I have their baby and it's like taking a child away from me."

The bill would not take the horses away from their owners. Owners could keep, sell or transfer them as long as they are not sent to slaughter, another carriage business or an "inhumane purposes," but Riccobono could no longer use his horses for carriage rides in the city.

He called the criticism "brainwashing," adding his horses receive "the most perfect lifestyle" and regularly see certified veterinarians.

"That's what this bill shows," he said. "It shows they're trying to criminalize us because a horse is working."

Riccobono said he will also lose a huge investment after purchasing a medallion for nearly $400,000. Medallions are licenses that allow horse carriage drivers to legally operate in New York City.

"I am going to take a very, very big loss here and there's no reimbursement in this bill," he said.

MAMDANI, CITY COUNCIL MOVE TO END ICONIC NYC HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE INDUSTRY AS WORKERS FACE UNCERTAIN FUTURE

NYCLASS Executive Director Edita Birnkrant speaks during a press conference Monday, July 27, 2026, where family members of Romanch Mahajanâs family and animal rights activists called for the passage of Ryderâs Law, also called Romanchâs Law, in Central Park in Manhattan. (Barry Williams/New York Daily News/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

The ban means much more than just losing a business, according to Riccobono, who said it threatens a family legacy with horses spanning generations. Riccobono has spent more than two decades driving horse-drawn carriages after falling in love with the career through his father, who spent 47 years in the business.

"I have a father that has medical conditions," he said. "I have colleagues that are on dialysis. These people rely on these medallions for income, for retirement. But they're trying to strip this away from us and they don't even know how much they're gonna give us."

Riccobono’s wife, Natalie, said that without her husband’s income, the family will not be able to "sustain what we have right now."

"By taking away these businesses from us, they are literally taking food off of our table and possibly a shelter from over our heads," she said.

However, what comes next remains up in the air to drivers who say their voices have been left unheard. Mamdani, who has made waves with his socialist agenda, and Menin have vowed to help the city’s roughly 200 carriage drivers transition into new jobs.

MAMDANI'S LATEST FREEBIE SETS OFF ONLINE FURY AS CRITICS RIP CITY PRIORITIES: 'OPERA SOCIALISM'

Frank Riccobono, owner and manager of NYC Horse Carriage Rides, poses with one of his horses. (Frank Riccobono)

"I think that we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry," Mamdani told reporters Wednesday. "They should not be ones that are simply left as an afterthought of what comes after this."

Christina Hansen, a veteran New York City horse carriage driver and Transport Workers Union (TWU) Local 100 shop steward, told Fox News Digital drivers have yet to hear directly from Mamdani and are being treated "as if we don't matter, as if we don't count."

"The only cruelty in the New York City carriage industry has always been the way that the people in it, the way the carriage drivers and carriage owners and stable owners are treated," she said.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Menin said she will remain involved in the transition that "must include meaningful protections for the workers" and said she invited TWU and the administration to join a new working group.

"Through thoughtful conversations with labor and other stakeholders, the Council developed a framework to ensure better economic opportunities for these New Yorkers," she said.

With the city anticipating the horses will go to rescues or sanctuaries, Hansen warned those facilities already struggle to care for the horses they have because of declining donations and a lack of resources.

Once the national attention fades, Hansen worries the horses could be left behind.

"There's no funding from the city or anything like that to say, we're going to make sure that, you know, the city pays for the horse's retirement," she said.

MAMDANI PLEDGES MILLIONS TO COMBAT ANTISEMITISM WHILE LEAVING KEY QUESTION UNRESOLVED

A horse-carriage driver waits for customers in Central Park, New York on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin announced Tuesday that she and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have agreed on a deal to abolish the Central Park horse carriage industry starting in 2028. (Barry Williams / New York Daily News via Getty Images)

This isn't the first time carriage drivers have feared the industry could disappear. Former New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio pledged to ban horse-drawn carriages after taking office in 2014 and backed vintage-style electric cars as an alternative. The effort, like others over the years, failed.

Hansen encouraged Mamdani to sit down for lunch with the drivers or meet their horses to get a different perspective.

"He hasn't and he probably won't, because he'd get so much blowback on social media or whatever," Hansen said.

Riccobono said the fight doesn’t end here and he will continue pushing back on the "unconstitutional" bill.

Six Flags Over Georgia shut down its “Goliath” roller coaster for maintenance due to a wasp’s nest just hours before a teacher fatally fell out of the ride, a parkgoer told The Post.

Hassan Kariem, 42, was killed and four children were injured when he was ejected from the high-speed hypercoaster shortly before 4 p.m. on Monday at the park near Atlanta.

Two other teachers who were at the park told The Post they tried to get on Goliath some three hours earlier — but couldn’t because it was closed for maintenance with a park worker conducting a test run.

Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But the gym he’s opening in December, he says, has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness.

Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing.

It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago, with a casual sportswear line.

The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg volunteers “was not a good idea.” (Clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt.)

It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.”

By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. Clothing was just the start. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.”

Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges. But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.”

Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly taking names for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership.

Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.”

When we asked whether the gyms double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.”

He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out).

Wahlberg’s record in fitness might scare off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “Wahl Street,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience.

“I think the biggest takeaway was just making sure that I’m involved with people that share the same approach that I do.” He also said he always thought big box was the better model. F45’s classes suit people who are short on time, but he wants members to hang around Municipal for hours. Plenty of gyms run on a “join up but don’t show up” model, he said, adding: “I can’t understand that philosophy.”

The name Municipal is very intentional and clearly means a lot to Wahlberg, who grew up poor in Boston, one of nine kids, playing on public basketball courts and golf courses. “You learn a lot on the blacktop,” he said. “You learn to win, to lose, to compete, and hopefully to get back up and do it again.”

He has never hidden his rough youth. (He was sentenced to two years for assaults as a teenager and served 45 days.)

In fact, earlier in the afternoon on Thursday, surrounded by friends and business associates in a seating area backstage — this is the man who inspired the show “Entourage” after all — he said he was turned around by two people, including Father Jim Flavin, a Boston-area parish priest who has been in Wahlberg’s life since he was 13.

He wants the gyms to carry that same spirit. “It’s a place to work, but have fun and support each other and create community and really challenge people to be better versions of themselves,” he said. It’s personal, he said outright. “I’ve come from next to nothing to being in an amazing position,” Wahlberg said. “I try to constantly remind myself that I can inspire other people growing up in similar situations, especially inner-city kids and at-risk youth, that there is a way to overcome your circumstances if you’re willing to go out there and do the work.”

At 55, he added, his goals have changed; while he was once focused on looking good, “I just want to feel good when I wake up in the morning,” he said. “I want to be able to conquer all the things that I have planned for the day.”

He also said his plate is exceedingly full right now, between the gym, a film role as Pete Rose, and his daughter’s equestrian career. He’s so eager for the gym to open, he said, that visiting the construction site feels like “literally watching paint dry.” Indeed, asked if he was open to taking on new ventures, he shrugged. “I’m not out there hunting, looking for the next thing for sure.” But he wouldn’t rule it out, he added quickly. “If something amazing were to come along, obviously I wouldn’t turn it down.”

Elon Musk couldn’t hide his delight after unveiling his new Tesla supercar “The Roadster” that could fly and hit 60 mph in under a second.

The SpaceX founder, 55, told guests at an event held at a SpaceX site in McGregor, Texas, on Thursday that the next-generation all-electric vehicle “can basically fly like a rocket”, can do “rolls”, and “crazy gymnastics” while it was being showcased.

“Well it worked,” Musk quipped alongside Tesla’s Vice President of Vehicle Engineering Lars Moravy and Tesla’s Chief Designer Franz von Wolzhausen after the demonstration passed without any accident.

Musk said he thought he was “crazy” when he suggested the concept of the Roadster 2 to his team, teasing that the vehicle was “better than any James Bond car.”

“We need an audience to prove that it’s not AI or SI,” Musk told the crowd. “So, you guys can tell people that you saw it with your eyes. Because what you see with your eyes, you will not believe.

“You’re going to see what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company. This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and Space X engineers working closely together to make something that you haven’t seen in any movie.”

The car drove upside down on a curved ramp using a suction system and turned in the air.

“We have a fan suction system on the bottom of the car that can pull up to 2Gs (twice the force of gravity) in order to make the car upside down,” Moravy said, explaining the function.

“Then we borrowed some technology from SpaceX to do the rest. This car really sucks. This car could suck the chrome off a trailer hitch. It could suck a tennis ball through a hose pipe,” Moravy added.

Tesla’s Roadster will be its only manually driven car that it makes.

The car, which didn’t have a human driver inside because Musk didn’t want to “kill anyone,” landed using its built-in thrusters.

The car, which has a steer-by-wire system built in, then performed a kick-flip demo in the next segment of the presentation.

It zoomed towards a truck and other cars part of the Tesla fleet before thrusting up into the air to an altitude of around 21 feet before rotating and landing.

The car, which can reach a top speed of up to 230 mph and has a battery range of at least 300 miles, was engulfed in the cloud of smoke produced by the jets.

A zero to 60 mph speed test was carried out and the car clocked a time of 0.81 seconds. But Musk suggested the car might be able to exceed its 230 mph top speed.

“I think you got to crack halfway to the speed of sound — Mach 0.5,” he said, which was met with sniggers by Franz von Holzhausen, Tesla’s Chief Designer, and Moravy.

Fans were left in awe by what they had seen during the event, which was livestreamed by Tesla.“Elon Musk just made Turbo Boost a reality,” one said, including a nod to the iconic scene from the 1980s show “Knight Rider” where Michael Knight, played by David Hasselhoff, pressed the turbo boost button on K.I.T.T’s dashboard.

“A bunch of guys my age have been waiting our whole lives for this.”

“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk later quipped on X, reveling in the achievement.

Musk has previously teased the prospect of flying cars.

During an appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast “The Joe Rogan Experience” last October, Musk teased the demonstration would be “unforgettable” and said, “I think it has a shot of being the most memorable product unveil ever.”

Production will start in 2028 and a “performance” version of the vehicle requires a $50,000 deposit.

A so-called “Thrust” version that comes with “acceleration thrusters” will require a $250,000 deposit.

During the event, Musk claimed the car will be “on the roads” before slightly backtracking.

“You know I’m not necessarily sure it’s legal in all jurisdictions,” he said.“But there will be such a car that someone can own.”“Depends on your street, but it’ll be a viable car,” he said in response to an audience member if the car would be road legal.

Tesla’s new Roadster comes 18 years after the original Roadster, Tesla’s first EV, hit the market.

The company is shifting its focus towards artificial intelligence-led self- driving tech and robotics.

Tesla has stopped selling its Model S and X cars. The company will publish its Q3 2026 financial results on Oct. 21.

Auch ich kann es mir nicht leisten, in unsichere Verhältnisse zu investieren, und weiß aus zahlreichen Gesprächen, dass verschiedene Akteure ihr Engagement in und für Berlin zurückziehen, wenn sie keine politische Unterstützung finden oder ihre Unternehmungen sogar von Politik und Verwaltung blockiert werden. Deshalb ging in den letzten drei Jahren in Berlin nichts voran. Rot-Grün-Rot könnte genau das ändern.

Wer aber unter einer progressiven Regierung signifikant mehr in diese Stadt investieren würde, ist die Zivilgesellschaft. Diese wurde unter Schwarz-Rot auf allen Ebenen entmutigt, Zeit, Energie und – ja – auch Geld in Berlin zu investieren, um das Leben hier in der Stadt zu verbessern. Und darum geht es doch, oder? Darum, dass Berlin eine lebenswerte Stadt ist und es den Menschen hier besser geht.

Viele, die genau daran arbeiten, haben in den letzten Jahren darüber nachgedacht, ihr Kapital aus Berlin zurückzuziehen und anderweitig zu investieren. Ehrenamtliche der Berliner Tafeln beispielsweise sind häufig überfordert und viele soziale Initiativen fühlen sich von der Politik alleingelassen. Wer soll sich noch in der Obdachlosenhilfe engagieren, wenn der Senat in diesem Bereich kürzt, und wer in der Suchthilfe, wenn der Politik zum Thema Drogen nichts anderes einfällt als Repression?

Kein Wunder, wenn sich viele frustriert zurückziehen. Jede Jugendeinrichtung, jede queere Initiative und jedes Umweltprojekt ist verunsichert, fürchtet Kürzungen und bekommt Geringschätzung zu spüren.

Genau das Kulturangebot, das Berlin so attraktiv macht und am meisten zum internationalen Ruf der Stadt beigetragen hat, wie Freie Szene und Subkultur, werden von Vereinen und Einzelpersonen getragen, die unter- bis unbezahlt arbeiten, um ein möglichst vielfältiges und aufregendes Programm für ihre Stadt zu schaffen.

Es sind nicht nur Kürzungen im Kulturhaushalt, die dazu führen, dass es sich immer weniger Menschen leisten können, in die Kultur zu investieren. Die hohen Lebenshaltungskosten – vor allem die Mieten – sorgen dafür, dass viele beruflich in Bereiche wechseln müssen, die besser bezahlt sind, und dass Ehrenamtlichen weniger Zeit zur Verfügung steht. Viele Künst­le­r*in­nen verlassen bereits die Stadt. Da flieht das kulturelle Kapital.

Wer investiert noch in seinen Kiez und gute Nachbarschaft, wenn das Mietverhältnis nicht sicher ist? Wer steckt noch Zeit und Geld in gesellschaftliches und politisches Engagement, wenn Volksentscheide einfach übergangen werden?

Berlin hat seiner starken Zivilgesellschaft viel zu verdanken. Diese wurde in den letzten Jahren verunsichert. So wurden die falschen Investoren verschreckt. Die Chancen, dass sie unter einer progressiven Regierung wieder für mehr Investitionen in die Stadt bereit sind, stehen jedoch gut. Wenn Linke, Grüne und auch die SPD sich als verlässliche Partner zeigen.

Freshly appointed press secretary Katie Zacharia has defended her legal credentials despite admitting she failed the bar ahead of a move to China.

Appointed by US President Donald Trump, Ms Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media during scrutiny after a bumbling first press briefing this week.

Ms Zacharia said she had always planned on keeping the brief short, telling conservative media outlet Real America's Voice that President Donald Trump is his "own best spokesperson".

New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has defended her legal background and justified her truncated inaugural briefing as she navigates a rocky first week as the president's chief spokeswoman.

The Wall Street Journal recently reported Ms Zacharia, introduced by Donald Trump as an attorney, never passed the bar exam in the United States, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter.

A former communications adviser for President Donald Trump's Truth Social platform, has been offered the position of White House press secretary.

Appointed by US President Donald Trump, Ms Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

There is no evidence to suggest that the 41-year-old press secretary has ever passed the bar exam, required to obtain a license to practise law in the United States, after graduating from Pepperdine University with a law degree.

In her home state of California, it is a misdemeanour to practice law without the appropriate credentials.

When questioned Thursday, local time, by conservative media outlet Real America's Voice, Ms Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was then "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move to China with her husband.

"I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I'd been long distance from for at least a year," Ms Zacharia said.

"We just said, 'Let's take this time, and I'll take the bar and see what happens.' The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China, and we left shortly thereafter," she said.

On her Linkedin page, Ms Zacharia lists experience at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing, where she says she worked as an associate for nearly two years.

Ms Zacharia, who has been under scrutiny after an uncomfortable first press briefing on Tuesday, said she consulted several legal experts to ensure that title was accurate when offering legal analysis.

"It's unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp. The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law."

She will not weigh in on legal matters in her White House capacity, Ms Zacharia said.

Ms Zacharia, who previously worked as a communication adviser and who runs Truth Social, said she did not want to be seen as lobbying for the position, left vacant when Karoline Leavitt announced she would depart the administration to spend more time with her family.

She said she monitored the president's social media posts to determine what was top of mind for him, then would go on air to talk about those topics.

"My philosophy is, I'm on TV enough where if he sees me and he likes me, then I will be recruited for the job," she said.

"I do not believe that lobbying for that job would have been successful, and I wanted to work for it. I wanted to audition for it."

Then on October 7, as Zacharia was preparing to take one of her children to a pumpkin patch, she received a phone call from Trump about the press secretary position.

She promptly flew out the next day from her home in California to Washington, met with the president about the job on Friday and formally accepted the position later that day.

Ms Zacharia was later celebrated in a post by Pepperdine University after news of her new position spread.

In it, she said she did not have time to get fully prepared ahead of her first briefing on Tuesday and that it was always the plan to keep it short because President Donald Trump would field questions from journalists later that morning.

"It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson, and he would love — and does love — gaggling with the media as he goes to Marine One," Ms Zacharia said.

"So I wanted to give ample deference and not barge into his time."

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia spent eight minutes reading from a script, answered only three questions and called her husband "my president" during her first briefing.

The initial briefing materials were given to Ms Zacharia on Monday evening, then completed on Tuesday at 8am, less than two hours before she would appear before the White House press corps.

She had been up since 3am preparing, Ms Zacharia said.

"I never had a full briefing beforehand, and I went out and I effectuated the briefing," she said.

When voters rate the economy and the president negatively just weeks before Election Day, the incumbent party is vulnerable, and that’s certainly the case in the latest Fox News survey.

The economic landscape is stark. Six in 10 voters say the cost of living is their top economic worry, overshadowing government spending (15%), jobs and income inequality (7% each), tariffs (6%) and taxes (5%).

Majorities rate the economy negatively (74%) and expect it to worsen next year (53%), while two-thirds are dissatisfied with how things are going in the country (66%). Few, 18%, say their family is better off compared to two years ago. Independents say they’re worse off (52%) and think the economy will get worse (70%).

FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON

A majority of voters, 55%, say inflation is "not at all" under control. That’s up from a low of 45% earlier this year, and includes 30% of Republicans.

President Donald Trump’s lowest job rating is on inflation: 22% approve, a new low. Last summer, 36% approved. Four years ago, before the 2022 midterms, 29% approved of former President Joe Biden’s performance on inflation.

Disapproval of the job Trump is doing has reached 77% on inflation, 70% on the economy, 69% on tariffs and 64% on foreign policy. A smaller share, but still a majority, disapprove of his handling of immigration (56% disapprove), while border security is the only issue that is close to positive (50% approve, 50% disapprove).

Trump’s overall job approval is 36%, his lowest ever in a Fox News survey for either term. It had been holding steady at 39% since May. The decline is mainly driven by decreases among voters under age 45, those with annual household income below $50,000, non-White voters, and those without a college degree.

FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS

Approval stands at a low of 76% among Republicans. That’s down 3 points since last month, 12 points since September 2025, and 16 points since early in his second term (March 2025).

As in most midterms, voters are prone to punish the party in power: 7 in 10 say they will vote to send a message to Trump, with nearly twice as many expressing opposition (47%) as support (25%).

If the election were today, 54% of voters say they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district and 45% would support the Republican. That is outside the margin of error and is a wider lead than last month when Democrats were ahead by 51%-44%. The race narrows among those saying they are certain to vote, with the Democratic candidate ahead by 52%-46%.

The survey finds about the same number self-identify as Democrats (43%) and Republicans (41%), and both parties feel equally certain about voting (62% and 64% respectively), while more Democrats (61%) than Republicans (52%) say they are extremely interested in the election.

Party loyalty is solid: 98% of Democrats support their party’s candidate, and 94% of Republicans back theirs. Independents favor the Democrats by 26 points.

The Democratic candidate is the choice among Whites with a degree, those under age 45, women, union households and Hispanics. The Republican is ahead among Whites without a college degree (White men without a degree in particular), those 65 and over, voters who attend religious services regularly, military veterans and White evangelical Christians.

While 43% of Hispanic voters supported Trump in the 2024 election, just 31% prefer the Republican candidate this year.

"When the country is this closely divided in terms of partisanship, slight differences in defection and turnout rates can make all the difference," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Republicans have time to close these apparent gaps, but it’s getting late."

Meanwhile, Democrats lead on 10 out of 13 issue concerns.

The top five voter concerns are government corruption (60% extremely concerned), inflation (58%), gas prices (50%), government leadership (49%), and healthcare (48%). And double digits more trust the Democrats than the Republicans to handle each of those.

Republicans retain the advantage on crime (by 10 points) and border security (R+8), while views are closely divided on immigration (R+3). The Democrats are seen as better on healthcare (D+22), inflation (D+16), gas prices (D+12), voting rights (D+12), election integrity (D+12), government leadership (D+11), what’s taught in public schools (D+11), artificial intelligence (D+10), government corruption (D+10) and foreign policy (D+9).

Republicans have lost ground on key issues compared to four years ago, when more voters trusted them by 21 points on border security, 13 points on inflation and 9 points on foreign policy.

Other issues that voters are extremely concerned about are the Iran war (42%), immigration (35%), crime (34%), voter suppression (32%), AI technology (32%), what’s taught in public schools (29%), voter fraud (28%) and border security (25%).

While corruption in government and inflation are the top two worries about both parties, far more Democrats (72% and 70%) than Republicans (47% and 49%) are extremely concerned.

The issue that helps explain the Democrats’ advantage isn’t an issue at all. By a 14-point margin, more voters think the Democrats will do a better job "fighting for people like you." Majorities of White voters with a college degree (53%), men (52%), women (60%) and non-White voters (77%) think Democrats will fight for them. Whites without a college degree are split 49-49%.

Despite their issue advantage, just 35% say Democrats have a clear plan for dealing with the country’s problems, and 33% say the same about the Republicans. That reverses the Republican advantage from July 2025, when 43% said the Republicans had a clear plan compared with 33% for the Democrats.

There’s deep dissatisfaction with lawmakers: 15% approve of Congress, while 84% disapprove. Remarkably, that’s above the low of 9% approval in October 2013.

Both parties are viewed negatively. The Democratic Party is underwater by 16 points (42% favorable, 58% unfavorable), while ratings of the GOP are net negative by 23 points (38% favorable, 61% unfavorable).

Yet, favorable ratings fail to translate directly into vote choice. One third of those backing the Democratic candidate (31%) dislike the party, while 23% of those supporting the Republican dislike the GOP. Among the 26% who dislike both parties (double haters), Democrats lead 62%-36%.

Here’s how polarized the parties are: Just 16% of Republicans say that Democrats love America and want what’s best for the U.S., and even fewer Democrats, 6%, think Republicans do.

Compared to four years ago, the number of voters saying Democrats want what’s best for the country is up four points, while fewer say Republicans love the country now by 6 points.

Fifty-one percent of voters have a favorable view of capitalism compared with 32% for socialism. Compared to a year ago, positive ratings of capitalism are down 2 points while they are up 5 points for socialism. Eight in ten of those with a positive view of socialism support the Democratic candidate, while 6 in 10 of those viewing capitalism favorably back the Republican.

Voters who plan to cast their ballots early favor the Democratic candidate (by 19 points) as do mail voters (D+33), while the candidate choice splits among those voting in person (early or on Election Day).

Six in 10 oppose U.S. military action against Iran, and they back the Democrats by 56 points.

Drug development has long relied on animal models, but differences between species mean what works in animals doesn’t always translate to humans, and most drugs still fail during development. Intero Biosystems, a Denver-based startup, is developing human intestinal organoids, lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, as another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. Researchers and pharmaceutical companies are increasingly looking for models that better reflect human biology to supplement animal testing and reduce their reliance on it.

Intero, which spun out of the University of Michigan, says its organoids differ from simpler models that replicate only part of the gut. They contain multiple cell and tissue types found in the human intestine, which the company believes makes them a more human-relevant model for testing drugs and other compounds, co-founder and CTO Madeline Eiken told TechCrunch.

“Most drugs fail clinical trials, and I think it’s pretty easy to appreciate that we are neither mice nor flat layers of cells,” Eiken said.

The startup’s flagship product, GastroScreen, is a human intestinal organoid model that it sells to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds. Each organoid is about one millimeter across, and the company ships roughly 100 at a time in a tube, co-founder and CEO Charlie Childs said. Customers can use them as healthy intestinal models or induce disease-like conditions to test how the tissue responds to different compounds.

“We’re literally shipping mini living organs in the mail to people,” Childs said.

Beyond the organoids themselves, Intero sells the supplies needed to grow and work with them, such as the nutrient mixes that feed the cells and the chemicals used in experiments. It also runs studies for customers, including designing custom experiments, performing lab tests, and delivering the resulting data. Much of this work focuses on drug safety and disease research. For example, a customer can expose the organoids to a drug candidate to see whether it could harm the gut, or use organoids modeling a gut condition to see how the tissue responds to a compound.

Founded in 2024, the startup now has seven employees and just under 10 customers after raising a $2.3 million pre-seed round last year. It generated more than $400,000 in revenue from the fourth quarter of last year through the third quarter of this year, the CEO noted.

Regulatory changes have also helped drive interest in alternatives to animal testing. In April of last year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) laid out plans to reduce its reliance on animal testing in drug development, promoting alternatives including organoids, organs-on-chips (small devices that mimic organ functions) and AI-based computational models as potential alternatives.

In March of this year, the FDA issued draft guidance outlining how drug developers should validate new approach methodologies, or NAMs, a term of non-animal testing methods, when using them to support regulatory submissions. The guidance provides a framework for validation but doesn’t endorse any specific method. Whether a NAM can support a submission depends on factors including the method, how it is used, and the data provided.

Changes in U.S. law that allow drug developers to use non-animal testing methods in some cases have made pharmaceutical companies more willing to explore technologies such as organoids, Eiken told TechCrunch. Companies once hesitant about the technology are now looking to bring organoids in-house, she added.

Intero isn’t alone in trying to build more human-relevant models of the gut. Altis Biosystems develops stem cell-derived intestinal models, while InSphero offers patient-derived intestinal organoids for gastrointestinal toxicity testing. Other peers like MIMETAS take a different approach with organ-on-chip technology, using microfluidic systems to recreate aspects of the environment inside human tissues.

Intero says it sets itself apart from competitors in the complexity and scalability of its model. Unlike intestinal models grown from tissue collected through procedures such as colonoscopies, GastroScreen is derived from induced pluripotent stem cells, which are adult cells reprogrammed to become almost any cell type and can be generated from a blood sample, Eiken explained. That approach gives the startup the potential to personalize its models to different patients and scale production more easily, she added.

When asked what evidence shows GastroScreen can predict human drug responses more accurately than existing animal or cell-based models, Childs said the company is still building that evidence and is now in the second stage of a three-stage validation process. Having first shown that GastroScreen contains the key tissues of the human gut, Intero is now testing well-known drugs with documented effects in humans. GastroScreen has shown expected responses to drugs that reduce intestinal inflammation and to compounds known to damage the gut, Childs told TechCrunch. In the final stage, the company will compare GastroScreen’s results directly with pharmaceutical companies’ existing animal and clinical data. Those studies are underway with several pharmaceutical companies, using both existing compounds and new drug candidates, Childs said.

Intero doesn’t use AI to build its organoids. Instead, Childs sees an opportunity to use the organoids to generate the biological data AI models need, and the company plans to license such datasets to pharmaceutical and AI companies.

In the near term, Intero is focused on scaling production. It can currently make a few thousand organoids at a time and is working to automate manufacturing, with the goal of producing hundreds of thousands per batch, Childs said. Longer term, it wants to move into personalized medicine, using a patient’s cells to create organoids that could test different drugs before treatment. Its most ambitious goal is an artificial intestine, a vision that Childs said would build on the manufacturing scale and patient-specific data generated through its organoid technology.

While announcing that Norway would be hosting a Gaza aid meeting, President Donald Trump joked he thought he was getting the Nobel Peace Prize.

Alfred Nobel intended the peace prize for those who had done the most to advance peace among nations. Instead, it is increasingly handed out to the international activist class: people who say the right things, back the right causes and appeal to the political instincts of a handful of parliamentarians in a rarefied progressive bubble.

This year’s award to Navi Pillay is a case in point.

Pillay is best known for chairing the U.N. commission of inquiry that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza. Her selection will inevitably be read as an endorsement of a U.N. culture in which hostility to Israel is not a liability but a badge of moral seriousness.

NOBEL PEACE PRIZE AWARDED TO UN JURIST WHO ACCUSED ISRAEL OF COMMITTING GENOCIDE IN GAZA

Chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, South African Judge Navi Pillay speaks during a press conference in Geneva on September 16, 2025. The Inquiry Commission on Sept. 16, 2025 accused Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza in a bid to "destroy the Palestinians" there, and blamed Israel's prime minister and other top officials for incitement. (Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images)

But there is more to Pillay’s record than the commission’s fixation on Israel.

When Denmark’s embassy in Pakistan was bombed after Danish newspapers republished the Muhammad cartoons, former Foreign Minister Per Stig Møller reportedly said Pillay’s response was not to defend free speech, but to suggest censorship and restrictions on it.

Her reaction to Charlie Hebdo was much the same. Pillay reportedly called the magazine "doubly irresponsible" for publishing Muhammad cartoons. She is said to have described them as "malicious and deliberately provocative" and said she "fully understands why people wish to protest strongly." When Islamists answer speech with threats, violence and murder, Pillay’s first instinct seems to be to scold those who exercised their right to speak.

In 2022, she defended fellow U.N. commissioner Miloon Kothari after he referred to a "Jewish lobby" controlling social media and questioned whether Israel should even be a member of the United Nations. Kothari later apologized. An event in Pillay’s honor at Berlin City Hall was canceled after the mayor withdrew her support.

WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM

Anti-Israel protesters holding antisemitic posters in Alberta, Canada, on April 13, 2025. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via AP)

There are more reports of uncomfortable episodes. Pillay is said to have declined to attend the 2010 Nobel ceremony for the imprisoned Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo, citing a scheduling conflict in Geneva as Beijing pressured foreign governments to stay away. At Durban II the previous year, she remained seated while Mahmoud Ahmadinejad delivered an antisemitic tirade against Israel and Western delegations walked out. She condemned his speech later, but admitted that she had been "naive" about the Iranian president.

A review of Pillay’s first two years as U.N. human-rights chief found no public statements from her on abuses in dictatorships such as Cuba, North Korea, Eritrea, Saudi Arabia, Sudan or Belarus.

This is the person the Nobel Committee now presents as a model of human rights, freedom and peace.

The prize has a long history of such decisions.

AMBASSADOR JEFF BARTOS: UN MUST ABANDON ANTI-AMERICAN, ANTI-WESTERN LEGACY OF DURBAN CONFERENCE

Exterior views of the International Criminal Court on October 9, 2026, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Pierre Crom)

In 1994, Yasser Arafat was awarded the Peace Prize despite a political career built around hijackings, murder and the glorification of violence against civilians. In 1973, Henry Kissinger and North Vietnam’s Le Duc Tho received it for negotiating a Vietnam ceasefire that quickly fell apart. Tho refused the award because peace had plainly not been achieved.

In 2007, the prize went to Al Gore and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Climate change may be an important issue; it is not, however, what Nobel had in mind when he wrote of peace among nations.

Barack Obama received the award in 2009, less than nine months into his presidency and before any significant diplomatic achievement. Even Obama seemed embarrassed by how premature it was.

A view of the rostrum where the Nobel Committee's chairman, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, will announce the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize for 2025 in Oslo, Friday, Oct. 10, 2025. (Rodrigo Freitas/NTB Scanpix via AP)

The European Union won in 2012, not for a particular peace agreement or diplomatic breakthrough, but for a lofty view of Europe that appealed to the Oslo establishment.

None of this is an argument against human rights, international law or humanitarian work. It is an argument against pretending that every fashionable cause belongs under the heading of furthering world peace.

There is a difference between speaking the language of peace and doing the hard work of making it. The latter involves deterrence, diplomacy, compromise, alliances and often dealing with people one does not like. It is not always glamorous and rarely produces applause in international conference halls.

Consider the Abraham Accords. They normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states, creating embassies, direct flights, trade, investment and security cooperation. They replaced formal hostility with working relations between governments that had long treated one another as enemies.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Prime Minister of Israel Benjamin Netanyahu, U.S. President Donald Trump, Foreign Affairs Minister of Bahrain Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani and Foreign Affairs Minister of the United Arab Emirates Abdullah bin Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan wave from the Truman Balcony of the White House after the signing ceremony of the Abraham Accords on the South Lawn of the White House on September 15, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong)

Some may dislike Jared Kushner or the Trump administration. That is beside the point. Kushner did more to advance peace between states than many of the campaigners and organizations celebrated by the Nobel Committee in recent years.

Yet it is almost impossible to imagine the committee rewarding such an achievement. Association with Trump alone would make Kushner unacceptable to the small political circle that controls the prize.

Jared Kushner, son-in-law and advisor to President Donald Trump, arrives for a joint news conference between U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the State Dining Room at the White House on September 29, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That is the problem. The Nobel Peace Prize is decided by five people appointed by Norway’s parliament. They have the power to pronounce who represents the world’s highest moral ideals. Too often, they use it to reward people who share their own progressive assumptions.

The Stockholm-based Nobel Foundation cannot simply reclaim the prize. Nobel’s will assigns responsibility to a committee appointed by Norway’s Parliament. But the committee can be criticized, and it should no longer be treated with the automatic reverence it enjoys.

Alfred Nobel created an award for exceptional achievements that furthered world peace. The Norwegian committee has turned it into an annual seal of approval for causes it happens to favor.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A Peace Prize that cannot tell the difference no longer deserves the name — much less the respect it still receives.

Daniel Schatz is a political scientist, author and international affairs expert. He holds a Ph.D. in political science and is a former visiting scholar at Harvard, Stanford, Columbia and Georgetown universities.

ex-boyfriend-murders-girlfriend-suitcase:
By ELIOT FORCE, US NEWS REPORTER

Published:  08:35 AEDT, 14 October 2026   |  Updated:  08:47 AEDT, 14 October 2026

A New York man has admitted to murdering his ex-girlfriend, dismembering her body and keeping her severed head in a suitcase along with a flower.

Damon Foy, 50, strangled his ex-girlfriend Alberta Dale, 44, to death sometime between March 31 and April 1 in 2024 soon after she broke things off with him, according to court records reviewed by the Daily Mail.

He then chopped up her body in his home and disposed of everything but her head, which he kept as a kind of sick memento in his apartment in Kerhonkson, a town about 100 miles north of New York City.

Dale had an order of protection against Foy, and the couple had a history of domestic violence. Police began investigating Foy on April 1 after Dale's family reported her missing and requested a welfare check at his apartment.

Officers discovered Dale's severed head in a carry-on suitcase tucked away in Foy's closet on April 2 and arrested him.

He was soon indicted on charges including second-degree murder, aggravated criminal contempt, concealment of a human corpse, criminal contempt, criminal mischief, assault, strangulation and weapons possession.

Foy pleaded guilty to second-degree murder last week. Prosecutors dropped his other charges in exchange for the plea.

Under the agreement, Foy faces 23 years to life in prison, which is two years below the state's maximum sentencing guidelines of 25 to life for second-degree murder. Foy's sentencing hearing is scheduled for December 16.

Alberta Dale, 44, was strangled to death by her ex-boyfriend in 2024. He then chopped up her body and kept her severed head in a suitcase with a flower

Damon Foy, 50, admitted in court last week to murdering Dale. He is now facing 23 years to life in prison and will be sentenced in December

Dale's family reported her missing on April 1 after they had not heard from her for a while and were concerned for the woman's safety, as they were aware of the domestic violence she suffered and the order of protection she had against Foy.

Police conducted two welfare checks at Foy's apartment that day, but did not see Dale. They did note, however, that her car was parked in front of the home.

Foy told officers that Dale had left the home in an Uber or a Lyft a day earlier because she had no money for gas or to fix her car, which is why it was parked out front.

He said that Dale had been at the residence to pick up some of her belongings, but he was not there at the time or when she left because of the order of protection. He added that the last time the two had spoken was over the phone 24 hours earlier.

The next day, a local found a phone on the side of the street and turned it in to police. Detectives quickly determined that it had belonged to Dale.

Around that time, an assistant district attorney also told police that Dale had previously told a staff member at the Ulster County Crime Victims Assistance Program 'that if she went missing, it was because [Foy] killed her.'

Six armed officers returned to Foy's apartment on April 2 and searched the residence with his permission. He had been drinking before they arrived, and he continued to drink and become increasingly intoxicated during the search.

The officers reported a strong smell of bleach in the residence, an open bottle of bleach on the kitchen counter and a pail with a brand-new mop in the corner.

Police found Dale's dismembered remains in Foy's apartment at this complex in Kerhonkson, New York

In one of the two bedrooms on the second floor, the bathroom was 'immaculately clean,' officers observed. An open bag with rubber gloves was inside the master bedroom.

As police searched the residence, Foy told an officer: 'I'm at the point now where I gotta call a lawyer.' He also said: 'I loved this girl.'

Foy was standing in front of a closet, and an officer asked him to move so he could search it. Inside, there was a suitcase that was 'quite heavy for the size of the bag,' police noted.

When a deputy shined a flashlight on the suitcase, he saw what appeared to be dried blood on it. When asked what it was, Foy got defensive, held up his hands and said: 'See, no defensive wounds.'

A detective asked Foy if Dale was in the suitcase, to which he replied: 'Are you out of your mind?'

The officers then remained in the residence while waiting for a warrant to search the suitcase. During the wait, Foy whispered to one of the detectives: 'I killed her. She's in there, I killed her.'

Once police received the warrant and opened the suitcase, they found Dale's severed head, but the rest of her remains were missing. A flower was also inside.

When a detective interviewed Foy in custody the next day, he asked why Foy had placed the flower in the bag.

The murderer said, 'I loved that girl' and that he was trying to figure out 'what still happened last night to take s*** over the top.'

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk as President Donald Trump speaks after a White House meeting on AI, September 29, 2026.Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty

The world’s richest man has a vision of the universe’s future with little role for humanity—and is rushing ahead to have his AI company build it.

Elon Musk said in an X post on Sunday that a huge semiconductor factory planned by Tesla and SpaceX in Texas will have an output of at least $1 trillion—rivaling the GDP of some of the world’s larger economies.

Musk has made similarly grandiose projections that are, depending on one’s interpretation, somewhere between ambitious and absurd. He has a long track record of overpromising. In recent SEC litigation, in fact, Tesla’s legal team resorted to arguing that his exaggerations are “corporate puffery.”

The Terafab project, which recently broke ground 70 miles northwest of Houston, is planned to build chips for Tesla cars and humanoid robots, and for the newly-merged SpaceX and xAI. Currently, the design of advanced AI chips is dominated by Nvidia, and their fabrication by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC).

Musk’s famously erratic statements should be taken with a heaping of salt. But his companies do build more electric vehicles than any domestic competitors, and are responsible for the majority of launches into orbit in recent years. So it’s worth wondering: what vision of the future does Musk want his Texas chip plant to help build?

“We aspire to be a galactic civilization,” Terafab’s site says, and “harness all the energy in a galaxy.” But Musk’s recent statements raise a question about who, exactly, the “we” is—including a post he made last week that “Propagating super intelligence to the stars is a great success condition for a biological bootloader.”

A rough translation of what he seems to mean: humanity would fulfill its cosmic purpose by building AI—under Musk’s leadership—that tramples us all on its way to colonizing the universe.

Musk once professed to oppose such ideas, including when he helped found OpenAI with the stated mission to “advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole.” But AI successionism—the belief that humans are merely a stepping-stone in cosmic evolution on the way to a “worthy successor”—is a growing movement, now with more support from a man with unimaginable wealth and power. xAI did not immediately respond to a query on whether AI successionism represents company policy.

For now, the coming of a machine-god that devours its creators and colonizes the stars is still just a prophecy, feared by some and much anticipated by others. That vision of humanity would probably have served as little consolation to the 780,000 real, breathing people estimated to have died in the first year of DOGE’s cuts to foreign aid.

The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump, even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.
