“No one is above the law.”

That’s what House Democrat Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said after the Biden Justice Department indicted Donald Trump nearly a year after an unprecedented raid on his Mar-a-Lago estate. But now that one of their own has found herself the subject of a federal search, Jeffries and his party are singing a different tune.

The search at issue happened early Monday morning at the Washington, D.C., residence of Rep. Ilham Omar, D-Minn. According to sources who spoke with Fox News, federal Homeland Security Investigations agents executed the judicially authorized search as part of a “criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.”

Omar has faced notable allegations of corruption through the years, some of which rest on “extensive evidence suggesting that the Muslim representative legally married her flamboyant brother before a Christian minister,” as Federalist Senior Contributor Ben Weingarten reported.

Omar predictably cast Monday’s search on her estate as “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement” — a talking point quickly adopted by Jeffries and fellow Democrats. But such rhetoric is a significant departure from Democrats’ gleeful response to the Biden FBI’s 2022 raid on Mar-a-Lago, which came as part of Jack Smith‘s illegal classified documents lawfare against Trump.

Presidential wannabe and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., released a video message on Monday decrying the search of Omar’s home as a “targeting” of Trump’s “political opponents.” He also seemingly suggested that the move was based on the fact that Omar is Muslim.

That response is a complete 180-degree turn from the one Khanna gave following the FBI’s Mar-a-Lago infiltration. Appearing on MSNBC, the California congressman defended the Biden administration’s actions as “non-political” and claimed that the FBI had “some probable evidence about possible wrongdoing” since it got a judge to sign off on the search warrant.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., characterized the search of Omar’s residence as “a disgusting abuse of power” and “a dangerous sign of an authoritarian president who will stop at nothing to distract you from his deep unpopularity with the American people.” When it came to the raid on Mar-a-Lago, however, Jayapal applauded the Biden administration and said that Trump “should be in jail.”

Former Rep. Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y., similarly came rushing to Omar’s defense by claiming that the search of her home is designed to satisfy Trump’s base, whom he called “blood-thirsty” and “racist.” Yet, when pressed by CNN after the Mar-a-Lago raid about whether Congress should investigate Trump over the classified documents issue, the ex-Squad member defended the raid and fervently agreed by saying, “Oh, absolutely. Trump should be investigated for many things.”

Omar’s Islamist sister-from-a-different-mister and fellow Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., also threw her “Trump is grossly abusing his power” hot-take out on social media. The America-hating congresswoman notably defended the Biden DOJ’s raid on Trump’s home with Democrats’ played out “No one is above the law” schtick.

Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., is another Democrat now criticizing the feds’ Omar search after previously trotting out the Trump is “not above the law” talking point to run interference for the FBI’s Mar-a-Lago raid.

kyiv_air_raid_alerts_relentless_russian_:
Kyiv residents have lived under Russian drone and missile attacks since the start of the war, but this summer the attacks became a daily occurrence. Since late August, Russian forces have been attacking the city day and night, and air raid alerts constantly disrupt residents’ plans. Dozens of civilians have been killed in the capital over these months, and hundreds have been injured. As winter approaches, residents are preparing for power outages and heating problems. Meduza spoke with Ukrainian journalist Denys Trubetskyi, who writes for Die Zeit and other European outlets, about how doctors, business owners, and other Kyiv residents live and work under relentless attacks, and whether the coming winter could be much harder than previous ones.

— You were born in Sevastopol, but now you live in Kyiv and cover Ukraine for German-language outlets. When did you move?

— My career in German media came about pretty much by chance. I’ve never lived permanently in Germany or another German-speaking country, but at some point I started learning the language because I was interested in German sports and politics.

I got into journalism 14 or 15 years ago as a sportswriter, working for fairly big Ukrainian outlets like Football.ua. In 2012, Ukraine and Poland hosted the European soccer championship, and I met German colleagues while covering the German national team’s matches.

Then Ukraine entered a very interesting period politically: Maidan, the annexation of Crimea, which affected me directly because of where I’m from, and so on. I’d always thought about moving to Kyiv, and I’ve lived here since 2015. That’s also when I started working as a political correspondent for major German outlets — Die Zeit and Table.Media — as well as Swiss and Austrian publications.

— In late August, Russia began attacking Kyiv and the Kyiv region almost nonstop — at night and during the day. How is the city coping?

— To understand that, you have to look at Russia’s whole strategy of total war against Ukraine. I should explain why I call it total war. You can debate whether Russia is using all its resources for mobilization. When it comes to the war economy, it isn’t using all its resources yet.

But in the air war, Russia has been using every resource available since the fall of 2022. It’s sending pretty much everything it produces at Ukraine, including Kyiv. The jet-powered drones that have been pounding Kyiv since August are so new that some were built just two weeks ago. They sometimes stockpile ballistic missiles, but overall, attacks on the current scale wouldn’t be possible without using missiles fresh off the production line.

On September 11, 2022, Russia launched the first wave of attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The strategy was meant to put as much pressure as possible on civilians. Since then, Russia has tried all kinds of ways to pressure Ukrainians — trying to knock out the country’s energy system, for example. But it’s come to realize that plunging half the country into a total blackout for a couple of weeks is very difficult.

So since last winter, Russia has focused on Kyiv. It’s the number one target for attacks behind the front lines. Kyiv and its metropolitan area account for roughly 15% of the population currently living in Ukrainian-controlled territory.

Last winter was the harshest in 20 years. Temperatures sometimes dropped to minus 25 degrees Celsius (minus 13 degrees Fahrenheit). Entire districts of Kyiv, especially on the left bank of the Dnipro, went weeks without electricity or heating. But this summer also turned out to be the hardest in the city’s history.

— What made it so hard?

— Two things coincided. First, [in winter] the genius U.S. president launched his “very successful” Operation Epic Fury, which caused a major weapons shortage. That had a serious impact on air defense. The PAC-3 MSE missile used in Patriot systems is the most effective against ballistic weapons. In July, Ukraine was receiving small batches of 15 to 20 missiles. We don’t know how things stand now, but those July figures are unlikely to have changed much.

Second, Russia increased production of its ballistic missiles. It used to produce up to about 60 standard ballistic missiles a month; now it’s up to 75. There are also missiles that follow a quasi-ballistic trajectory, like the Zircon. Roughly speaking, we’re talking about production of around 80 to 100 ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles a month.

Ukraine has almost nothing to shoot them down with. And several Patriot systems are stationed in Kyiv — that’s an open secret. Obviously, once shortages developed here [in air defense], Russia started firing at Kyiv, because a new opportunity had opened up for its military.

Then there’s the situation with jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5. Ukraine had more or less been mentally prepared for attacks like these since the beginning of the year. Technically, there are ways to shoot them down, but it’s extremely difficult to find a solution that can be used on a large scale against drones flying at up to 650 kilometers per hour (about 400 miles per hour). And to make sure that solution doesn’t cost one and a half to two times as much as the Gerans themselves.

— How has this crisis affected everyday life in Kyiv?

— From May through the end of summer, ballistic missile strikes happened every third night on average. That’s really hard on your mental health and your day-to-day life.

Quite often, the strikes came before an air raid alert was even issued. But ballistic missiles fly so fast that many people barely have time to get down to a shelter, even after hearing the alert: A missile can hit one or two minutes after the alert. And if you’re outside at that moment, say, on your way to a shelter, that can be more dangerous than staying in the hallway.

You go to bed and you don’t know which night it’ll happen. In practice, a strike can come at any moment. When it happens every day, it’s hard to describe it without swearing.

— After the attacks intensified, The Guardian and The Washington Post described Kyiv as a frontline city. Do you agree?

— Things are different here. Kyiv is still a city behind the front lines, even if it’s the “number one target” behind them. FPV drones, artillery shells, and so on don’t reach us here. I wouldn’t use that particular term [“a frontline city”], although I understand it from a journalist’s perspective, and the situation [in Kyiv] is very difficult.

The problem with the endless launches of jet-powered drones is that it’s basically one endless attack that’s been going on since August. Without exaggeration, several people are killed and dozens are wounded every day. Of course, the chance of you personally getting hit is still small. But it’s increased considerably. There was a time when your risk of dying in a car crash in Kyiv was much higher than in an air attack. Now it’s the other way around.

I’m noticing that a lot of people around me are at their limit. They’re thinking about the coming winter. People who have the option of leaving for the winter are looking into whether they can afford it. I can’t do that: You can’t work as a Kyiv correspondent without being in Kyiv.

My friends were looking at apartments in Ivano-Frankivsk and Chernivtsi. Prices have naturally gone through the roof. You can describe Ukraine’s economic situation in one sentence: People have become much poorer. And we can say with certainty that food, internet, phone service, and so on will inevitably get much more expensive. Finding the money for an incredibly expensive apartment somewhere in western Ukraine is very difficult.

The economic side of this is very important right now. Many employers are suffering from the attacks — almost every industry has been affected. People’s wages are being cut while everything is getting more expensive. It leaves people feeling paralyzed.

Some people cope better than others in stressful situations like these. Among the people I know, the number taking sedatives or seeing a psychologist or psychiatrist has multiplied several times over.

— If you walk around Kyiv on a weekday now, what’s changed since the summer? What’s the first thing you notice?

— There’s a lot more destruction. Kyiv has 1,200 high-rise buildings, and I think about a third of them have been damaged over these four and a half years. Not always anything hugely dramatic, but at least a window blown out here or there.

There are fewer people in the city, though you might not notice it. The thing about Kyiv is that as some people leave, new people arrive — from Sumy or other cities [near the front lines].

There aren’t any official figures yet, but I’ve noticed it’s easier to park and fewer people are going to cafés and restaurants. You see fewer people on the streets, too, though that may be because so many are being switched to remote work.

And another thing you notice is that people are much more on edge.

— More and more people are working remotely?

— Yes, wherever that’s possible. Universities have been switching to remote learning on a fairly large scale. Schools haven’t been able to resume regular in-person teaching since September 1 — that’s very difficult with so many hours of air raid alerts every day.

— Which parts of the city are suffering the most from the attacks?

— Right now, all districts are suffering about equally. For example, Russia has recently been specifically targeting Kyiv’s gas stations. Literally any gas station could become a target, and you could happen to be nearby — stuck in traffic, for instance. Jet-powered drones can reach Kyiv from Russia’s Bryansk region in half an hour, depending on the model, and can fly around the entire city in three or four minutes. In that situation, there’s nothing you can do.

Russia has also been attacking Ukrainian data centers recently. Take the strike on the National Academy of Sciences [on September 28]: One of the offices of Ukrtelecom, a Ukrainian internet provider, is in the building next door. That same day, there was a strike on another Ukrtelecom office, which shares a building with the private clinic Dobrobut. Another strike [on September 25] hit a data center in Shuliavka, in an office building. There were terrible scenes there, too — bodies were literally lying in the street.

Russia isn’t holding back — I’m saying that without exaggeration. It’s not necessarily setting out to strike civilian facilities in these particular cases, but this is no longer collateral damage. It’s part of the military strategy. Russia can strike a gas station or a large office complex during the workday. It apparently intends to stick with this tactic. And with everything flying so fast, you don’t even have time to do anything.

— You’ve already said that internet and communications services in general could soon get more expensive in Ukraine. Are people already feeling the effects of attacks on data centers? Has internet service in Kyiv gotten worse?

— There are local disruptions, yes. At one point, roughly 100,000 subscribers in Kyiv and the Kyiv region lost internet access. But I still find it hard to understand exactly what this campaign is meant to achieve. The military’s internet infrastructure isn’t entirely independent of these data centers, but they [the Ukrainian armed forces] have their own infrastructure and networks, plus Starlink. These attacks seem more aimed at the civilian economy. Ukraine relies heavily on digital services.

How effective are they really? You might find yourself unable to pay for something by card, but there won’t be a total catastrophe. Ukraine may have one of the most decentralized networks of internet providers in Europe, or even the world — there are about a thousand operators in the country. Of course, there are big companies, but overall it’s a very extensive network.

— Are businesses managing to adapt to round-the-clock attacks and the changed conditions?

— It varies a lot. I’ve spoken with people running many large restaurants and food-service chains. They all have different views of the future, but they agree that restaurants in shopping malls won’t survive this winter: It’s dangerous to have employees come to work there during an air raid alert, even a yellow-level one.

There are reasons to believe Russia will strike shopping malls. So not only restaurants but probably all retail businesses in those malls will close down. And shopping malls are an important part of Ukraine’s economy. Kyiv has Respublika and Blockbuster Mall — they’re among the largest shopping malls in Ukraine and [Eastern] Europe.

Business owners — whether they sell clothing, run restaurants, or do something else — are trying to find solutions. But nobody can predict with complete certainty what things will look like in winter, so everyone’s improvising.

More generally, businesses are trying to adapt: A red alert means we don’t work; a yellow alert means we try to work somehow, because otherwise you could go crazy.

— Can a red alert last for hours?

— No, actually. That’s more likely with yellow alerts. This is a deliberate Russian tactic: launching small groups of jet-powered drones one after another. One arrives, gets shot down, then another is launched. It’s all done either to keep a yellow alert going almost indefinitely or to have another yellow alert issued 20 minutes later.

A red alert means either a truly massive drone attack or a specific missile threat.

— How much have Kyiv residents’ daily routines changed since attacks started happening during working hours?

— There is no routine — everyone’s improvising. Meetings are constantly being rescheduled and canceled, but businesses somehow manage to keep working. I’m amazed myself at how the cafés on my street manage to open on time. If you want to get a coffee at a café that opens at 8 a.m., somehow you can.

We’ve been through all sorts of things in four and a half years. But never this level of anxiety. Now it’s constant. People see it all happening. Very often, jet-powered Gerans fly right overhead. This will sound surprising, but that’s a good thing, because it means you won’t be directly hit. Most likely.

I’ve seen a lot over these years, but when this superfast thing that sounds like a quiet jet aircraft races over your head, it really gets to you.

— How has life changed for families with children?

— Everything’s become harder for them, because the children are effectively learning remotely all the time. Officially, it’s hybrid or in person, but the reality this school year is distance learning.

And this is another area where the internet situation matters. Because if attacks on energy infrastructure intensify, cell service and internet access could go down.

But the city has been through that before.

— The daily attacks must also have affected hospitals. How are they operating now?

— As a rule, surgery doesn’t stop during an alert — it all depends on the specific situation. During a red alert, hospitals try to move anyone they can to a shelter. During a yellow alert, they’re more likely to keep patients where they are, and 80% of Kyiv’s air raid alerts are yellow. Nobody moves intensive care patients anywhere. Ambulances and intensive care units keep working all the time.

As for strikes on hospitals, I wouldn’t say hospitals are being deliberately targeted at this point. But honestly, with the current strategy of terror — let’s call it that — we can’t rule out Russia moving on to that. Take the strike on the private clinic Dobrobut: The clinic wasn’t the specific target. Though perhaps Russia didn’t mind it getting hit, either.

There could be serious problems with medicines in the future. Some medications could be in short supply: There have been strikes on a facility in Kyiv belonging to Darnytsia, a major pharmaceutical company. This is primarily part of the economic war, but attacks like these show that Russia doesn’t care much about civilian lives. I don’t think that needs explaining anymore in 2026.

There’s also collateral damage. When warehouses are attacked, absolutely everyone gets hit — book publishers, manufacturers of all kinds of things. Quite a few warehouses storing medicines have also been destroyed. That doesn’t mean there’ll be a catastrophe, but shortages of certain medicines could develop.

— You mentioned that Russia is heavily attacking warehouses in Ukraine. In late August, Agriculture and Food Minister Taras Vysotskyi said that about 90% of the country’s grocery-chain warehouses had been destroyed. Can you see that in the selection of products in stores?

— Yes, it’s changing. That’s especially true of perishables, because there are virtually no refrigerated warehouses left in the Kyiv region [because of Russian attacks].

I can’t say we’re facing an across-the-board shortage of fish, meat, or milk. But the selection has shrunk, and exactly what’s missing from stores depends directly on what was damaged two, three, or four days earlier. For example, right now you can barely find cola in Kyiv supermarkets, because the Coca-Cola plant in Brovary was hit very recently.

I don’t think there’s a risk of famine. Ukraine’s agricultural sector has enormous capacity, despite all the problems of 2022. But shortages and major price increases are almost inevitable. We can’t yet tell how severe they’ll be. But you’ll certainly be able to get through the winter eating, say, buckwheat.

There’s an effort now to reorganize logistics so that more goods go straight from suppliers to supermarkets. But the vehicle fleets that retail chains and suppliers needed and maintained in the 2000s no longer exist.

There’s still the option of importing food from the EU. We saw a similar situation in 2022 with gasoline and food. Back then, Russia was destroying Ukraine’s few oil refineries, and now Ukraine depends almost entirely on gasoline from Europe.

— In August, Ukrainian media reported that air raid alerts were bringing Kyiv’s transportation system to a standstill. The metro had effectively stopped carrying passengers, and buses and trolleybuses were overcrowded. Kyiv residents were flagging down cars in the street and asking drivers to give them a ride to the other bank. How is public transportation working now?

— That was actually one of the reasons for dividing alerts into yellow and red levels. All city-run surface transportation keeps operating during yellow alerts. That’s dangerous, of course, but otherwise the city simply can’t function.

Previously, though, large numbers of passengers on buses and trolleybuses would be made to get off at the nearest stop. If you can’t get to a shelter, that’s hardly safe, either.

The metro is a little different. Kyiv has three lines, two of which connect the left and right banks. During yellow alerts, one of those stops running, and the other becomes severely overcrowded.

— Has planning a route become harder?

— I’d strongly recommend avoiding trips from one bank to the other whenever possible. Especially from the left bank to the right. The city center is on the right bank, so large numbers of people travel there for work in the morning and return in the evening.

That’s another reason so many people are being switched to remote work. There’s the general safety concern, but also a very specific everyday problem: With constant traffic jams, people can easily be an hour late. There’s no point sitting in traffic.

— Since the beginning of October, the Russian military has struck bridges over the Dnipro several times, particularly the Northern and Southern bridges. What consequences could those attacks have for the city?

— Completely destroying bridges over the Dnipro is virtually impossible — we can see that from many other bridges in Ukraine. Despite continuing attacks and damage, the bridge over the Dniester estuary in Zatoka [in the Odesa region], the bridge over the Dnipro in Zaporizhzhia, and the Antonivskyi Bridge in Kherson are all still standing. Ukrainian forces struck the Antonivskyi Bridge during their counteroffensive in the fall of 2022, when Kherson was still occupied.

We’re talking about strategically important bridges, not small structures somewhere on the Siverskyi Donets, which really can be destroyed.

Still, if intensive attacks on Kyiv’s bridges continue, serious logistical problems will naturally develop. According to Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry, roughly 600,000 vehicles cross Kyiv’s main bridges every day.

The city is now considering setting up pontoon crossings and ferries, but as I understand it, the infrastructure needed for that isn’t ready yet. And it would be hard to replace the Southern Bridge fully that way, for example. It’s particularly important for transportation and logistics: A significant share of freight passing through the capital crosses it, and it also carries a metro line.

— You regularly see headlines about air raid alerts lasting for hours. According to Ukrainska Pravda, Kyiv had one of its longest air raid alerts on September 28: It lasted more than nine hours. How does the city change during an air attack?

— It depends. If you walk around Kyiv during an ordinary attack, when there aren’t explosions right around you — whether you’re downtown or elsewhere — the city won’t look much different from normal. Life doesn’t stop. It’s an ordinary workday: People go about their business, drink coffee, and go places.

When there’s a confirmed threat of ballistic missile strikes, things are a little different. You can see people trying either to take cover with two walls between them and the outside or to get to a shelter. Again, it varies from person to person and depends on where you are.

What has really changed is that quite a few people, including people I know, are choosing to spend every night in a shelter — in the metro or an underground parking garage, for example. For many, that’s hard mentally, but a friend of mine, for instance, says she’s learned to fall asleep without worrying about what might happen.

Signs of a massive combined strike — an attack involving cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, and drones — usually appear several hours [before the strike itself]. You can tell whether an attack is coming from the movements of strategic bombers inside Russia.

At times like that, Kyiv’s metro is packed. The record for the number of people spending the night in the metro has been broken many times. The current record is 56,000. Realistically, that’s the maximum the metro can accommodate. Experts give higher figures, but after this summer’s combined attacks, you get the impression those are only possible on paper.

— Does Kyiv have enough shelters? Are they equipped for attacks lasting hours?

— The situation is pretty bad. Kyiv has about 4,500 shelters. It’s hard to say whether that’s a lot or a little. Not all of them are in good condition, and, let’s put it this way, not all of them are actually accessible.

During a jet-powered drone attack, conventional shelters — the metro, basements in schools and government buildings, and so on — aren’t all that helpful. They’re important, but Kyiv has almost none of what you see in Kharkiv and Odesa, for example. There, you can see portable concrete shelters on the streets that provide decent protection from drones.

Why are there almost none in Kyiv? That’s partly down to domestic politics. I don’t want to get too deep into it, but President Zelensky and Mayor Klitschko have been at odds for a long time. Different authorities block each other’s decisions to some extent.

I don’t want to take anyone’s side. But why almost nothing has been done about portable shelters in four years remains an open question. Kyiv’s mayor bears a great deal of responsibility here.

— What’s happening in Kyiv’s shelters during these hours-long alerts?

— Sometimes in the evenings, people try to get [into the stations] before the metro closes so they can lay out their mattresses and other things. Sometimes there’s a fight for spots.

Apart from these rather comical situations, I don’t think the atmosphere is that bad. It probably doesn’t compare anymore with the start of the war, when people held impromptu concerts in the stations. But even though everyone’s on edge, you can still feel people supporting each other. They share coffee and sandwiches, get to know each other, and so on.

Several times, I’ve gone down into the metro specifically as a journalist, to see how it all works and how people behave. And you really can still see some of that unity.

— In September, the Kyiv Post reported that Kyiv residents were increasingly ignoring air raid warnings. What do you think about that?

— You have to understand that it’s impossible to respond to every air raid alert for four and a half years. At some point, you could just go crazy. During yellow alerts, you could theoretically spend 18 hours in a shelter, but, as you can imagine, almost nobody does that.

But at night, when the chance of a ballistic missile strike is fairly high, people do go to shelters. I’d say that since May 2026, there’s actually been a noticeable increase in the number of Kyiv residents who don’t ignore air raid alerts.

— You’ve already mentioned attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Last year, some districts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks at a time, and temperatures often dropped below minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit). What’s the outlook for this winter?

— It’s obvious there’ll be problems with energy supplies. Russia is trying to cut Kyiv off from the country’s power grid by striking both thermal power plants and power lines. Frequent repeat attacks make it harder to repair the damage. Kyiv could end up spending a week or two either with no electricity at all or with power for just a few hours a day. Hospitals, public and private, have long been ready for this. They largely prepared during the first winter of the war: They have generators and fuel reserves, so things are more or less okay on that front.

Air defense is also in worse shape now, for the reasons I mentioned at the beginning. But the weather is expected to be better this winter. Electricity consumption has also fallen. I think this winter will be more or less like the last one. It won’t be good, but I’m not expecting an outright apocalypse.

There could be problems with the sewer system — that’s very dangerous, and you can’t really prepare for it. If that happens, it’ll be a new experience for Kyiv residents.

— Last year, 600,000 people left Kyiv because of power and heating outages. Should we expect a similar mass exodus this winter?

— First, I want to point out that Klitschko’s figure of 600,000 was pulled out of thin air. People did leave, but there wasn’t a noticeable exodus. This winter will probably be different, since a whole range of factors will come into play.

Obviously, for people who have relatives [in other cities] or a house in some village where they can at least heat with firewood, that’s an option. But many people’s ability to travel is limited — primarily, I’m talking about military mobilization. There are checkpoints outside Kyiv, and if your paperwork isn’t all in order, you won’t get very far by car. So some people effectively won’t be able to leave Kyiv. And their girlfriends, wives, and children often stay with them.

And as I’ve already said, prices have risen so much that many people can’t afford to rent an apartment somewhere in western Ukraine.

— Can those who stay in the city prepare for winter?

— There’s nothing new here. Obviously, you can’t put a gasoline generator on the balcony of an apartment building, because your whole apartment could burn down. But people generally already have their power banks, EcoFlow portable power stations, and all that equipment ready.

I’m not saying everyone does, because there are people who don’t put much effort into it and just take things as they come. But people who wanted to prepare for winter have mostly been ready for a long time.

The Department of Justice is seeking to indict former Trump White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson for “lying” to Congress about the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, according to new reporting. The news comes years after The Federalist exclusively exposed Hutchinson for her contradictory claims on the subject.

Punchbowl News’ Laura Weiss reported on Thursday claims from unnamed sources that the DOJ Civil Rights Division “brought evidence to a federal grand jury on Tuesday and is expected to present more evidence and additional witnesses later this month” in its pursuit of the sought-after indictment. The sources also reportedly told Weiss that Hutchinson “has not been subpoenaed to appear before the grand jury” at this time.

In her June 2022 congressional testimony, Hutchinson made a series of grandiose claims about President Trump and her former White House colleagues regarding their conduct during the Jan. 6 riot. Among the many salacious allegations was her claim — based on “third-party conversations” — that the president “tried to violently hijack the presidential limousine to drive himself down to the rioters on Jan. 6,” as The Federalist summarized.

“As an American, I was disgusted. It was unpatriotic,” Hutchinson told Congress of the Jan. 6 events. “We were watching the Capitol building get defaced over a lie, and it was something that was really hard in that moment to digest.”

Hutchinson’s incredibly suspect testimony was quickly shot down by key figures privy to the events of that day. That includes the driver of the president’s limousine, who testified under oath that Trump never did what Hutchinson alleged.

Other witnesses and former White House officials aren’t the only ones who have disputed Hutchinson’s far-fetched claims, however. Communications from Hutchinson herself show the former Mark Meadows aide completely undermining the sob story she told Congress.

Federalist Editor-in-Chief Mollie Hemingway and Tristan Justice exclusively reported in these pages on roughly 18 months’ worth of private chats “between friends from the [first] Trump White House” showing how Hutchinson “dramatically changed her story about what she knew and how she felt about what she witnessed as a White House staffer.”

The communications documented Hutchinson discussing “with other targets of the [J6 House Committee] probe about how little information she had about any wrongdoing that day, and lamented how corrupt the politicized committee was.” “Far from being upset with Trump,” Hemingway and Justice wrote, “Hutchinson repeatedly spoke in favor of [Trump] and his presidency.”

[READ: House Republicans Expose J6 Committee’s Lies, Cover-Ups, Scandals In New Report]

In one text message sent three months after the Jan. 6 riot, for example, Hutchinson said that she’d “rather shoot myself dead into the Potomac than see marine one flying around this city without 45 again.” Other communications showed Hutchinson telling a former colleague after she was subpoenaed by the J6 Committee that she had nothing to offer the “phony” committee.

Additional text messages revealed Hutchinson trashing committee members like then-Rep. Liz Cheney, R-Wy., whom Hutchinson would later go on to embrace as part of her J6 flip-flop.

Hutchinson also attempted to target Hemingway in her web of falsehoods. The former aide dishonestly contended that The Federalist editor-in-chief illegally obtained classified materials from Meadows, a claim which Hemingway denounced as “false” and Congress found to be “entirely uncorroborated.”

The Department of Justice did not respond to The Federalist’s request for comment.

staten-islander-arrested-booting-car:

A Staten Island man was arrested after he took the law into his own hands and placed a wheel-locking parking boot on a car parked illegally outside his home.

Aaron Hardy, 52, of Stapelton, had grown tired of drivers parking in front of his driveway, which he said would often include sex workers and johns, and installed a “No Parking” sign on his fence.

“When I first moved down here, they used to come down there and prostitute. They used to come down there and do all types of stuff. They had drugs, and all that other stuff,” Hardy told The Post.

“They see a dead-end street and they’ll come down there and they’ll prostitute. I get up every morning and see condoms all over the place.”

When he spotted a Jeep Grand Compass ignoring the sign earlier this month, the vexed man turned vigilante — applying a boot to the vehicle and leaving a handwritten note on the windshield on the morning of Oct. 2, the NYPD said.

“I seen you looked at the do not park sign and still park there $25 to take the boot off,” the note read, according to Gothamist, which first reported the story.

He claimed he initially got the idea from a cop, after numerous complaints to police and 311 failed to deter the allegedly sex-crazed scofflaws.

“An officer told me like this: ‘you didn’t hear it from me,’ but I’m going to give you a suggestion – you can go on Amazon and get yourself a boot.’ I got this idea from an officer,” Hardy said.

Although usually deployed by parking enforcement agents, wheel-locking boots can be purchased by anyone and are widely available online for about $50.

The cul-de-sac crusader also alleged that he was only targeted by police because the driver of the Jeep was dating another cop.

“I never had no problem until we had a shiesty police officer get involved,” Hardy said.

“He didn’t like the fact that I put a boot on his girlfriend’s car. That’s what this is about.”

Hardy, who told The Post he operates a car wash business from his home, pleaded not guilty to coercion, tampering, larceny and weapons charges and was released without bail ahead of a December court date.

The weapons charges were handed out when he booked at the 120th precinct house, where officers found Hardy was allegedly in possession of a stun gun, according to police.

Hardy defended his actions in a phone interview Sunday afternoon.

“If I park my car in my little driveway, if anybody park in front of my house I can’t get my car out without hitting their car. That’s why I put up signs,” he explained.

Connecticut-based pizza expert Colin Caplan examines the influence of Italy's celebrated 50 Top rankings and reveals why cultural preferences and distinct regional traditions make choosing a universal winner difficult.

The 50 Top Pizza rankings of 2026 highlight restaurants from coast to coast, though what makes a pie worthy of the top spot is still a matter of taste.

New Haven, Connecticut-based food historian and pizza expert Colin Caplan told Fox News Digital that what constitutes the "best" pizza really comes down to personal preference.

Ranked lists such as those published by 50 Top Pizza are helpful for expanding palates and introducing people to restaurants and dishes to try, he noted, but there's usually some subjectivity at play.

"50 Top Pizza is a very well-respected Italian-based, chef-based site that really goes and finds what they think is the best," he said, but suggested the organization might have a slight bias toward certain pizza styles that align with its Italian roots, such as Neapolitan.

“I looked at my informed mail, and it was supposed to have my great-grandchildren’s ballot,” Brown said. “It was mailed. It should’ve been in my mailbox that day.”

Brown only learned about the theft through a neighborhood app, leaving her unsure whether the ballots had been snatched along with the other mail.

“I was panicked because they weren’t going to be able to vote,” Brown said.

Former staffers say he drove them to tears. Colleagues say he’s a bully. The Bradford campaign says his passion is just what this city needs.

The first person to stand up and speak at Brad Bradford’s July 15 crime and safety townhall said he wanted to buy a gun.

The declaration didn’t seem to perturb the audience of roughly 40 people gathered in the small, brightly lit hall at Glenview Presbyterian Church in North Toronto. Mayoral hopeful Brad Bradford was seated, listening, at the front of the room, his features arranged into a look of grim concern. It had been just four days since a shooting at a street festival on St. Clair Avenue West had killed two and injured five others, and the forum was supposed to be an opportunity for residents to air their concerns about violence in Toronto. Held in one of the city’s wealthy garden suburbs, Lawrence Park South, the conversation was dominated primarily by fears about property theft and break-ins. Hence, the gun. Fears of a home invasion had driven both of the speaker’s grown children to get their gun licenses, he told the room. “I’m going to get my gun license,” he said, his voice steely. “It’s time to be proactive. We can’t be reactive. We can’t just wait.”

His anger was not out of place at the townhall. It did not matter, in this room—the first public event after Bradford’s campaign launch—that break-ins in the city had in fact plummeted during the pandemic and have never returned to their pre-2020 levels. Nor did it matter that, after rising briefly between 2022 and 2023, they’ve gone down during Olivia Chow’s time as mayor. What mattered to Bradford was how you felt. When Toronto’s deputy chief of police said after the St. Clair shooting that Toronto remained one of the safest cities in the world (gun deaths and injuries have trended steadily downward since 2019), Bradford seized the opportunity to criticize the city’s leadership. “People don’t experience life in a spreadsheet,” he repeated, first in a campaign video set to tense violin strings, then at a press conference. “They ask one simple question: do I feel safe?”

The moment—criticized by some as a cynical exploitation of tragedy early in the lead up to the Oct. 26 municipal election—appears to have solidified a principle of Bradford’s campaign: feelings trumped facts. And the overarching feeling that has characterized his run at mayor seems to be anger. Anger at incumbent mayor Olivia Chow, primarily. But also, in some ways, anger at the police force, and at the visible crisis of homelessness and addiction on city streets. It’s a feeling shared by a not insignificant number of Torontonians.

Publicly, Bradford’s image is characterized by a relentless drive to win in the race for mayor, and particularly to win against Chow. There’s little else that one really knows about the candidate or his interiority. In wanting to learn more, I spoke with his former staff, with his colleagues and critics on city council, with constituents and old friends and mentors. Many of them struggled to pin down what Bradford really believes, or who his friends on council are, or what changed in his two-term arc to the political right. They agree he is driven, and capable of being incredibly hardworking. But former staff allege that Bradford has screamed and sworn at his employees, sometimes pushing them to tears. Colleagues describe him as a bully on the council floor. And almost everyone I spoke to identified, under layers of unyielding energy and intensity and ambition, that Brad Bradford seems pretty angry.

Join the thousands of readers who've signed up for our free newsletter and get award-winning local journalism delivered to your inbox.

"*" indicates required fields

Bradford’s most famous war, and the one that has most fuelled his critics, is with himself. First-term Beaches-East York councillor Bradford, in particular, has been a scourge to the campaign of mayoral hopeful Bradford.

When he was first elected to represent Ward 19, Bradford was an eager, bike-riding city planner in his early thirties, with a young family. He enjoyed the rare dual endorsements of both the mayoral frontrunners, John Tory and progressive Jennifer Keesmaat. His biggest priority, he told the Toronto Star after his win in 2018, was road safety.

Bradford was, perhaps, overestimated as progressive by virtue of his age—in his first term, he voted with Mayor Tory 93.7 percent of the time. But he took vocal stances on things that he has since had to publicly, repeatedly disavow. In 2020, he voted alongside the City’s progressive bloc in favour of cutting 10 percent of the police budget, and later that year, largely in favour of a raft of policing reforms. In fact, he was one of the small number of councillors who voted in favour of consultation with municipal bodies representing Black and Indigenous communities in establishing these reforms. Today, the hiring of 1,000 police officers is one of the cornerstones of his campaign.

While he voted in favour of renaming Yonge-Dundas Square to Sankofa Square in 2023, Bradford spent the early part of his campaign this summer criticizing the move, and proposed renaming it Toronto Square. And of course, there’s the bike lane issue. Bradford’s early identity was so tied up with bike-riding that it was the one thing people knew about him if they didn’t know anything else. Now, he’s proposing the removal of bike lanes on part of Bloor Street West that he himself voted to implement, and promising not to build bike lanes on arterial roads (he says he remains supportive of the lanes on Adelaide, Richmond, and Sherbourne Streets, which he helped initially vote in).

In the press, Bradford has characterized these changes of heart not as ideological, but as a response to evidence that has emerged in the aftermath of the decisions. “We were able to see and feel the real-world feedback,” he said about the Bloor Street West bike lanes in an August press conference. “It became clear that council, including me, got this one wrong.”

“Some people are going to want me to double down on a bad take…I will not do that.”

Early in his time as councillor, Bradford’s policy ideas weren’t tied to any particular side of the political spectrum. He was an action guy—he seemed to really care about bike lanes, road safety, and housing—and he was adept at navigating the bureaucracy of city hall using the experience he’d gained as a planner with the City.

This was the context in which I first noticed Bradford, when I investigated the road safety records of city councillors in the 2018-2022 city hall term. The Beaches-East York councillor was leagues ahead of his colleagues in improving road safety in his ward because he regularly waived long, bureaucratic processes in favour of simply installing speed bumps or stop signs because the community wanted them. “The local residents on the local street know their street better than the bureaucrats at city hall,” he told me in 2022. “If they think traffic calming measures are necessary, I’m going to be there to support them, and move that through the machinery of government.”

In my conversations with former Bradford staffers and with his colleagues on council, I’ve been searching for a particular turning point, a catalyst that helped form the Bradford we recognize today—or even a clear answer on when that transformation really happened. No single answer emerges. It’s not just that Bradford is distinctly more right-leaning now than he was even a mere four years ago. Perhaps more importantly, it’s that he today appears to be driven not by an enthusiasm for the policies he’s advocating for, but by a contempt for the ones he’s advocating against.

First-term Bradford wavered between passionate and aggressive, says Jessica, a former senior staffer who worked with Bradford through part of his first and second terms. “But I think rather than staying true to that,” Jessica says, “he’s definitely leaned quite heavily into the anger, frustration, aggression.”

For this story, I independently spoke with three former staffers from Bradford’s office who were willing to share their experiences with me. Their stories were verified against each other, and using contemporaneous correspondence from that time sent via email and text. The Local viewed messages sent and received by the sources at the time that mentioned Bradford’s anger, yelling, and instances of staff crying. In politics, employees are expected to never speak openly about current or former employers—the staffers quoted in this story have been given pseudonyms to protect their employment.

In the earlier years, there was a puerile, bro-y energy in the Bradford office, the staffers say. (This atmosphere became more professional, and more demanding, in his second term, sources tell me.) Bradford would change into his cycling kit and get on his exercise bike in the office, they say, sometimes having staff read him prep notes while he worked out. Jessica and another staffer, Tim (also a pseudonym), both recall him employing the term “BDE”—big dick energy, a slang term that captured the public imagination for a hot minute in 2018—when he wanted his staff to pursue something aggressively. They say he would frequently do things an employer doesn’t usually do: ask about peoples’ love lives, share personal details, pal around with the staff.

These purported quirks could, if one were feeling generous, be chalked up to the tone-deaf idiosyncrasies of a man who had grown up playing sports. (In his youth, Bradford was a figure skater—a talent that many only found out he had after he made a video with Tessa Virtue this year. He played rugby in university, and following a knee injury, took up cycling and co-founded a competitive team, Toronto Hustle.) But the staffers paint a less generous picture, of a boss who wasn’t afraid to occasionally venture to the outer boundary of appropriate office behaviour.

Towards the later part of that first term, Tim tells me, Bradford began to show a disdain for the people who disagreed with him. “It kind of became this constant barrage of, ‘let’s openly complain about people who disagree with us,’” Tim says. No one was off limits: constituents, average-joe social media commentators, fellow councillors, he adds.

There were times when Bradford would come back from having an argument at city council or a committee meeting and would perch at the edge of a staffer’s desk in the main office, Tim says, and lead the office in a group discussion about how his opposition was wrong and he was right. Tim and Jessica both say that he was harsher about female councillors, and on occasion, that they heard Bradford use the word “bitch” to describe them.

Jessica says that Bradford “couldn’t talk to certain staff without being really belligerent, yelling or screaming at them.” It wasn’t uncommon, she adds, for staff to cry during or after these encounters. Sometimes, to some people, he would apologize, she says, but his actions did not meaningfully change in the time she worked for him.

“Brad kind of created an environment of fear where he yelled and swore a lot at staff, and would throw mini-tantrums if he didn’t feel like he was getting what he needed,” says Tim, describing some of the incidents as akin to “verbal abuse”.

A former staffer who declined to be quoted for this story described having the same experience working under the councillor—that he would lose his temper easily, yell and swear, and, they feel, fail to conduct himself as an employer should.

I ask Bradford about these allegations on a sunny Monday morning in mid-September, over coffee at the Marriott bistro across from city hall. Bradford, who is compact, clean-cut, and perpetually clad in business casual, is unfazed by the question. He puts his coffee—black, no milk, no sugar—down. “I don’t think I’ve really had a lot of conflict with my staff.”

“[But] I hold myself to a very high standard when it comes to performance on the job,” he says. His voice is level, and sincere—he’s not grandstanding. “You know, we all need to perform. We owe it to the people who have invested their trust in us to lead. So I’m not a guy who does well with mediocrity. I’m not a guy who responds well, if the effort doesn’t match the urgency of the issues that we’re dealing with.”

Prior to publishing, The Local sent the Bradford campaign a detailed list of every allegation from former staff. “You spoke with 3 former staffers, unnamed. Brad has worked with hundreds of staff, colleagues and volunteers over 8 years at City Hall,” wrote campaign spokesperson Laryssa Waler. “We’re not going to spend the final weeks of the campaign responding line by line to anonymous accusations from people who won’t attach their names to them.” Neither Bradford nor the campaign denied any allegations.

The next day, the Bradford campaign attempted to connect me with a former staffer. After I described the allegations in this story, the staffer decided not to go on the record.

The Local then heard from two current staffers who describe having good relationships with Bradford. Both describe the office as a high-intensity workplace, but they say they’ve never heard Bradford swear at his staff, or refer to a fellow councillor as a “bitch.” Craig Ruttan, Bradford’s chief of staff the last three years and current deputy campaign manager, says he “can’t recall” a time when Bradford’s actions made staff cry, and that he hasn’t heard or experienced Bradford yelling and berating employees in the way he’s seen in other councillors offices. “Can I say, definitively, [that] I’ve never heard him yell? No,” he continues. “There have been some times where something quite bad happened, and he had a response to it. But I wouldn’t say it’s something that was typical or characteristic of him.”

Heather Purdon, who has worked as office manager for Bradford for two years, says that while she’s seen Bradford get upset and yell, she’s never seen him yell at staff, nor make anyone cry. She described Bradford as patient and supportive. (Purdon did not respond when asked whether she is working for Bradford’s current campaign.)

Some of Bradford’s colleagues on council attest to his temper. Gord Perks, outgoing councillor for Ward 4 — Parkdale-High Park, 20-year veteran at city council, and prominent ally of Chow, had one of the most visibly tense relationships with Bradford of anyone on council. Over the years, the two have exchanged sharp words, eye rolls, and occasional passive-aggressive snubs. “From day one, he’s been very competitive with other members of council, and been quite an attention-seeker. That’s been a consistent pattern all the way through,” says Perks. “The one thing that’s changed, though, is he’s gotten even angrier.”

At least while the livestream cameras are on, city council tends, on most days, to be a fairly subdued, collegial place, dominated more by finicky bureaucratic process than by impassioned arguments about principles. But Bradford has occasionally attracted attention for his demeanour on the floor of council—for sparring with progressive councillors like Alejandra Bravo and Gord Perks, for example, or for the time he described Toronto-Danforth councillor Paula Fletcher’s behaviour as “hysteria.”

According to Perks, it’s not beyond Bradford to swear at his colleagues off-mic. “He storms around like a bull, and tries to use swagger and intimidation to get his way,” he says.

When I ask Bravo, she is measured in her response. “He doesn’t work well with his colleagues,” she tells me, “and it will be challenging for him to be able to govern with a majority of council.”

Perks and Bravo are, of course, part of Chow’s progressive coalition. For this story, I also tried to speak to councillors who had a more positive relationship with Bradford, like Stephen Holyday or Jon Burnside, or those who have endorsed Bradford for mayor, including James Pasternak and Vincent Crisanti. Holyday declined to speak; everyone else did not respond to multiple attempts to reach them.

Jennifer McKelvie, former city councillor for Ward 25 — Scarborough-Rouge Park and current Liberal MP for Ajax, joined council at the same time as Bradford, in 2018. “He’s smart, he works hard, and he cares,” she told me.

During her time at city hall, McKelvie worked with Bradford on key policy pushes, she tells me: the legalization of multi-tenant housing, setting a goal to build 285,000 homes over 10 years, reducing red tape and zoning barriers to build faster. She has now endorsed him for mayor.

When I ask her about the allegations of bullying and anger fellow councillors and former staff have raised against Bradford, she says, “I’ve also seen how very kind he is to the residents…I know there’s many employees of his that are currently working on his campaign and also hold the utmost respect for him as well.”

Observers say that Bradford’s anger—and his willingness to make it known to others—escalated during his 2023 run in Toronto’s mayoral by-election.

Among the sources I spoke to for this story, the consensus was that Bradford hadn’t necessarily entered the role of city councillor aiming to one day be mayor. But it seemed his unrelenting ambition needed a natural home after his tenure on council ended (Bradford has been committed, throughout his time as councillor for Beaches-East York, to only being in that office for two terms). The 2023 revelation of former Toronto mayor John Tory’s extramarital affair and subsequent resignation seemed to present the perfect opportunity. Despite Bradford’s close working relationship with Tory, the outgoing mayor endorsed then-councillor and former deputy mayor Ana Bailão.

Toronto-Danforth councillor Fletcher, another councillor who has had an openly adversarial relationship with Bradford, describes him as disruptive, rude, and belligerent once he began campaigning. She was particularly struck by it because she felt they’d gotten along well when working on the Danforth bike lane before the pandemic. “There was a marked change once he decided to run for mayor,” she says.

Fletcher points out that historically, she didn’t align politically with former mayor John Tory, but that disagreements with his allies on council didn’t have to mean animosity between colleagues. “I may have an argument with one of the councillors, but afterward, it’s very genuinely friendly,” she says. “I did not find that with Councillor Bradford, once he decided he was running for mayor. He was in fight mode every minute.”

In June of 2023, Bradford lost his first run for mayor. He came eighth in a crowded field of 102 candidates, winning only 1.28 percent of the vote, sandwiched, astonishingly, between a right-wing media commentator and an actual Holocaust denier. He’d gotten fewer votes city-wide than he had the previous year in just his own ward. It was a loss so humiliating that even some of his critics were surprised. Bradford himself seems resigned to recognize some humour in it: both at the safety townhall from July, and during our interview, when he mentions the first time he ran for mayor, he looks off to the side and laughs a little.

After Chow’s election win, it seems much of Bradford’s ire and intensity turned towards her. On the floor of council, he has become Chow’s most vocal opponent, frequently disagreeing with the mayor despite the futility of whatever motion or argument he’s trying to make—perhaps specifically so that he can be seen, on record at city council and under the watchful eye of the livestream, as council’s primary foil for Chow. At the last council meeting before the election, held at the end of July, the two had a terse exchange over how much Chow may have known about the province’s plans to expand the island airport before they were announced. “I don’t know where you’re at, at this point,” she shot back a little defensively, in response to his question, and in reference to Bradford’s prior support of a longer runway. “At some point, you need to make your decision clear—what side are you on?”

“Let’s not confuse the issues,” he retorted. “You sound confused.”

She was visibly peeved, a side of the mayor the public doesn’t often see. The contrast between this exchange and the one before it—Chow’s interactions with the rather soft-spoken, unassuming Etobicoke Centre councillor Stephen Holyday, who frequently votes against her and also had questions about the airport—were night and day.

In February of this year, Bradford spent $13,602 on a telephone townhall for constituents of Beaches-East York, opening the phone lines for them to call in with grievances about Chow’s budget. No other councillor did anything similar, or for this much money—except the mayor’s office. More than a year ago, Bradford was on the cover of the Toronto Sun wielding a baseball bat he claimed to keep under his bed at night to protect his family from—there’s that familiar threat again—armed home invaders. He was making an impression on the public, giving them a chance to know him ahead of his second run. It is, perhaps, the most overt years-long campaign for mayor that this city has ever seen.

If you spend any time with Bradford, you do notice traits that are well suited to the role of mayor. He’s a remarkably well-spoken person. When he chooses to be, he can be affable, even charming. There is a consensus, even among his most vocal critics, that he is extremely hardworking. The selling point is: what if his churning, unyielding drive were harnessed in service of improving the city?

“I was terribly impressed with his enormous work capacity and energy, and ability to meet so many people, and be so sharp, and connected, and involved,” says Kent Hakull, a friend of Bradford’s from his Masters degree at the University of Waterloo. The two of them were student leaders with the Canadian Association of Planning Students, organizing and attending urban planning conferences and events while working on their degrees. While they haven’t stayed in touch much over the past 14 years, and Hakull, a soft-spoken city planner in Haugesund, a small coastal municipality in Norway, doesn’t keep up with Bradford’s politics, he does remember the distinct impression a young Bradford had made upon him.

In their small program of 30 or 40 students, “He was extremely inviting, open, curious,” Hakull says. Bradford gave the outward appearance of a pure extrovert—“he got to know everybody quite quickly, and developed friendly relations really fast.” In fact, when Hakull in his work today has to meet new people, work a room, he uses the skills he learned from Bradford. “People think I’m an extrovert, and I often credit that to Brad.”

Bradford’s ambition and his skill were apparent to Hakull even then. One night, driving back from a conference together in Bradford’s little car, the Norwegian remembers telling Bradford, whatever he did, to aim high. “I think he had the ambition of being a leader,” Hakull says. At that stage of their life, there were a million possibilities for where that could take them.

Many of the better traits Bradford projects outwardly make him a natural fit for political leadership. In fact, it’s puzzling to me that he doesn’t mine his inarguably compelling personal history to build a public persona with more layers to it. Even the story behind his full name, which is in fact Bradford Bradford—he was named for his mother’s last name, but then changed his own last name to match hers after his parents split—is a humanizing detail that could engender sympathy from voters.

During the July safety townhall, Bradford briefly mentioned his father in the context of addiction treatment for people in crisis. “People who are struggling need treatment. You know, my dad left us when we were six. He had some issues with addiction and mental health.” And then, before the supporters in the room could get to know Bradford any further as a person—rather than as a politician—he pivoted to talking about his drug treatment policy. (Bradford has campaigned on mandatory treatment for people experiencing addiction, which many health professionals and critics say is not backed by science: some studies have found that people experiencing addiction who are forced into treatment are more likely to relapse upon release, and have higher risks of adverse health outcomes and death.)

When I ask him about his family history in person, he’s similarly reticent. “Without getting into too many of the personal details of my own family’s experience,” he prefaces, before gently turning to policy. There are only two things he always mentions. The first is his family—two daughters and his wife, urban planner Kathryn Randle, who all frequently appear on his social media and in campaign material. And the second is his appreciation for his mother, who made the decision to raise three kids under six on her own. “I saw how hard she worked, the sacrifices that she made, everything that she did to provide for us, and all the challenges that come with it,” he tells me. Another graceful pivot, like political figure skating. “I think that gives me a firsthand perspective of what it’s like for so many families here in the city…”

The walled-off part of Bradford’s public persona is an interesting choice in comparison to Chow’s open-book approach to talking about her family and the strife that shaped her childhood: the abuse her mother and brother faced at the hands of her father, who also struggled with mental health issues. We live in an age when the most successful mayoral campaign in public memory is New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s—a candidate whose smiley, man-of-the-people optimism far more resembles Chow’s (famously dance-friendly, however one may feel about that) campaign than Bradford’s. He seems to recognize this tension, though I don’t get the sense he’s rushing to kiss any babies on the campaign trail. He mentions it briefly, laughing, when we meet: “Yeah, the Star was saying I need to smile more.”

In pre-election polling, 40 percent of city voters favour Bradford. In his own ward, if there are many supporters, they’re being drowned out by his vocal critics. In the 2023 mayoral by-election, only 4.7 percent of voters in Beaches-East York voted for their councillor, leaving Bradford sixth in the ward’s ranking. Many feel that he’s neglected the ward in favour of his three-year run for mayor—constituents I spoke to from the ward described him as impossible to get a hold of, and ineffective at managing the tasks that a city councillor is meant to, like clearing snow from a school bus lane used by paratransit for elementary school children. Despite Bradford’s campaign team sending out a press release criticizing Olivia Chow for her inaction at 500 Dawes Road, an apartment building known in the ward for its appalling living conditions, tenant organizer Ryan Endoh told me that Bradford didn’t respond to their advocacy work for years before it became a broader issue taken up by the mayor’s office. “I gave him every opportunity,” Endoh says. “I don’t actually think that he’s ever really committed himself to doing anything consequential or meaningful.”

Bradford also appears to have broken from the prior mentors who helped put him in the role he has now. His relationship with former mayor John Tory is unclear, and politicos close to Tory have distanced themselves from Bradford. Nick Kouvalis, in particular, who had a hand in both Tory and Ford’s ascent to mayor, told the Toronto Star earlier this year, “There is zero chance that I will work for Brad. I would sooner help Olivia defeat Brad.” (Kouvalis did not reply to my multiple requests for comment). Jennifer Keesmaat, who endorsed Bradford in his first run for council, said on social media earlier this month that Bradford “just makes things up, even when the facts are readily available.” (Keesmaat did not reply to multiple requests for comment.) Mary-Margaret McMahon, current Liberal MPP for Beaches-East York and city councillor for the ward preceding Bradford, told me, “He’s not the person I thought he was when I endorsed him.”

Bradford has instead surrounded himself, in this phase of his political life, with a team of mixed Liberal- and Conservative-affiliated advisors and staff who, for the most part, lean further to the right. His campaign manager, John Sinclair, was former deputy chief of staff for federal Conservatives leader Pierre Poilievre, and Bradford has hired members of Premier Doug Ford government’s communications and press staff.

Those advisors have helped Bradford construct a platform that emphasizes crime, and saving voters money on taxes. Besides that, he wants to establish a 15-minute money-back guarantee for delays on the TTC, and remove 12 km worth of Scarborough priority bus lanes, while also pushing for the suburb’s Eglinton East LRT. He’s talked about job creation for young people. He proposes the bureaucratic-but-genuinely-impactful elimination of the municipal land transfer tax for homes under $1.1 million (which critics say could take hundreds of millions of dollars from the City’s already flagging coffers).

His mayoral run has had mixed reception even among presumed supporters. Despite Bradford being the law-and-order candidate this election season, the head of the Toronto police union has praised Chow and criticized Bradford. Many assume that Doug Ford would align with Bradford, but there’s no sign this is the case—in fact, Ford gave a peculiar wink-and-nudge almost-endorsement of Chow earlier this fall, only to walk it back the next day. But Bradford is endorsed by the centre-right non-profit A Better City Toronto. “Anybody who comes to this role with a clear-eyed assessment of the state of the city, to say, ‘Things aren’t working right now, and I have a plan to fix them’—to me, that is a powerful candidate,” the organization’s executive director Kelly Aizicowitz told me.

Vastly outperforming his 2023 self, Bradford has found definite purchase with a few groups this election season. People who are alienated by the visible crisis of homelessness and addiction on city streets, and who feel that this crisis is the result of a culture of permissiveness at city hall (particularly through the existence of safe consumption sites), rather than, say, a chronic underfunding of social services and a housing affordability crisis. People who harbour a specific resentment against the Bloor West bike lane, or Scarborough rapid transit bus lanes. Some who are passionately pro-Israel, and want the police and the City to crack down on the regular pro-Palestine protests that have taken place in the city since Israel’s bombing of Gaza began; others who feel Chow has failed them on the more than doubling of antisemitic hate crimes reported to the police since 2022; and some who feel both. (Bradford’s reception at the candidates’ forum on antisemitism in early September was fervent—the only time distant third-place candidate Chris Alexander received anywhere near as much applause was when he admitted he was open to withdrawing from the race, which he since has.)

But beyond those narrow constituencies, the central bet of the Bradford campaign is that there are enough people in Toronto who are as angry as he is. Traffic in the city is terrible. The cost of living is debilitating. There is a distressing, sometimes frightening crisis of addiction in the city. These are real issues—complicated issues, issues that should make you upset. Bradford seems to hope that, coloured by frustration and fear, voters will attribute all of that to one person, and to her decisions.

Whether this sentiment is pervasive enough to win Bradford the mayor’s race is uncertain. According to some polls, Chow’s lead has grown slimmer over the course of the race, currently sitting somewhere between four and eight points, with Alexander’s withdrawal almost certainly sending some voters towards Bradford. The race is closer than any re-election campaign for an incumbent mayor in decades. If Bradford’s apparent anger really does reflect enough of the city he wants to lead, he’ll finally have the seat he’s single-mindedly coveted these last few years.

There’s something Kent Hakull mentioned about going to school with Bradford that stuck with me long after our conversation. In grad school, he explained, they learned that in planning, “leaders cannot be only skeptical of developers.” It’s a belief that Hakull and Bradford shared in these formative years, that they maybe still share, he said. It’s a lesson that applies to city planners, but also to anyone who wants to be a responsible leader. “Being close to power, being close to actors of both ‘good’ and ‘bad’, essentially requires skill,” said Hakull. “You have to know who you are and where you stand.”

Bradford has mastered the first part, being close to power. For the people I spoke to who have known him, worked for him, or once voted for him, it’s the second part, about knowing where you stand, that makes them worry.

Clarification—Oct. 10, 2026: This article was updated to add that Craig Ruttan is deputy campaign manager for Brad Bradford.

A massive drug bust on Skid Row has sparked a war of words between a Los Angeles City Council member and the city’s top federal prosecutor.

Dozens of FBI agents and cops descended on the notorious downtown neighborhood Thursday as part of a sweeping crackdown on the sale of fentanyl, meth, cocaine and PCP.

The California Post was on the scene as investigators seized drugs, guns, cash and luxury cars, making dozens of arrests in a probe that exposed the alleged tricks dealers used to hide their deadly trade — including disguises, storefronts and sidewalk tents.

But Councilmember Ysabel Jurado, whose District 14 includes Skid Row, blasted the operation, claiming homeless residents were prevented from returning to their tents to retrieve their belongings, medication and other necessities.

“Law enforcement has described the operation in Skid Row as targeting drug trafficking. But that doesn’t remove the responsibility to protect residents’ rights and well-being,” Jurado wrote on social media.

“Residents have reported being kept from returning to their tents, obtaining their belongings, accessing essential medication, and reaching the services they depend on every day to survive.”

Jurado argued that Skid Row is home to one of the city’s largest populations of “seniors, people with disabilities, and Black residents,” and said its residents deserve the same treatment as people in any other Los Angeles neighborhood.

“But we’ve continued to treat it as the afterthought of our policies,” the councilmember wrote. “Living in a neighborhood that society wrote off does not make you a criminal.”

“It does not make you unworthy of city services, mental health, and representation from your government.”

The councilmember also said Skid Row’s homeless residents deserve “protection from exploitation and violence” and “dignity and accountability from the institutions responsible for their safety.”

The 50-block area is home to roughly 6,000 homeless people and has long been plagued by open-air drug dealing and violence.

Dubbed “Operation Free Skid Row,” Thursday’s crackdown involved multiple agencies, including the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration and Los Angeles Police Department. Authorities said 28 alleged dealers were charged with federal drug offenses, while agents served more than 40 search warrants.

But US Attorney Bill Essayli, the region’s top federal prosecutor, wasn’t having Jurado’s criticism.

Essayli accused the councilmember and the nonprofit Los Angeles Community Action Network (LACAN) of contributing to the neighborhood’s problems by opposing law enforcement efforts.

“They are fiercely anti-law enforcement and focus their efforts on protecting criminals who exploit the homeless. Under their watch, gangs and thugs run Skid Row, supplying the worst drugs imaginable, stealing money, and raping or killing anyone in their way,” Essayli wrote Friday.

“Rather than working with LAPD to arrest drug dealers, LACAN advocates handing out millions of dollars’ worth of needles and crack pipes while harassing officers.”

Essayli defended the operation, saying investigators had obtained judicial authorization for the searches and carried out the crackdown professionally.

“We are proud of yesterday’s operation that charged 28 people with federal drug dealing and served more than 40 search warrants (all done professionally with judicial authorization). If the councilwoman disliked yesterday’s actions, she will be very displeased in the months ahead,” Essayli added.

Democrats lost the 2024 elections in part because of their eroding support among Latino voters, a constituency that was once a reliable segment of their base.

That November, Kamala Harris won the Latino vote by three points, according to the Pew Research Center. In 2020, Joe Biden carried them by 25 points.

This year, swing districts with large Hispanic populations could help decide which party controls the House. And Democrats are scrambling for ways to win those voters back.

One new effort comes from the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, also known as BOLD PAC. In February, they launched a program to personally connect social media influencers with voters.

"We're turning to trusted voices in local communities that have followings giving them information and then allowing them to create content in a way that is organic and authentic," said Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., who chairs BOLD PAC.

That includes Latina content creator Alexa Flores, who not long ago mostly posted about beauty tips and fashion. But the Arizona resident shifted to politics in response to the Trump administration's immigration policies.

She says she wants Latino voters to understand their impact if they vote.

"My job is to get people to understand that so that they can go and move that needle," said Flores, who has nearly 500,000 followers across her platforms.

Her job now includes "get-out-the-vote" events with BOLD PAC in swing districts around the country. Flores, for her part, will appear at a wine tasting event in Las Cruces, N.M. – where Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez is locked in a close race against Republican Greg Cunningham. She'll also appear at a Día de los Muertos event with lowriders and voters in Tucson, Ariz., where Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza is trying to unseat GOP incumbent Juan Ciscomani.

BOLD PAC says it is not paying content creators for posts. Instead, they're providing stipends of $1,500 for flights, hotels and other travel costs for each event.

Sánchez says content creators could help bridge a gap for her party. Thirty percent of Latinos regularly get their news from influencers on social media, according to Pew Research Center. That's more than any other demographic.

"So whether that's ... Instagram or YouTube or TikTok, that's how they're getting their information," she said. "So we need to be in those spaces."

Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., chairs BOLD PAC. She says content creators can help bridge a gap for her party. Above, Sanchez speaks on immigration at the U.S. Capitol on May 10, 2023.
                
                    
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

Democratic strategist Stephanie Valencia says Democratic efforts to win back long term support from Latino voters is going to be an uphill battle. Valencia is co-founder of Equis Research, which estimates that roughly a third of Latinos are considered independent voters.

Of those, more than 40% think neither party cares about people like them.

"One election cycle is not going to solve the problem that Democrats have had and a frayed trust with Latino voters that has developed over the last several election cycles," Valencia said.

In 2024, Latinos shifted right in response to what they saw as liberal immigration policies and a focus on foreign intervention over domestic policy under former President Biden. Flores, the Arizona influencer, says she hopes for more awareness that Latinos are having a growing impact on major pieces of American life.
