The icons of social media apps, including Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and WhatsApp, are displayed on a mobile phone screen(Image: PA)

Children aged as young as 14 are being treated for social media addiction, a top rehab boss has warned.

Growing numbers of kids are being treated for the disease by psychiatrists after becoming hooked on attention-grabbing apps such as TikTok and Instagram. In an exclusive interview, Jan Gerber, founder of world-leading recovery clinic Paracelsus Recovery, told the Mirror: "This is a massive epidemic.

"The algorithms are being designed to hijack the reward system [in the brain]. These are all dopaminergic activities. Scrolling is one thing, but collecting likes or comments that's levelled up - that's all designed to get people hooked.

Jan Gerber, founder of rehab clinic Paracelsus recovery described the issue as "a massive epidemic"(Image: Supplied)

"And when the brain is still being formed, it's much more vulnerable at a younger age and at that young age they're not equipped to resist that. It's like digital crack cocaine."

Mr Gerber said he has been approached by parents of children even younger than 14, but legally cannot treat them at his clinic in Switzerland. He added he is also seeing young patients becoming hooked on online gaming on phones and tablets before running up massive bills on their parents' bank cards after buying so-called loot boxes within games.

He said: "It's like going to the casino. You could win big, but also you can get nothing at all. It's designed to be it addictive."

Asked what warning signs of social media addiction, parents should look out for, Jan said: "The most obvious is the amount of screen time or app use time. Social withdrawal is another, like a faked headache or tiredness like I'm going to bed early and so on, but actually they're using the phone or tablet under the blanket. These are tell-tale signs.

The clinic is understood to cost £100,000 a week to attend

"And also hobbies being given up, causing social connections to basically fizzle out or not happen anymore."

Mr Gerber admits treating the disease is "super difficult" and "takes time". But he says doctors at his clinic have recently had success by treating young patients with a system of playing style cards to help them cope with and express their feelings.

Australia imposed a social media ban on under-16s in December and Prime Minister Keir Starmer is now poised to announce a ban for under 16s using sites like Facebook, Snapchat, Instagram and TikTok, on Monday.

Jan believes an outright ban is unlikely to succeed because it would likely make children want to experience it more. But he believes the government must take action and that moves such as restricting children's screen time to a maximum of one hour per day, may be more effective.

A self-confessed chatterbox in an increasingly loud world, Angela Garwood swapped conversation for stillness at a device-free silent retreat, hoping to discover what lies beneath the noise

A self-confessed chatterbox in an increasingly loud world, Angela Garwood swapped conversation for stillness at a device-free silent retreat, hoping to discover what lies beneath the noise

“It’s OK,” a fellow bather mouths with a reassuring smile. I squeal slightly as the water hits my waist before plunging in. It’s perfect. Refreshing without the usual razor-sharp iciness of British waters. I emerge feeling awakened and alive.

A group of us bob around, admiring the stunning white chalk cliffs of the Seven Sisters. Others sit on the shore. No one talks, as this would be breaking the rules. It’s a glorious Sunday morning and I haven’t spoken for more than 36 hours.

I’ve come to the Sussex coast to spend the weekend trying something I struggle with at times: keeping my mouth shut. As a performer, the notion of a silent retreat goes against so much of what brings me joy: using my voice and a love of words. I’m a talker. I revel in a witty exchange or an outrageous story.

Doubts aside, I’d arrived at Gayles, a beautiful converted family farm in Eastbourne, on a Friday afternoon, in the midst of a particularly full-on summer. Hoping to find stillness amid the chaos, I’d opted for something more radical than a spa day.

“It’s essential,” says Roz Robinson, 66, yoga teacher, former psychotherapist and host of the Walking, Yoga, Meditation, Silence retreats at Gayles. “You wouldn’t expect to drive your car for a year without having an MOT, and I don’t think we should be allowed to carry on without having, if you like, our own reset.”

“It’s such a precious space to be able to step into,” she continues. “To give yourself time to reflect, because there is so much noise in the outside world now.”

I’m shown to my room, a spacious double with views of the sea in a converted 1930s stable. Then the group, all 18 of us, mostly women, are given a tour of the grounds, which include a pool, tennis courts and cosy corners for quiet contemplation. Surrounded by 11 acres of rolling downland, there’s a comforting and unassuming family-home feel to Gayles, which has been in Robinson’s family for generations.

Demand for restorative escapes is surging post-Covid. Image: Laurie Griffiths

Poolside, Robinson requests “no bombing”. “Who bombs on a silent retreat?!” we ask. “Oh, it’s happened …”. We chuckle. Other rules include no alcohol, no Apple Watches – it’s device-free – and no aggressively strong perfume or deodorant if you’re sharing a room. Electric toothbrushes are allowed, but I later refrain from using my hairdryer.

A small wicker basket sits on a side table with a note inviting us to hand our phones in. It’s not compulsory, but we’re encouraged to do so. I place mine on the pile.

We are, for the initial meal, allowed to talk. Munching on our delicious, home-grown vegetable lasagne, I enjoy getting to know my soon-to-be-mute companions. We’re mostly first-timers and ages range from 30-something to 60-something.

“I walk away from here like I’m walking on air,” says Fiona Lomas, 54, a Brighton-based creative director on her 10th stay at Gayles.

Having the burden of small talk removed was refreshingly liberating. Food came alive

After dinner, we head to the cow shed, a tranquil yoga space converted from the original farm building. Candles are lit and I feel a child-like sense of ease, like I’m being taken care of. We each share why we’ve come.

The reasons followed similar themes: needing to switch off, wanting to try something new and seeking a connection with nature. One young professional in sustainability finance admitted “I’m not all that comfortable with silence.” A woman in her 60s just said: “I’m here … for me”.

I’m not alone in my desire for stillness. After taking a 68% hit in 2020, wellness tourism in the UK grew at an annual rate of 79% between 2020 and 2022, according to the Global Wellness Institute, more than twice the global average of 36%. The institute’s 2026 wellness tourism trends include ‘The Nervous System Reset’ and ‘In Search of Deep Rest’, reflecting growing demand for restorative escapes, nature and time away from digital overload. Condé Nast Traveller, meanwhile, named ‘silent travel’ one of its top travel trends for 2024.

Silent walks are 'a totally different way of experiencing nature,' says guest Fiona Lomas. Image: Laurie Griffiths

“If you need anything, I’m always here,” assures Robinson. “If you need to cry, or scream even, you can scream. Crying is a release. It doesn’t matter!”. There’s talk of resetting our autonomic nervous system, getting closer to our true selves, and healing. While the retreat isn’t religious, there’s a spiritual undercurrent.

We’re led through a relaxation exercise, before a momentous yet subtle declaration: “The silence has begun”. I leave the room elated by the challenge. A space opens up in my mind.

“I love that there’s no pressure to make conversation,” says Rebecca Hastings, 46, an international charity fundraiser. “I come for that deep quality of silence that happens in community, when people are together”.

We quickly found our flow as a group. In the kitchen the following morning, we dance around each other, waiting to stack the dishwasher or boil water, as if previously choreographed. Occasional smiles are exchanged, but interaction is minimal. I enjoy a smoothie before we embark on a five-mile sunny coastal walk.

In the silence, I was confronted, head-on, with my thoughts, which was unnerving yet empowering

“You will have some rubbish to work through,” says Robinson. Indeed. While my thoughts were louder than ever, so too was the aliveness of the nature surrounding me. I found the pattern of trees mesmerising and noticed when a flock of tweeting birds flew overhead. I felt held in the presence of everyone else and over time, a harmonious group synchronicity became apparent. We moved almost as one, stopping together and turning away every time someone left the line for a bush wee.

“The walks are always really interesting because you just see and hear things that you wouldn’t normally,” says Lomas. “It’s a totally different way of experiencing nature.”

We’re encouraged to rest, so I indulge in a two-hour nap, followed by some tea and cake. Yoga and meditation, which I’d grown fond of by this point, came later, then a temporary invitation to break the silence and share how we were finding the experience. Most stayed quiet, myself included.

The silence ends shortly before lunch on Sunday and I have mixed feelings. I was enjoying our peaceful cocoon, but welcomed getting to know the others.

“It’s amazing how connected you can feel to a group of people, even when you’re not talking,” I said in our final circle. We’d shared a unique experience and I’d miss their familiar faces. Together, we’d created our own silent bubble, and I’d come to appreciate existing within it. It was, as Robinson described, a ‘warm silence’.

'We think of silence as being empty, but I learned there’s a richness to that space,' says writer Angela Garwood. Image: Derry Robinson

“At our source, we are quiet, loving, joyous communicative beings,” she reflects. “Donkeys standing in a field are all connected, they’re not chatting all the time.”

Having the burden of small talk removed was refreshingly liberating. Food came alive. There’s a depth of stillness that’s hard to reach when you’re constantly making conversation.

We think of silence as being empty, a void that needs filling, but I learned there’s a richness to that space. A palpable, yet peaceful energy that sits within us, always. In the silence, I was confronted, head-on, with my thoughts, which was unnerving yet empowering.

It wasn’t easy. Huge life uncertainties surfaced, including big questions I had no immediate answers to. I noticed everything: my mind drifting from the past to the future, or simply being unduly self-critical. I felt tension in my body as I moved between yoga poses. There were moments I briefly broke the silence, alone in my room, to give myself the odd pep talk or cry. I surrendered to whatever came up.

The silence created space to hear what I already knew deep down. I needed to come up for air amid my frantic life; to stop, and breathe.

“We look for answers out there, when really the answers are in here,” says Robinson in her closing lesson. “Be kind to yourselves, each and every one of you.”

I left Gayles reenergised, determined to build stillness into my days and commit to the practice. One breath at a time.

Lee will attend the NATO summit in Ankara on Tuesday and Wednesday at the invitation of NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, national security adviser Wi Sung-lac said during a presidential office briefing Friday.

Seoul also hopes to improve cooperation with NATO in emerging military technologies including drones, artificial intelligence and space systems.

Lee will also attend the NATO Summit Defense Industry Forum, which brings together government officials and defense executives to discuss industrial production, investment and technological innovation.

He is scheduled to deliver a keynote address during a session titled "Shared Values, Stronger Industrial Base" and participate in a panel discussion.

Lee will attend an official welcoming dinner hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife Tuesday evening.

The South Korean president plans to hold bilateral meetings Wednesday with leaders of countries that have significant potential for defense and other economic cooperation. The presidential office said the schedules for those meetings were still being coordinated.

Wi said the visit would establish a foundation for South Korean defense companies to expand into NATO markets and participate in more resilient international supply chains.

South Korea is not a NATO member, meaning its weapons and communications systems must meet alliance standards to be integrated smoothly with equipment operated by NATO countries.

"We need to advance partnerships that strengthen interoperability in line with NATO standards so South Korean defense products can be exported smoothly to NATO allies," Wi said.

South Korea has increased defense exports to European countries in recent years, particularly Poland, which has purchased K2 tanks, K9 self-propelled howitzers, FA-50 light combat aircraft and Chunmoo multiple-launch rocket systems.

The government has set a goal of making South Korea one of the world's four largest defense exporters.

Wi said Lee would use the defense industry forum to emphasize South Korean manufacturers' technological capabilities and ability to deliver weapons quickly.

"We will directly communicate the excellence and rapid procurement capabilities of South Korea's defense industry to NATO allies and partners," Wi said.

The government also hopes South Korean armed forces and private companies can participate more actively in NATO innovation networks involving drones, space technology and other emerging defense systems.

Wi said such participation could give South Korean organizations opportunities to acquire critical technologies, conduct joint research and strengthen their ability to respond to future conflicts.

Mongolia state visit

Lee will travel to Ulaanbaatar on Thursday after completing his NATO schedule.

He will meet Mongolian President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh for a summit followed by an exchange of agreements and memorandums of understanding and a joint news conference.

Lee will deliver a keynote address Thursday evening at a South Korea-Mongolia business forum attended by government officials and business leaders from both countries.

The forum will focus on expanding cooperation in resources, supply chains, infrastructure and other industries.

Mongolia has significant deposits of coal, copper, rare earth elements and other minerals important to advanced manufacturing and clean-energy technologies.

South Korea, which depends heavily on imported energy and industrial resources, has sought to diversify its supply chains by expanding cooperation with Mongolia and other mineral-producing countries.

On Friday, Lee will visit a memorial honoring Lee Tae-jun, a Korean physician and independence activist who supported Mongolia's medical development and Korea's independence movement while living in the country in the early 20th century.

The president will then attend a luncheon with members of the Korean community in Mongolia.

Mongolia established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1948, becoming the second country after the Soviet Union to recognize Pyongyang. It has maintained relations with both South and North Korea.

SpaceX said this week that it will build natural gas power plants to supply electricity to the Terafab semiconductor factory it plans to build in Texas, according to a report from Bloomberg.

Riley Trettel, who leads energy and data center development for SpaceX, said in a public meeting on Wednesday that his company will be “bringing our own power” for the project, which will also include “very large battery arrays.”

Notably absent from the Bloomberg report — and other SpaceX announcements related to Terafab — is any mention of terrestrial solar power for the facility. Tesla, which is also a solar developer, is a partner in the project.

Despite his investments in solar power, SpaceX and Tesla’s CEO Elon Musk has bet heavily on natural gas lately. The xAI data centers in Memphis run almost exclusively on the fossil fuel. Musk also recently bought a company that specializes in natural gas power plants, and SpaceX has said it plans to buy $2.8 billion worth of gas turbines over the next three years.

Terafab will be built in Grimes County, which is about 45 miles northwest of downtown Houston. SpaceX, which recently went public in an IPO that raised $87.5 billion, received a 100% tax abatement from the county in exchange for spending at least $5 billion by 2030 and creating at least 1,800 full-time jobs by 2035. Texas is also providing $30 million in incentives.

The initial phase of the fab unit is expected to cost $16.8 billion, though SpaceX had previously estimated it would cost $55 billion. The fab is intended to build chips for data centers that will be run by SpaceX and its xAI subsidiary.

The AI data center boom has driven a surge in proposals for new natural gas power plants across the industry, which has in turn driven up costs for natural gas power plants by 66%. Google, Meta, and Microsoft have all announced massive projects in recent months.

Texas has been ground zero for these “bring your own power” data centers, and more than 70 gigawatts of capacity has been charted out.

Such schemes are intended to speed up project development while addressing concerns about rising electricity prices for consumers, but natural gas turbines can release significant amounts of pollution. SpaceX subsidiary xAI has been sued over its use of unpermitted natural gas turbines in one of the most polluted parts of the country.

SpaceX’s shares fell to just above $135 on Wednesday, the price that CEO Elon Musk and his company chose ahead of its blockbuster June 12 IPO that raked in nearly $86 billion.

The company’s stock spent much of the day below that IPO price, at one point dipping beneath $133 per share, before it traded back up to finish at $135.27.

The dip on Wednesday followed a steady decline in the month since the company went public. SpaceX initially saw its stock price rise to more than $200 in the days after it went public, briefly giving it a valuation that rivaled tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft. Its shares have lost value basically every week since reaching that high point.

Some of the volatility is attributable to the fact that just 4% of the company’s total shares are trading on the Nasdaq. That small “float,” as it’s known, combined with an immense amount of constant attention on the company, has created wild swings during the first month of trading.

The markets also appear to be sobering up on CEO Elon Musk’s grand vision for the company, part of a broader deflation in tech stocks over the last month. Not only has SpaceX’s stock traded down, but also bonds the company sold in the wake of the IPO are suffering.

A prolonged downturn for SpaceX could have wider effects because the company’s stock price is a sign of how investors view the (literal) otherworldly promises Musk has made about what his company can accomplish. SpaceX’s IPO has also set the table for other Big Tech companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to go public. Both of those companies have filed confidentially for an IPO. While neither has set a date to go public, SpaceX’s stock is being closely watched to gauge how successful those IPOs could be.

SpaceX is about to face another early test of the durability of its stock price. On Thursday the company will test launch its Starship rocket for the first time since the IPO. Starship is still very much in development, which means it is prone to failures — the result of SpaceX’s “fly, fail, fix” approach.

This will be the first Starship flight since it experienced a booster failure in May. And once again, the company does not plan to try to recover the Starship booster or upper stage on this flight, instead opting to have them simulate a landing in the Gulf of Mexico. That means both parts of the overall Starship rocket system will end in an explosion no matter what, even if they don’t run into any problems during the flight plan.

On 30th July, Europe’s right-wing populists received manna from heaven as images emerged of 78,000 people arriving on the shores of Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in North Africa. Having spent years warning that the continent faced an existential threat from an “invasion of migrants”, scenes of young men scrambling up the rocks to this small city-state gave them political dynamite.

No one can claim that what happened in Ceuta was not a disaster, with a death toll that some have estimated at more than 100.The local population also faced the near collapse of their public infrastructure, with hospitals, the sanitation system and migration centres overwhelmed. For Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez, this was a worst-case scenario. Having bucked Europe’s punitive trend on migration by regularising the status of 500,000 undocumented migrants in Spain, his liberal approach came under instant fire from those who sought to link it to the crisis.

These attacks were not entirely without basis. A few weeks before, the Spanish Supreme Court made a ruling that appeared to outlaw “hot returns” (a return without due process) for those who arrived in Ceuta from Morocco by sea. Reports suggest that social media misinformation about this ruling may have fuelled the sudden crossing, as well as a laissez-faire approach to enforcement by Moroccan border guards.

Nevertheless, within 24 hours, around 70,000 of those migrants had returned voluntarily to Morocco, and none of them are known to have reached the Schengen area. This, however, did not stop a vicious row breaking out in Europe, as 22 European member states signed a letter criticising Sánchez’s regularisation policy as a “pull-factor” for the influx and demanding tougher border controls. Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni even called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, and neighbouring Schengen states tightened border checks with Spain. Things looked bleak for Sanchez and his outlier migration policy, as he hit back at several countries for their “selfish” and “polarising” response.

On 4th August, however, in an emergency video call, EU interior ministers praised Spain for coping with the crisis. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen commended Sanchez’s “swift handling” of the situation, while Danish immigration minister Morten Bødskov said he was “very satisfied” with Spain’s response. This was in contrast to earlier comments by Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, who sided with Meloni. EU commissioner Magnus Brunner said the crisis was “a test of our European resilience and of the security of our external borders”. But “for the time being,” he said, “Europe has passed this test”.

Europe is already undergoing its biggest migration reform in a decade

Europe’s politicians would do well to listen to him. The bloc is already undergoing its biggest migration reform in a decade, which has angered human rights groups. In June, the New Pact on Migration and Asylum came into force, introducing measures including: pre-screening checks before entering EU soil; accelerated procedures for rejecting asylum claims; and a mandatory solidarity mechanism to lessen the burden on “frontline” states for migration, such as Italy and Greece.

“For people escaping conflict, persecution or economic insecurity these reforms will mean less protection and a greater risk of facing human rights violations across Europe—including illegal and violent pushbacks, arbitrary detention and discriminatory policing,” said Eve Geddie, Amnesty’s head of the European Institutions Office and director of advocacy.

Europe should be more concerned with addressing these serious human rights risks than demands for further punitive measures. Take, for example, calls from Greek premier Kyriakos Mitsotakis to tackle the potential "instrumentalisation" or “weaponisation” of migration by states such as Morocco. These concerns are not unfounded. Given a recent deterioration in relations between Rabat and Madrid, and the seeming impossibility of such a mass crossing occurring without the consent of border guards on the Moroccan side, it is possible that Morocco was using the Ceuta crisis to send a particular message.

However, the solutions that hardliners are proposing may only exacerbate the problem, such as agreeing new migrant return hubs in countries outside the EU. “Externalisation regimes that rely on partner countries only exacerbate the threat of so-called weaponization," writes Helena Hahn, policy analyst at the European Policy Centre, as they increase the EU’s dependency on outside actors to control flows of people. This is not to mention that the pact already has a clause that gives member states extra time and flexibility to respond to cases of influx or “instrumentalisation”, which helped enable Spain to promptly deal with the Ceuta crisis.

But the debate rages on in Europe and beyond, with Donald Trump and other Maga politicians chipping in to criticise Spain. When I first saw the scenes in Ceuta, I feared they would ring the death knell for Sánchez’s progressive migration policy in Europe. He has, however, stood strong.

While Spain and the EU more broadly must calmly find ways to address the causes of Ceuta and prevent a repeat, this tragic incident cannot be used to advance a hardline migration agenda.

And those of us who want to see a more humane approach to migration should continue to watch Sánchez’s ambitious approach to regularisation with hope and interest. The test for that particular policy is yet to come, when 500,000 people gain legal status, and the impacts on Spain’s economy and social fabric begin to emerge. Ceuta was a fraught and tragic moment, but it was not that test.

Steven Spielberg has always been the master of awe and his new film Disclosure Day is no exception. If only he trusted his intuition.

Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day begins with a literal punch in the face. The opening scenes of the film have a kinetic rush: with minimal exposition, we are introduced to Daniel Kellner (Josh O’Connor) and his girlfriend, Jane Blankenship (Eve Hewson), who are being held hostage.

The crisp nocturnal cinematography by Janusz Kamiński and Sarah Broshar’s brisk editing recall the paranoid landscapes of the Mission: Impossible films and Christopher Nolan’s noir fantasies, yet the seamlessly classical mise en scène is undeniably the work of Spielberg. It’s as if the septuagenarian director is daring the audience, wanting to make it clear he is far from over the hill.

Daniel is on the run from his former employer Wardex, a shadowy security organisation with links to the FBI. For decades Wardex has been involved in covering up evidence of extraterrestrial contact. Daniel and a handful of his colleagues have come across damning evidence of the merciless interrogation and torture of aliens. This renegade group of rebels, led by Hugo Wakefield (Colman Domingo), want to unleash their trove of recorded evidence to the world. Wardex’s attempt to sabotage their disclosure, led by Noah Scanlon (Colin Firth), forms the narrative spine of the film.

The visceral excitement of the filmmaking is too often let down by the heavy-handedness of the script. The screenplay is by David Koepp, who wrote one of Spielberg’s most successful films, Jurassic Park (1993), but it’s tone-deaf when it comes to dialogue. After Daniel and Jane have made their escape, they find haven among Catholic nuns. Jane was a novitiate when she was younger and when Daniel reveals why Wardex is chasing them, her reaction is to doubt the readiness of the world to hear we are not the supreme beings in the universe. Her arguments are banal and Daniel’s response is equally trite. The writing is so shallow you can sense O’Connor and Hewson straining to build a rapport: their relationship never feels believable.

Disclosure Day raises questions of doubt and existential meaning but too often the playing out of these tensions is reduced to mawkishness and a strained Christian mysticism. The film’s most effective moments are those that reveal the anguish of the aliens. When Daniel first shows Jane recordings of Wardex’s cruelty to the extraterrestrials, Spielberg keeps the visuals and sound elliptical and doesn’t linger over the images. His restraint underscores his talent and responsiveness as a filmmaker: the effect is shocking. After the powerful impact of such scenes, returning to another car chase or more of Noah’s cat-and-mouse pursuit of the fugitives becomes exasperating.

When Spielberg concentrates on the story’s central question – how we might approach other alien beings with empathy – the film comes close to achieving beauty.

Thankfully the film has Emily Blunt. She plays Margaret Fairchild, a Kansas City TV weather presenter who is always hoping for a better job, a better life to come along. When a northern cardinal swoops into the apartment she shares with her boyfriend, she looks at the bird and suddenly can speak in perfect Russian. Margaret, like Daniel, had an encounter with the extraterrestrials when she was a child, an experience she has repressed. Her strange new powers will prove central to the success or failure of the renegades’ attempts to outmanoeuvre Wardex and expose their cover-up.

There’s an element of the ridiculous in the onset and scale of Margaret’s emerging superpowers, yet Blunt is such a capable performer she can play both the comedy and apprehension in her character’s inexplicable transformation. When we first meet Margaret, she is a ruthless woman on the make. Her character softens as the story progresses, yet the toughness that Blunt reveals in her first few scenes is never completely sacrificed. Her ability to combine humour with stubbornness is a rare talent: her likeability always feels earnt. We don’t ever feel she’s sucking up to us. She keeps us invested in Disclosure Day even at its most ludicrous or sentimental.

Initially I was unconvinced by Josh O’Connor’s performance. His thoughtfulness, his almost reticent screen persona, seemed at odds with the action tropes of the film’s opening act. Once Daniel is saved by Margaret, O’Connor visibly relaxes as an actor. Blunt’s control seems to act as a tonic and allows O’Connor to reveal Daniel’s vulnerability – he still possesses a core of childlike awe. The idea he’s prepared to sabotage his security because he has witnessed another being’s suffering suddenly makes sense.

The rendering of awe has always been a pivotal part of Spielberg’s filmmaking. Disclosure Day isn’t necessarily a sequel to his early masterwork Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977), but undoubtedly there are echoes and resonances with that earlier film and his wondrous fantasia E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982). These connections are consciously embedded in the film in the lighting and design, particularly in two key scenes that directly refer to one of the most haunting sequences in all of Spielberg’s oeuvre, where the child is taken up by aliens in Close Encounters. It’s impossible not to be reminded of the chilling scenes of E.T.’s capture by government agents when we glimpse the footage of the Wardex agents interrogating and experimenting on the aliens in Disclosure Day.

There’s too much going on in this film, as if the filmmakers never quite trust the simplicity of the story they wanted to tell. That anxiety is reflected in John Williams’ self-derivative score, which becomes increasingly bombastic. The supporting cast can’t do anything with their roles, which are lazily sketched and written. There’s also a desultory subplot about the possible outbreak of a world war, although we never sense any real threat of nuclear Armageddon.

When Spielberg concentrates on the story’s central question – how we might approach other alien beings with empathy – the film comes close to achieving beauty. There is a real power in the final disclosure, where we see how the world might respond to such a revelation. It’s fantastical – even absurd – but as with Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Jurassic Park and E.T., there’s a real pleasure in giving ourselves over to wonderment. Being reminded of the awe one felt as a child at the hope for magic and fantasy is no small thing. It’s one of Spielberg’s greatest gifts as a filmmaker.

Spielberg has nothing to prove. Four years ago he directed The Fabelmans, one of his greatest films. It’s an autobiographical film about a young man discovering his vocation for film, and its elegiac and humane script was co-written with Tony Kushner. Spielberg and Kushner collaborated on 2012’s Lincoln, a film of great ambition but formal inconsistency. The Fabelmans left behind the grand sweep of history and mined the essence of what ignites inspiration and how talent is both shaped and compromised by familial loyalty and conflict, to create a tender, mature work. I don’t think a young person could have looked back so forensically on the pain visited on a child by divorce yet been so unequivocally generous to both parents. It is remarkably free of bitterness – the work of filmmakers who trusted their story and intuition.

The opening scene of The Fabelmans is of the young director-to-be being taken to his first film, Cecil B. DeMille’s overblown epic The Greatest Show on Earth. The child becomes obsessed with how the director managed to convincingly show a train colliding with a car on screen. In that child’s working out of how to achieve those effects we see the emergence of filmmaking instinct and talent.

Spielberg is still trying to make The Greatest Show on Earth. In the final scenes of Disclosure Day, he almost gets there. Yet that first experience might be as much a millstone as it is an inspiration: Disclosure Day doesn’t need the train crash, the car chases, the implausible shoot-’em-up games. They mar its effectiveness and compromise its story. This film is a very particular kind of failure: the work of a great filmmaker trying to second-guess himself.

I’m not alone in considering The Fabelmans a great film, but it was a commercial flop. It’s possible that, even after all these years, that box-office failure spooked Spielberg. Maybe it’s the price that comes with chasing popular success. In trying to please everyone, you forget how to listen to your instincts.

Disclosure Day is screening in cinemas nationally.

spielberg-et-interview-age-of-celebrity-:
Veteran interviewees are forever trotting out the same anecdotes in response to unoriginal questions – until one fearless disruptor dared ask if ET had moist skin

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

For the most part, Steven Spielberg has avoided most of the indignities of the modern day press tour. He hasn’t had to subject himself to any spicy chicken wings, or summon any witticisms when presented with a cloche-covered sausage roll. Unlike many other celebrities, he hasn’t chosen to promote Disclosure Day by answering softball questions while simultaneously fashioning a Lionel Richie-style clay approximation of himself for YouTube. For this he should be applauded.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Instead, Spielberg has spent this promotional cycle on something more suited to his stature. A maestro tour, if you will, on which he gets to position Disclosure Day against a body of work that is second to none. Publications have run long oral histories about his entire career. He was a guest during the prestigious final week of Stephen Colbert’s talkshow. He was interviewed by the New York Times about the exact texture of ET’s skin.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

That last one really did happen. A clip of the interview has gone mildly viral, featuring interviewer Rachel Abrams straight-out asking Spielberg “Was ET slimy or dry?” before suggesting that this is a decades-old conundrum that had long foxed everyone she knows. To his credit, Spielberg answered the question with tremendous gusto, if a little bewilderment. “ET was a little moist but never slimy,” he replied, after shaking his head. He then explained that, while “ET was only dry when he got sick”, it would be wrong to call him slimy. Xenomorphs are slimy, he pointed out. “ET never had tendrils of drool.”

Now, why Abrams asked this question is another matter. The good faith interpretation is that Spielberg has spent the last half-century in the public eye, and been interviewed so many times that he has developed a tendency to become something of an anecdote jukebox, reeling out the hits unprompted. This is something that afflicts only the truly famous but it can be debilitating. There are, after all, only so many times that a person can hear Ringo Starr’s “I thought it was you three” story.

Viewed from this perspective, there is real value in extracting genuinely new information from A-list celebrities. The fact that ET is now canonically moist maybe adds something to the cultural conversation that wasn’t there before? If so, the question deserves to be commended. However, if Abrams just asked a deliberately dumb question to the director of Schindler’s List because she knew it would get clicks, then that is another matter entirely.

We must also question why the subject arose in the first place. Abrams’s justification that it was in the public interest, since it had long been a discussion within her social group, rings a little false, because presumably everyone in her social group has eyes and can see perfectly well for themselves that ET isn’t slimy. It’s right there! All through the film! We know what texture ET’s skin is because ET is a visible character throughout the entire movie. As everybody knows, ET’s skin is clearly pleather or pleather-adjacent, like the skin of a Mediterranean grandmother. There is certainly no slime there. If there was, then the film would have included a scene of Drew Barrymore skidding about in ET’s slug trail, or the climatic hug scene between ET and Elliott would have ended with Elliott looking down at his slime-covered clothes and tutting, “These were new on today.”

But none of that happened so we can reasonably ascertain that ET isn’t slimy and this was a stupid question to ask. Still, the new media landscape loves nothing more than a replicable format, so perhaps this is something we’ll see more of in the future. For all we know, the New York Times is working on a series called Famous Auteurs Answer Self-Evident Questions as we speak, and this time next week they’ll drag Martin Scorsese in to ask if Jake LaMotta had 12 ears, or Paul Thomas Anderson to ask if Daniel Day-Lewis is secretly a mouse. For the avoidance of doubt, I hope this happens.
spooky_maryland_attractions:
Jack-o’-lanterns are gearing up for creepy, snaggletoothed smiles, pumpkin spice lattes galore are on the horizon and haunted houses are dusting off their doorsteps.

Fall is here along with the spooky season when countless kiddos and adults will test their courage at haunted attractions or run for the hills. But Halloween-leaning fun doesn’t have to be synonymous with bed-wetting fear.

Little tykes still have a chance to get in on the entertainment whether simply dressing up at an event or exploring a corn maze.

These attractions and events across Maryland allow kids to participate without the risk of getting too scared.

Attendees at the ZooBOO! Festival, which kicks off Friday, are encouraged to wear family-friendly costumes while participating in mostly free activities throughout the Maryland Zoo. There will be face painting, sack races, costume contests on Saturdays and Sundays, and food trucks and vendors.

ZooBOO!, which takes place most weekends in October, is included with the price of zoo admission or a membership. Children under 2 are free. Tickets range from $28 to $33.

The Maryland Zoo is located at 1 Safari Place in Baltimore.

Survival isn’t guaranteed at the Terror Trail in Davidsonville, which is recommended for courageous kids over 8 years old. The Boo Loop, where no one will jump out, is designed for the younger kids, with static displays and a scavenger hunt with prizes. These offerings are only open Fridays and Saturdays throughout October. Attendees are invited to dress up as they enjoy the attractions and food truck.

Terror Trail tickets are $30 and Boo Loop tickets cost $10. Proceeds support the Arundel Volunteer Fire Department Station 7, and ticket discounts are available to first responders, teachers, veterans, medical professionals and those who bring a canned food item.

The AVFD Station 7 Terror Trail is located at 2701 Davidsonville Road in Davidsonville.

Until Nov. 8, families can head to Weber’s Cider Mill Farm in Parkville to experience all things fall with a smidge of spooky, including a family-friendly skeleton walk, a hay maze, farm animals and play structures. For an additional cost, kids can have their faces painted or get a glitter tattoo. And for your fall food fill, apple cider donuts, apple slushies and more are on the menu.

Tickets are required for anyone 2 years old and up. Weekday festival admission starts at $12, while the weekend costs $15. Or you can get unlimited entry on weekdays with a season pass that’ll run you $35. Admission pricing is subject to change throughout the season.

Weber’s Cider Mill Farm is located at 2526 Proctor Lane in Parkville.

For a controlled encounter with the dead, the Burying Ground at Westminster Hall is usually open daily for self-guided tours from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., according to Westminster Hall’s website. Edgar Allan Poe’s large marble grave site is a popular stop within the grounds. There are also catacombs that can only be explored through a guided tour.

For $5 a person, Westminster Hall is hosting a catacombs tour on Oct. 31 from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. Baltimore Heritage also provides a tour of the catacombs for $10-$15.

Westminster Hall and Burying Grounds are located at 551 W. Fayette St. in Baltimore.

Baltimore City Recreation and Parks is offering an opportunity to drive through terror on Oct. 16 from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m. Pack the kiddos in the car, choose your time slot and schedule a date with horror as a portion of the 745-acre Druid Hill Park is turned into a roadway of doom. The event is open to all ages, and there are subtle ways to maximize or minimize the scares.

For an intense, scary experience, keep the doors unlocked and the windows down. For a less frightening time, make sure to do the opposite. Keep at least a half-gallon of gas in your tank since you’ll have to wait in line in your car to enter.

Each car costs $13.

Druid Hill Park is located at 3001 E. Drive in Baltimore.

starbucks-korea-tank-day-furore:
Coffee chain to hold ‘historical awareness’ training after backlash against marketing campaign that evoked 1980 military crackdown.

Save

Share

Starbucks stores in South Korea will close early next week so employees can receive history instruction after a botched marketing campaign triggered a public backlash, the US coffee chain’s local operator has said.

The move comes after Starbucks Korea provoked a furore last month with a marketing campaign that evoked one of the most painful chapters in the country’s march to democracy.

The coffee giant’s use of the wording “Tank Day” and “5/18” to promote a range of coffee tumblers outraged South Koreans by evoking a military crackdown on May 18, 1980, against a pro-democracy uprising in Gwangju.

Starbucks Korea CEO Son Jung-hyun was fired over his role in the PR disaster, which Starbucks’s global headquarters said was “unintentional” but “never should have happened”.

In a statement on Monday, Starbucks Korea operator Shinsegae Group said all outlets nationwide will close at 3pm (06:00 GMT) on Monday next week so employees can participate in “historical awareness and social sensitivity” training.

Shinsegae Group said the move will mark the first time that stores have shut early all at once across the country since Starbucks launched in South Korea in 1999.

Shinsegae Group Chairman Chung Yong-jin and top executives will separately undergo training on Wednesday, the retail conglomerate said.

“The move is intended to take the incident as a lesson and prevent similar cases from recurring across the group in the future,” Shinsegae Group said.

The Gwangju Uprising was a major catalyst in the democratisation of South Korea, which held its first free elections in decades in 1987 after a succession of military-led administrations.

Led by student protesters opposed to the rule of military strongman Chun Doo-hwan, the democratisation movement was violently crushed when Chun deployed the military to retake control of the southwestern city.

Government figures put the death toll at more than 200 people, but activists and historians have estimated the true figure to be more than 2,000.

South Korea is home to more than 2,000 Starbucks outlets, making the country the second biggest overseas market for the Seattle-based chain after China.

starmer_arson_conviction:
Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has said he is pleased "justice has been done" after two men were convicted of arson attacks on property connected to him.

Ukrainian national Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Ukrainian-born Romanian national Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were found guilty on Monday of conspiring to carry out arson attacks on property and a car in 2025.

Shortly after the verdicts, a BBC Panorama investigation revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks.

Speaking from the G7 summit in France, Starmer said he was "very pleased for my family's sake" that the men were convicted.

He told reporters: "Obviously it was a bad attack, and all the details have now come out in court and justice has been done".

But Sir Keir said the attack on his property needed to be seen in the "broader context" of Russia's war in Ukraine.

He cited Ukrainian successes in regaining territory and the impact of sanctions on Russia, and said it was the moment for the G7 to "ramp up the pressure" on Moscow.

The UK has announced a fresh wave of 70 sanctions on Russia targeting the Kremlin's "shadow fleet" used to move Russian oil and gas, and the finance networks used to evade Western sanctions.

That decision followed the boarding of an alleged Russian shadow fleet oil tanker in the English Channel on Sunday.

Prosecutors found the arson attacks were carried out in 2025 after a suspect was recruited online by Russian-speaking Telegram user "El Money" who promised him payment.

A BBC Panorama investigation uncovered evidence suggesting he is a 23-year-old Russian diplomat Evgeny Lyukshin, the son of a senior official who has been schooled in information warfare by spies and propagandists.

The BBC found that "El Money" offered Russian citizenship in return for other attacks, and glorified Putin in messages. Accounts based in Russian also spread disinformation on the motive for the attacks.

Earlier on Tuesday, Sir Richard Moore, the former head of MI6, warned the Russian President Vladimir Putin is "trying to intimidate" the UK with sabotage, arson and cyber attacks on British streets.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Richard said proxy attacks showed Britain needed to have a "discussion" about "the balance of resourcing for security and defence".

The government and intelligence services have not yet said the Kremlin was behind the incident, but Sir Richard commended the BBC's reporting and said "we shouldn't be surprised at all" if Russian involvement was confirmed.

Sir Richard claimed Putin was under pressure over the war in Ukraine which meant he was "quite keen to expand the battlefield a bit" by using sabotage, cyber attacks and arson in the hope it would be "disruptive, distracting and intimidating to those of us who are supporting Ukraine".

Sir Keir said in April that "the use of proxies by hostile states in this country is a growing concern and a real concern", and the UK must "deal with malign state actors".

Sir Richard, who left MI6 last year, said the UK should address the concern by "doubling down" on its support of Ukraine, improving cyber security and investing in "good intelligence" to disrupt Russia's activity.

"There is a criminal justice element" to tackling the threat, he added, saying "thugs" who were recruited online must "go down for a very long stretch" if found to have acted as proxies for hostile states.

It follows the resignations of Defence Secretary John Healey and Armed Forces Minister Al Carns last week, who quit the government over a dispute with Sir Keir over funding for the military.

Writing on X on Monday evening, Carns said the arson attacks and subsequent disinformation campaign showed the UK needed to rethink its approach to defence.

He said defence was "the thread underneath everything now" and the incidents showed "why resilience matters".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch also condemned the arson attacks and said "no one should face intimidation, threats or attacks because they hold public office".

She added: "Democracy is settled at the ballot box, not through fear or violence and definitely not through foreign interference from hostile countries."

starmer_defence_spending_claim:
Earlier this year the former prime minister told MPs that ministers were increasing defence spending by Â£270bn

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, the Wales Office and the Ministry of Defence (MoD) used misleading figures about how much the country would spend on defence, a watchdog has said.

In March Sir Keir told MPs that ministers were increasing defence spending by Â£270bn. The two other departments later repeated similar claims in June.

But the UK Statistics Authority say that is wrong, as the figure is the proposed overall amount the government plans to spend between 2025 and 2029. The Wales Office deleted a post on X that had contained the claim.

A UK government spokesperson said: "We have previously acknowledged this phrasing and took immediate steps to ensure it was not replicated."

Downing Street and Sir Keir's office said they had nothing to add. The authority said steps taken by the Wales Office and the MoD should reduce the risk of the claim being made again in future.

Sir Keir resigned from Downing Street in July, when he was succeeded by Andy Burnham.

In March Sir Keir told the House of Commons liaison committee: "We have already committed to 2.5% in 2027, and we will hit that. That means that, in this Parliament, we will spend Â£270bn more on defence than we would otherwise have done."

Similar claims were made by an MoD spokesman in June, and by the Wales Office X account, which said on 3 June: "The UK government is increasing defence spending by Â£270bn over this Parliament to strengthen our national security."

BBC Wales was told that the figure originated in the MoD, rather than the Wales Office, which was led by the then-Welsh secretary Jo Stevens at the time.

The Wales Office, which is a part of the UK government, oversees the system of devolution and aims to be a voice for Wales within Westminster.

In a letter to Tory shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge, UK Statistics Authority's interim chair, Penny Young, said: "We agree that it is incorrect and misleading to describe the Â£270bn as an increase in defence spending over the course of this Parliament, or to describe it as an extra Â£270bn.

"The Â£270bn represents the proposed overall spending on defence over the lifetime of the current Parliament, from 2025-26 to 2028-29."

According to the letter, the Wales Office told the authority the figure used "was a mistake and was amended as soon as it was noticed".

"In addition, Wales Office has told us it has reviewed its press office lines in relation to this topic, and its quality assurance process for press lines, to ensure that this mistake is not replicated elsewhere," Young said.

She added: "The MoD has taken steps to ensure that future communications use precise and consistent language when presenting defence spending figures."

Conservative Shadow Wales Secretary Mims Davies MP said: "At a time of growing global instability, the public deserves honesty and transparency about our defence budget.

"Labour ministers and civil servants in the Wales Office should be setting out the facts, not presenting figures in a way that risks misleading people."

By SAM FRANCIS

PRESENTED BY

Send tips here | Subscribe for free | Politics at Sam and Anne’s podcast | Listen to Playbook and view in your browser

Good Friday morning. This is Sam Francis.

DAN TO THE RESCUE: Keir Starmer’s grip on power this morning looks weaker than ever after John Healey’s resignation blew a hole through the PM’s strongest case for staying in No. 10: that in a dangerous world, he could still be trusted on national security. Healey’s central accusation, that Starmer had been “unable, and the Treasury unwilling” to fund the nation’s defense, was damaging enough on its own. But it was quickly followed by the resignations of Armed Forces Minister Al Carns and Healey’s PPSs Pamela Nash and Rachel Hopkins. With the Makerfield by-election and Andy Burnham’s expected return to parliament six days away, the threat to the prime minister feels close at hand. Dan Jarvis will need all the luck he can get.

Entering the lions’ den: Jarvis took up the poisoned chalice prestigious role of defense secretary at 9 p.m. and could have a hard landing. MoD officials confirmed late last night that his first outing will be a visit to the drone factory in Swindon later this morning— originally intended as the triumphant stage for the Defence Investment Plan launch, which now is presumably off, despite the fact that invites had already been sent out to major defense firms.

Watching brief: Plans were understandably in flux late last night as officials tried to salvage something presentable, with talk of a possible pooled camera and Jarvis potentially fronting up to the media in some form unconfirmed. FWIW, this is the same Swindon drone site my colleague Esther Webber reported last month had its opening held back so the prime minister could cut the ribbon alongside the DIP. The PM is no longer coming.

**A message from Palantir: At Palantir, what we value is helping our customers deliver better public services. Our software is driving up NHS operations, speeding up cancer diagnosis, tackling crime, preventing domestic violence and helping our armed forces protect our security. 17 per cent of our workforce is based here in the UK - and that’s what makes them tick.**

If anyone is able to ask Jarvis a question … they may well ask whether the DIP deal rejected by Healey is going ahead exactly as planned, or whether Jarvis accepted the job on the condition he could have a say on the detail (or at least read it top to bottom). Expect similar questions to Peter Kyle on the morning broadcast round and at the No. 10 Lobby briefing at 11.30 a.m.

DIP (probably) happens: The obvious clue in this is that No. 10 has rowed in hard behind the DIP as set out. In his exchange with Healey, Starmer insisted the current plan remained live, describing it as delivering “an unprecedented increase in defense spending in a sustainable way.” Exactly when anyone will actually see it, though, remains an open question ahead of next week’s G7 summit. And will any potential successor as PM stick to such a controversial plan? As Jessica Elgot points in the Guardian, Andy Burnham — should he make it from Wigan to SW1 — faces the exact same choices that drove Healey out. He’s not exactly put defense and foreign policy at the top of his pitches so far.

Healey big problem: The real hammer blow from Healey’s resignation was his implication that the prime minister wanted to give more funding to the Defence Investment Plan, but was too weak to pull rank on his chancellor. “This isn’t the beginning of the end, it has gone way beyond that,” one senior Labour adviser told the FT. Labour MP Graham Stringer told the Telegraph Starmer is a “dead prime minister walking.”

It’s just a flesh wound: Remember, Starmer wanted the DIP to be a central pillar of his legacy — a fully costed blueprint to show Labour was serious about the armed forces and that the U.K. was stepping up on the world stage. Instead, the plan’s credibility is now in tatters, despite Starmer wrestling somewhere between £10 billion and £13.5 billion from the Treasury — depending on who you listen to.

Can anyone solve it? But there is a deeper question as to whether any PM can produce a DIP that survives contact with the U.K.’s current finances while adequately girding us for a possible apocalypse. As the Guardian’s Pippa Crerar and Dan Sabbagh note, costs have spiraled under successive commitments from both Tory and Labour governments, compounded by longstanding weaknesses in MoD financial management. My colleague Emilio Casalicchio points out the original sin of the DIP was when the MoD discovered it had underestimated how much funding it needed as part of the Strategic Defence Review to the tune of £28 billion over four years. The Treasury found that figure simply unaffordable to find all at once and the haggling over that has led us here.

Although here’s a silver lining: Meg Hillier, the architect of last summer’s benefit cuts rebellion, told the i Paper’s Will Hazell that Labour MPs are now ready to back welfare reforms, following Alan Milburn’s youth joblessness review. Milburn himself is meeting a delegation from Singapore’s Ministry of Manpower in London today to learn why the NEET rate is 3.8 percent compared to Britain’s 13.5 percent.

Turner round for the books: Retired Air Marshal Andrew Turner told the FT the “DIP was unaffordable, which made it unannounceable” but argued it was “entirely plausible a new government and a new cabinet” might be able to make it work. Best of luck.

Brassed off: Do not rule out further departures today — albeit perhaps not from ministerial ranks. Chief of the Defence Staff Richard Knighton is now on “resignation watch,” according to the Daily Mail’s Jason Groves and Mark Nicol, after it emerged he had written directly to Starmer over concerns about funding for the DIP.

Straight out of central casting: One can only assume Knighton and the other chiefs will be on the blower to Jarvis, who arrived in Parliament in 2011 with what the BBC’s Brian Wheeler once dubbed “the dream CV” for a politician. Fourteen years in the Parachute Regiment, rising to major, an MBE and tours in Northern Ireland, Kosovo, Iraq, Afghanistan and Sierra Leone — before becoming the first officer since WWII to resign his commission to fight a by‑election in 2011. During the Corbyn years, he was often cast as the moderate the Tories would most fear. In the end, he sat out the leadership race, citing his young family.

Soft (boiled) power: Between 2018 and 2022 he also served as mayor of South Yorkshire, juggling the combined authority with his Commons role before giving up on double-jobbing and moving into government as security minister after the 2024 landslide. Those who played Playbook’s 2024 Christmas quiz will no doubt remember Jarvis also keeps rescue chickens, re-homed from the British Hen Welfare Trust, and brings eggs into Parliament to give as gifts. Perhaps he should start with the chiefs of the Army, Navy and RAF.

And why not give an egg to … Carns, who is on another interview round — this time post-resignation. He chatted to ITV’s Good Morning Britain a short time ago and should pop up on LBC at 7.20 a.m., the Today program at 8.10 a.m. and GB News at 8.45 a.m.

Time Healeys all wounds: Some observers have speculated Healey might want a tilt at the top job himself, although allies of Healey told the Sun there was “absolutely” no chance of him running for the Labour leadership. The Daily Mail hears the same. Though the Telegraph’s Ben Riley-Smith reckons Healey pulling the rug from under the PM — making him less able to contest any leadership challenge — could see the ex-defense secretary back in the MoD within weeks, should a leadership switch happen.

SCOOP — BLITZ SPIRIT: The prime minister is now facing the embarrassing prospect of explaining to allies at next week’s G7, including Donald Trump, why his own defense secretary felt he was not doing enough to keep his country safe. But international diplomacy also gives Starmer a chance to seize back some of the initiative. My colleague Esther Webber has caught a glimpse of internal documents showing the prime minister plans to roll out a blitz of announcements at the summit in France: on migration and Ukraine, as well as possible further Russian sanctions. In particular, she hears there could be a push to expand the U.K.’s Sandhurst deal with the French, designed to tackle small boats.

Trump card: The leaked details also suggest a coordinated effort to get Trump back on side in the run‑up to next month’s NATO summit in Ankara, with the push being led out of the U.K.’s Washington embassy. The U.S. president isn’t known for his love of NATO, nor does he tend to respond well to perceived pressure from allies — so, good luck, as they say, with that. Given the perceived wisdom in Westminster is that this may be Starmer’s final turn on the world stage, Playbook would gently suggest this could be the perfect chance for him to tell Trump what he really thinks. What could go wrong?

COOP, THERE IT IS: While the center of government continues in the trenches, the FCDO was keen to point out that Yvette Cooper is still working the diplomatic circuit, laying the groundwork for the G7. Cooper is in Paris to discuss Israel and Palestine with the French foreign secretary and civil society groups. Cooper announced sanctions on the settlers in the West Bank earlier in the week.

HEADACHE OF STATE: As flagged in yesterday morning’s lengthy spotted list, a fair chunk of Westminster — MPs, whips, No.10 staff, SpAds and, er, the Lobby — were out for a night full of cocktails on Wednesday. Playbook salutes everyone who got through yesterday’s avalanche of news nursing a hangover.

ALL QUIET ON THE WIGAN FRONT: The Labour and Reform campaigns in Makerfield are both hunkering down with no planned appearances today — but the most consequential by-election in a generation continues to make news.

SCOOP — SHIFTING FOCUS: A focus group for POLITICO in an Ashton-in-Makerfield pub has found Makerfield’s voters are angry and really want someone to feel their pain. And while some voters think Andy Burnham might make a difference, Reform UK and Nigel Farage are winning converts who want to  “shake up” the system.

Faith no more: Crime, immigration and the cost of living dominated concerns among a politically mixed group of voters — but the prevailing mood was one of deep cynicism. One participant, Bob, summed it up: in more than 90 years of voting, he had yet to encounter a “bloody good” politician. Read the full report by Tim Ross.

STICKING TO THE SCRIPT: The House Mag’s Sienna Rodgers has managed to get her hands on a Labour canvassing script that door-knockers are using in Makerfield, which intriguingly instructs them to say they are “out campaigning for Andy Burnham” rather than Labour. There are also several script cues that might raise eyebrows among Burnham’s soft-left power base, including telling potential voters that “Andy supports reducing net migration” and he believes “it is right to pursue root and branch reform” of the immigration system.

WIGAN OUT: Andy Burnham’s closest friends advised him to turn down the Makerfield seat, given how hard it looked to win, according to a fun deep-dive by the Guardian’s Jessica Elgot.

PARLIAMENT: Not sitting.

SCOOP —BANNED WAGON: My colleague Mizy Clifton has firmed up that the other pillar of Starmer’s legacy push, a ban on under-16s accessing social media, will be announced next week. Live-streaming, disappearing messages and functionalities that allow communication with adult strangers will also be banned for under-16s, and a social media curfew for 16-to-17-year-olds is also being considered. One slight snag: the definition of what counts as social media hasn’t yet been nailed down.

SCOOP — EARLY BIRDS: The Liberal Democrats are holding their first candidate “away day” today, training 28 prospective parliamentary candidates already picked for target seats. The party has moved earlier than ever on selections, part of a broader push to put itself on a more serious footing for a return to government. Playbook has been told Sheffield Hallam hopeful, 29-year-old councillor Sophie Crossthorn, recently named on the Sunday Times Young Power List, and South West Hertfordshire candidate Matt Sanders, a former Lib Dem adviser and one‑time sparring partner of Dominic Cummings during the coalition years.

Wetsuits at the ready: For more on how the Lib Dems have quietly rebuilt their press operation and central machine while Westminster tears itself apart (see previous newsletters for details), check out this long‑read by *checks notes* me. Anyone hoping that the Lib Dems getting serious about the next election means fewer Ed Davey stunts may want to look away now. The wetsuit is not going anywhere.

OWNING THE LIBS: Liberal think tank Bright Blue today publishes a cross-party essay collection arguing liberalism needs a reset after a populist decade. The book, including chapters from MPs like Liam Byrne, suggests a range of new policies, from ending the triple lock on pensions to introducing a “baby bonus” for all new parents and drilling for more north sea oil, to promoting Snus packets as an alternative to smoking cigarettes.

Fractured politics: Bright Blue is also hosting a talk at 3 p.m. with friend of the newsletter, psephologist Rob Ford, to discuss whether two-party politics is over.

UP CLOSE: Gary Klopfenstein, a U.S. fraudster accused of illicitly funding Robert Jenrick’s Conservative leadership campaign, met one of Jenrick’s current aides, Sam Armstrong, as part of a group to discuss the future of the Tory party before the alleged donations were made, the FT’s Rachel Rees reports. At the time, Klopfenstein had not been convicted of fraud. Jenrick’s lawyers told the FT the politician and his team complied with all electoral laws and Jenrick himself had no contact with Klopfenstein.

ON YER BIKE: Ministers want 60 percent of pupils in England cycling or walking to school by 2035 as part of Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander’s boost for active travel. The Guardian has a write-up.

CHAMPIONS! Economic Secretary to the Treasury Rachel Blake will announce in a speech to the Co-op Congress that she will appoint a champion for the co-op sector, with a recruitment process to follow.

WHAT THE GOVERNMENT WANTS TO TALK ABOUT: School students will learn how to plant a wildflower-friendly garden according to long-awaited plans for a natural history GCSE. The government has launched a 12-week consultation on the proposed subject content.

RETURNED: The party suspension of Lib Dem peer Chris Rennard has been lifted, as spotted by BylineTimes’ Josiah Mortimer. The peer had the whip removed in February after the party launched a new investigation into claims he sexually harassed female members. A Lib Dem spokesperson said the party’s independent complaints process decided to lift the suspension while their investigation is ongoing.

ENTERING THE RACE: Labour MP Steve Race is in discussions to take over the Labour Growth Group, my colleague Hannah Brenton reports. The MP for Exeter has floated taking the centrist group forward, after fellow MP Chris Curtis announced he was stepping down.

NOW LISTEN TO THIS: On this week’s episode of Westminster Insider, Sascha O’Sullivan asks: What is the point of political protest?

And keep your ears peeled For a bonus episode of Westminster Insider landing Sunday. Jack Blanchard was dragged away from his D.C. post by the tantalizing assignment of finding out who is the real Andy Burnham.

FUEL FOR THE WEEKEND: The King’s Birthday Honors list will be published on Saturday, with no doubt some political appointees. The Mirror’s Lizzy Buchan reports that Rugby Union star and motor neurone disease fundraiser Kevin Sinfield has been granted a knighthood.

THE KIDS AREN’T ALRIGHT: Young people are increasingly pessimistic about their future, with IPPR analysis finding that one in 14 young people believe they are likely to become long-term unemployed. This figure stood at just one in 50 in 2015.

SAFE AS HOUSES: Former Housing Secretary Angela Rayner is due to give a fireside chat from 3.50 p.m at the Propertymark One conference at Excel centre. Before she gets on stage Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride is due to give a speech, where he is expected to tell the room full of housing developers the Tory’s flagship plans to scrap stamp duty could mean 200,000 extra homes built over five years — a 25 percent boost on current building rates — based on modelling by the Adam Smith Institute.

COURT CIRCULAR: Four Palestine Action activists will be sentenced at 10 a.m. at Woolwich Crown Court after being found guilty of criminal damage at a U.K. site of Israel-based defense firm Elbit Systems. The hearing will see the judge decide whether there was a terrorism connection to their offense — despite the jury not being told of this possibility.

AND BREATHE: After two nights of chaos, protests held in some areas of Northern Ireland passed without incident following a “robust” police response, the BBC reports.

NUCLEAR OPTION: Donald Trump claimed that the U.S. has “ended the war” with Iran after asserting the two sides had agreed to a “very strong memorandum of understanding” including Tehran agreeing “never to have a nuclear weapon.” Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson has said the country did not yet reach a final decision on any agreement, according to state media. CNN has a live page covering the (ever-changing) details. Stop me if you think that you have heard this one before.

SCROOGE MCDUCK VIBES: Elon Musk is on the cusp of becoming the world’s first trillionaire as SpaceX debuts on the Nasdaq today at  a price of $135 a share. Fortune magazine has more on our brave new world.

BROMANCE: The World Cup is bringing together two potential 2028 presidential candidates  at Friday’s U.S. opener against Paraguay in LA, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and California Gov. Gavin Newsom sitting in the same box at kickoff at SoFi Stadium. Romantic! My POLITICO colleagues have the deets.

WHO SMELT IT, DEALT IT: The Pentagon resumed “normal operations” on Thursday after part of the U.S. defense headquarters went into lockdown in response to what spokesperson Sean Parnell called an “air quality issue” that required “precautionary measures” while officials investigated. Subsequent testing, Parnell wrote on X, found no issues.

**A message from Palantir: Palantir software is helping to deliver better patient care - including 110,000 additional operations to date, a 15% reduction in discharge delays, a 6.8% increase in the number of patients finding out whether they need cancer treatment within 28 days, and the safe removal of 797,728 patients from waiting lists. The same software is helping police forces in England to tackle crime too. The Metropolitan Police have used it to identify misconduct within the force and arrest officers. It has helped Bedfordshire Police to reduce the time taken to check whether someone’s partner has a history of violence by 85 per cent, identifying 1,000 vulnerable women in a single year. It is also being used to bring organised crime gangs such as F*** the Police to justice. A stronger NHS and safer streets. Values we can all agree on.**

starmer_phone_ban:
Tech companies such as Apple and Google have been asked by the UK government to block access to naked images on smartphones and other devices for under-18s.

Sir Keir Starmer has told firms to either activate built-in features or update software to prevent children from taking, sending or viewing sexually explicit images on their phones and other devices.

Speaking at London Tech Week, the prime minister said: "This is not an impossible challenge. These are some of the most innovative companies in the world and I believe they can solve it."

The government said it will bring forward legislation to force firms to activate the features if they do not comply voluntarily within three months.

This could include fines or, as a last resort, criminal liability for companies which do not comply.

The prime minister said the changes would apply to both existing and newly-sold smartphones and tablets in the UK.

"Legislation could cover operating system providers and others in the supply chain, such as retailers, and will not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age," he said.

In response, a Google spokesperson said it was "deeply committed to protecting children online."

"We are working constructively with UK partners to find effective, privacy-preserving solutions that deter the spread of harmful content while ensuring a safe digital environment for young people."

Apple has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.

It is unclear what action firms will take in response to Monday's announcement.

But a number of tech companies already have methods in place to try and prevent children from seeing or sharing nude imagery.

Apple recently began asking UK iPhone users to verify their age in a bid to make sure only adults access apps and sites for people intended for users over 18.

It also offers a service blocking nude imagery for children on several of its own apps including iMessage.

Its "Communication Safety" feature warns children who have a Child Account when they send or receive images and videos containing nudity across Messages, AirDrop and FaceTime.

The tool, which is turned on by default for those under 18 with a Child Account and which parents can enable for teens in iCloud Family settings, lets children report nude images or videos to Apple and also points them towards help and support.

Google's own Messages app, running across Android handsets, has similar settings in place to blur sensitive content for users supervised by a parent or guardian.

A number of third-party companies have also developed tech to detect and block children from capturing or sharing nude images.

The government has highlighted an AI tool developed by safety tech firm SafeToNet as showing how firms can safely scale on-device detection and blocking of nude images for children.

However some believe the government's call for firms to expand their own tools to apps they do not operate, and turn them on by default for all users, could impact user privacy - such as by making adults verify their age in order to opt out of or disable nude image blocking.

The UK has also already introduced laws to try to protect children online. Foremost is the Online Safety Act - laws and duties online platforms must follow - implemented and enforced by media regulator Ofcom.

However, child safety campaigners have urged the government to go further to stop children seeing or sharing nude images, amid concerns about online grooming and sextortion.

The government said 91% of online child sexual abuse reports recorded in 2024 contained self-generated content from children themselves and the average child now views pornography by the age of 13.

The plans would not prevent adults – anyone over 18 – from accessing naked imagery.

The news comes as Starmer is believed to be preparing to announce a crackdown on children's access to social media within days, including a speech on potential policy expected next week.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said tech companies "have a moral duty to act by making it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images. If they don't, we will legislate".

Technology Secretary Liz Kendall said: "Companies should switch these protections on by default, for every child, on every device. We are giving them three months to show us that they will do the right thing."

Andy Burrows, chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation, welcomed what he said was "an important step forward for child protection".

However, he criticised government communication around the announcement, alongside one of a potential ban on social media for young people.

"Number 10 needs to start urgently listening to experts and the evidence, rather than rush out hurried announcements for short-term expediency that will quickly unravel and continue to let tech firms off the hook for preventable harm," he said.

Following a national consultation, the UK is moving closer to restrictions on under-16s' social media use, with ministers consulting on measures ranging from age limits to bans on addictive platform features.

Silkie Carlo, director of Big Brother Watch, said: "Protecting children online is vital, but these are outrageous plans that will fail to address the underlying causes of online harm."

"Put simply, the Labour government is threatening ID checks for the internet. No-one in a democracy should need to show their passport just to get online."

Likewise, Open Rights Group have spoken of their concern of the infrastructure being expanded.

"This would turn every phone into a surveillance device," said Platform Power Programme Manager James Baker.

The government denies that the move would amount to surveillance.

However, Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, said it strongly supported the move, adding, "Time is up for big tech".

"Now government must focus on holding them to account to ensure this transformational change for young people's safety is quickly delivered," he said.

Labour MP Jess Phillips resigned as safeguarding minister at the Home Office earlier this year, accusing Sir Keir of being slow to threaten legislation on preventing children taking naked images of themselves, despite the technology being available.
