Congress faces a critical decision on the future of artificial intelligence as lawmakers debate potential regulations on Capitol Hill. Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the bipartisan push for guidelines.

Are we playing with the old playbook or a new playbook in the midterm elections this fall?

That’s unclear. It’s hard to determine simply because we’ve seen so much that’s "new" in politics lately.

Norms are cast aside. The American system quaked to its core in recent years. You’ve witnessed an American president win the election by prevailing in the Electoral College but losing the popular vote. To have that happen twice in 16 years (2000 and 2016) is astonishing, considering the fact that such an outcome only unfolded on three occasions before.

You then had a president impeached twice yet return to office a few years later. There was the Capitol riot as arguing continued about the 2020 election.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT

President Donald Trump arrives to host a dinner in the Rose Garden of the White House on Sept. 2, 2026, in Washington, D.C.  (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

If this is the old playbook, Democrats likely light up the scoreboard in November. The party of the president typically loses about 25 seats in a president’s first midterm. Midterm elections are frequently a referendum on the president. That’s why many Republicans are trying to keep President Donald Trump at arm’s length, considering that his polling numbers are anywhere from the mid-30s to 40% on a good day. Gas prices are high. Grocery prices are skyrocketing. The war in Iran lingers. There’s a trade war with one of America’s best allies.

On the old playbook, this portends a disaster for the GOP in this fall’s midterms.

But what if we’re using the new playbook?

President Trump — and sometimes Republicans aligned with him — have shown a remarkable resilience to defy political gravity and norms. Control of the House could come down to just a few seats. What if there are questions about election security and the validity of who won and lost? There’s redistricting. On paper, Republicans probably redrew about five to six seats nationwide in their favor.

If things are tight, we might not know which party wins the House on election night. Perhaps a few days down the road — if not later. That is, unless it’s a Democratic blowout.

And remember what we said a few moments ago about the president’s party losing so many seats in that first midterm? Yes, in a way, this is President Trump’s "first midterm." But not really. He experienced a midterm in 2018. Not that things went in the GOP’s favor that year. There’s no contemporary data on how the party of a president might perform after he’s been out of office and rallied to victory a few years later.

Also, the sheer reduction by both parties of seats which are in play mitigates political "waves" which crash across the political shoreline in House midterm races. Think 1994 and 2010 for Republicans. 2018 for Democrats. Thus, even though many of the factors favor the Democrats, the possibility remains it could be tough for the party to flip the House.

In 2018, the Democrats’ carried an approval rating of 44%. For this time around, it’s 37%. That rivals polling related to the president. In 2018, voters had had enough of President Trump and wanted a change. But because of the polling parity this year, it’s not so obvious that voters are so turned off by President Trump that they automatically gravitate to the Democrats.

Here’s another factor: turnout.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: WHAT’S IN AN ECONOMY?

The sun sets behind the U.S. Capitol Dome Sept. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

President Trump has worked hard to tell voters that he’s "on the ballot" this fall. That cuts two ways. President Trump’s presence on the ballot has historically driven people to the polls. In 2016, 60.1% of registered voters showed up. In 2020, an eye-popping 66.4% of all voters cast ballots. And in 2024, 64.3% of those registered to vote did so.

But considering the president’s unpopularity, the cognizance of voters that he’s "on the ballot" could also deter them from turning out. At least those who previously supported him. And those impacts ricochet down to House races. The president’s track record at turning out independent voters in races that count wasn’t great down ballot even as he won the White House in 2024.

Consider that, in the 2018 midterms, 50.1% of registered voters materialized. Just 46.1% voted in the 2022 midterms. It was 36.1% in the 2014 midterms — 41% in the historic 2010 midterms where Republicans won a record 63 House seats.

This "Trump on the ballot" initiative might not resound with voters. Especially since the president conceded — en route to his midterm convention in Dallas — that gas prices wouldn’t decrease until after the election. He also said the U.S. is stuck with the war in Iran through the midterms.

So, how do we know what to anticipate in November?

It’s really hard to read if there’s not a clear wave coming. The best way to postulate control of the House is by going race to race. And that is a painstaking process.

For instance, will Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo., have a district in which to run? Missouri Republicans tried to draw Cleaver out of his district earlier this year. Then a court ruled last week that the Show-Me State must use the old congressional districts, likely meaning that Cleaver was safe. Then another judge ruled that voters already cast ballots in primaries. So, the new maps were back, and Cleaver may be out.

All of this less than two months before the election.

MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING

Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol Dec. 16, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Is there a groundswell for Democrats in Iowa where the Senate seat and governor’s mansion are in jeopardy for Republicans? If that’s the case, Democrats might have a shot of claiming at least two if not three seats there: Republican Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Zach Nunn and maybe the seat that Rep. Ashley Hinson is vacating in her quest to become a senator.

How about Ohio? There are competitive gubernatorial and Senate contests. Does a Democratic surge boost Rep. Greg Landsman, D-Ohio? Do the accusations of spousal and child abuse bounce embattled Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio., in what is otherwise a relatively safe Republican seat?

Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, clung to her seat by fewer than 1,000 votes two years ago. But that was when President Trump carried the Buckeye State by 11 points and Kaptur’s district. Redistricting actually turned Kaptur’s turf slightly more in her favor. But the 80-year-old Kaptur was in a car wreck in August, inhibiting her ability to campaign. Is that a factor?

How well do Democrats perform in Virginia? Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., faces former Rep. Elaine Luria, D-Va., who she vanquished in 2022. Could former Rep. Tom Perriello, D-Va., who won in a 2008 upset in a differently-drawn district and promptly lost in 2010, unseat Rep. John McGuire, R-Va.?

Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, is retiring. Former Republican Maine Gov. Paul LePage is running for Golden’s seat. Does LePage benefit from Democratic chaos in the effort to unseat Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine? After all, President Trump won one of Maine’s three electoral votes in 2024, capturing that congressional district over former Vice President Kamala Harris.

We could bounce around the map, district to district, all day like this. But sans a wave, that’s what you must do to properly filet the House races.

Most conventional arrows point in the direction of Democrats winning the House this fall. Yet it probably shouldn’t be this close.

That’s why you have to go by the playbook.

The only question is if this is the old playbook or new playbook?

Reses built a close relationship with Vance starting with Vance’s successful 2022 Senate campaign in Ohio. Before that, he worked for Heritage Action, an affiliate of the conservative Heritage Foundation, and for Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. Reses was a constant presence on Vance’s campaign plane after Trump picked Vance as his running mate for vice president in 2024.

Several Cabinet members chimed in with praise for Reses.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, like Vance, is seen as a potential 2028 presidential contender, said Reses’ “intellect, leadership, and humor will be missed.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described Reses as having “been invaluable as we have fought to reshore critical industries and rebalance the economy from debt-driven consumption to production, saving, and investment.” And acting Attorney General Todd Blanche called Reses “tough, smart, hardworking, and loyal — the perfect combination to succeed in the Trump White House.”

Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s special envoy to the Middle East, alluded to Reses’ low-key stature and long-held aversion to the press.

Desperate US parents paying up to $20,000 a session for a procedure scientists say could be bogus

Autistic children as young as 18 months old are being injected with human stem cells derived from umbilical cords in unapproved, unproven and potentially harmful “treatments” that scientists warn are proliferating across the US under the active encouragement of the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr.

Clinics in Florida, Texas and other states are selling what they bill as “regenerative medicine” to families with autistic children who have intensive care needs. Parents who have taken their children through the process talked about their hopes and fears for a therapy that appears to be gaining ground in the US.

The procedure, which can involve the child being sedated with ketamine before receiving intravenous doses of millions of stem cells, costs up to $20,000 for each treatment. Families are often advised to return for regular top-ups.

Profoundly stressed parents are being wooed to the clinics with promises that a high-dose infusion of umbilical cord stem cells can lead to dramatic improvements in their children’s ability to speak, socialise, or avoid aggressive or self-harming behaviour. Yet there is no scientific evidence that the procedure works – the most comprehensive clinical trial staged so far, a placebo experiment conducted by Duke University, found insignificant benefits for most of the 180 children tested.

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) directly cautions parents that if they are being offered stem cell treatments outside an approved clinical trial, “you are likely being deceived and offered a product illegally”.

Though the Duke trial found minimal safety concerns with properly administered stem cell infusions, authorities continue to highlight the potential risks of under-regulated therapies.

The FDA warned in 2021 that it had received reports of complications following applications of umbilical cord stem cells and other related unapproved products leading to “blindness, tumor formation, infections and more”.

In his 16 months as the secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services within the Trump administration, Kennedy has undercut established scientific endeavors. He has fired thousands of federal health officials, dismissed longstanding scientific advisers, defunded $31m in autism-related research and attempted to shrink the recommended list of childhood vaccinations.

At the same time, largely unnoticed, he has given his backing to alternative health providers moving to fill the gap. Kennedy appeared by video link at the first two annual summits held in San Diego by Autism Health, a leading advocate of stem cell infusions for autistic kids.

At the summit last year, he told the audience that “your issue is no longer on the fringe”. At this year’s gathering in April, he promised to “create opportunities that extend across a lifetime” and to work with the stem cell providers “to drive solutions together”.

Those providers included Mike Chan, a Malaysian physician who presented the San Diego summit with a protocol that he practices from his clinic in Bangkok. It involves injecting autistic children in the buttocks with high doses of stem cells extracted from slaughtered sheep and rabbits.

“Man himself is an animal, the most intelligent animal. There are hundreds of drugs from animals,” Chan said in an email exchange.

Kennedy described the organiser of the San Diego summit, Tracy Slepcevic, as a “good friend”. In January, the health secretary appointed her to his remodelled Autism Coordinating Committee, which guides federally funded autism research.

Slepcevic is the mother of an autistic son and a proponent of alternative therapies for autism including stem cell infusions. She will be appearing alongside Eric Trump and Del Bigtree, the influential anti-vaxxer who was communications director of Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, on stage at the Christian nationalist ReAwaken America reunion in Tulsa next week.

Slepcevic unveiled at the San Diego summit a new experiment that involves injecting 120 autistic children with umbilical cord stem cells. The effort will begin next month in partnership with a major clinic in Tijuana in Mexico, a country that has historically taken a looser approach to stem cell regulation than the US.

Slepcevic did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.

Ed Clay, a former MMA fighter who founded the Cellular Performance Institute (CPI) in Tijuana, said that the clinical trial would be free to families and fully licensed under the Mexican federal health authority, Cofepris.

He said he had devised the exercise as a clinical trial with expert neurologists and pediatricians serving as investigators in the full-service hospital his company runs in Mexico, with the CPI investing about $2m to conduct it.

His team includes, he said, “21 PhD scientists and 42 medical doctors, including PhDs from institutions such as Harvard, Yale, MIT and Stanford”.

Clay said the clinical trial could be imported at later stages to Nashville and other US sites under full FDA licensing if early results in Mexico were promising.

While the CPI prides itself at using state-of-the-art medical technology, other stem cell providers now moving into autism treatment do not hold such standards. Clay said: “I would say our biggest competitor right now for CPI is the scammer and the many fly-by-night clinics operating in this space.”

Kennedy has said that he does not want to see a “wild west” of alternative therapies developing in the US. Yet in the same breath, he conceded that opening up the country to such providers will lead to “charlatans and people who have bad results, but ultimately you can’t prevent that”. The Guardian has contacted the US health department and the FDA but did not receive a reply.

Among the newly emboldened raft of stem cell providers targeting autistic kids is Better Stem, a Miami-based company run by Greice Murphy. She describes herself as an entrepreneur whose other ventures include the suggestively named “Biatch”, a range of “artfully crafted tequilas made for the woman’s palate”, and a Miami stem cell clinic offering infusions to address hair loss and erectile dysfunction. The Guardian contacted Murphy for comment, but she did not respond prior to publication.

Two months ago, she moved into the business of offering umbilical cord stem cell infusions for autistic children. Families are charged $300 for an initial consultation, followed by up to $15,000 per infusion.

Better Stem claims to be the first company in the US offering “legal, compliant access” to stem cell therapies under the “right-to-try” law signed by Donald Trump in 2018 during his first presidency. The clinic tells prospective clients that the legislation allows patients with a debilitating condition that has no cure, such as autism, to be treated with unapproved drugs.

In fact, the Right to Try Act is specifically limited to patients who are terminally ill and have been diagnosed with a “life-threatening disease or condition”. Autism does not fall under that definition.

“Technically speaking, the federal Right to Try Act covers terminal diseases and is not applicable to non life-threatening conditions even if they have no cure,” said Jeff Cohen, an expert in health law at the Florida Healthcare Law Firm.

Among the families who are being drawn to stem cell therapies are Taylor and her four-year-old son, Ollie, from Utah. At the end of this month, they will travel to Florida for an infusion of umbilical stem cells for Ollie, who is non-speaking and has been diagnosed with autism with high support needs.

The procedure will cost Taylor $12,500, which she has raised largely through donations from family and friends. She said that her heart’s wish was that people would come to understand “the weight these children carry in a world that was not designed to help them thrive”.

She has had family members chide her for seeking alternative therapies, which they have described as “a little bit crazy”.

Her view, though, is that “I have to at least try. For those who pass judgment, I hope they come to understand the lengths we must go, simply because no one else will.”

Almost 500 people turned out to the Greenway Parkrun on Saturday to pay tribute to Professor Richard Scolyer.

The former Australian of the Year died on June 7 after a three-year battle with aggressive brain cancer.

Mr Scolyer was an avid runner and achieved his 250th parkrun milestone almost a year ago to the day.

Nearly 500 runners took to Professor Richard Scolyer's favourite parkrun to honour his legacy following his hard-fought battle with brain cancer.

The former Australian of the Year recipient died aged 59 on June 7.

Posters of Mr Scolyer were hung around Richard Murdern Reserve in Haberfield in Sydney's inner west at the weekly Greenway Parkrun on Saturday morning.

Almost 500 people turned out to the Greenway Parkrun on Saturday morning. (ABC News: Digby Werthmuller)

At the start line, speeches were read and participants took a moment to reflect on the impact he had left on a community that loves to run.

This week's event was held in memory of Mr Scolyer an avid runner who competed in 250 parkruns, both in Australia and abroad.

Mark Scolyer reflects on his brother's impact on the running community. (ABC News)

His brother, Mark, a running enthusiast himself, said it was an emotional day for all involved.

Mark affectionately described his brother as "a daggy guy" who would "run up next to people and talk" at parkrun events.

"I've probably run here with Rich 20 times. We'd push each other and sometimes I couldn't keep up and sometimes he was having bad days and some days he couldn't run," he said.

Professor Richard Scolyer celebrates completing his 250th parkrun in 2025. (ABC News: Luke Royes)

Acting group run director Emily Hamilton said Mr Scolyer embodied the ethos of what the Greenway parkrun community was.

"He has been such an important figure for Australia and for cancer research," she said.

"But here in our community, he was one of those people that just really encouraged people to give it a crack and have a go."

Another participant reflected on Mr Scolyer's 250th parkrun, a milestone she watched him achieve almost a year ago to the day.

"I feel that he will always have a very special place in this community," she said.

Mr Scolyer first took part in the City2Surf 21 years ago with his wife and eldest daughter Emily (pictured). (X: Professor Richard Scolyer AO)

Every Saturday for the past eight years, Mr Scolyer ran the five-kilometre loop, which stretches around Haberfield, Leichhardt and Dulwich Hill in Sydney's inner west.

During his cancer battle, he had set himself a goal of completing 250 parkruns.

He marked the milestone in June 2025, despite having announced his cancer had returned months earlier in March.

"I guess it's part of my personality. Bit embarrassing, but wanting to get to 250 was something that pushed me along," he said of his feat at the time.

A renowned pathologist and melanoma researcher, Mr Scolyer died on June 7 after a three-year battle with glioblastoma.

He became a pioneer of brain cancer research when he volunteered as "patient zero" for an experimental immunotherapy treatment.

Mr Scolyer had volunteered to undergo experimental immunotherapy for medical research.  (Supplied: Instagram/@profrscolyer)

Mr Scolyer managed to stave off the disease for almost two years, while also supplying scientists with a wealth of knowledge to help shape the future of brain cancer immunotherapy.

In 2024, he was a co-recipient of the Australian of the Year award alongside Professor Georgina Long, for their ground-breaking melanoma research and treatment.

Chicago real estate developer Richard A. Stein constructed high-profile local projects like the Loop’s Franklin Center building, the Metcalfe federal office building, the University of Illinois Chicago’s campus expansion and the decommissioned Glenview Naval Air Station and Fort Sheridan military bases’ redevelopments.

Widely known as Richie, Stein built one of Chicago’s largest development companies and supported aggressive minority hiring for private-sector construction projects, with a commitment to diversity rarely seen by developers.

“He felt that every project was an expression of who he was, for all to see and judge,” said Julia Stasch, a former Stein & Co. president and chief operating officer. “So, he paid attention to every detail, making sure it was just right.”

Stein, 87, died of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on June 6 at his River North home, said his daughter Katie Balson. He previously had lived in Lincoln Park, Highwood and Glencoe.

Born in Chicago in 1939, Stein grew up in Highland Park and graduated from Highland Park High School. After earning a degree in hotel management from Cornell University in 1961, Stein briefly attended the University of Chicago Law School.

“I had always been interested in business, and at the time, it seemed to me that all corporate directors were lawyers,” Stein told the Tribune in 1985. “Two weeks into the semester, I asked a third-year law student if it ever got any easier. He said no … so I left law school and have never regretted it.”

Stein initially sold coal and heating oil to apartment building owners. The work “tided me over until I found something else to do,” he told the Tribune.

In 1963, Stein and a partner, Ray Klein, co-founded Littlestone Co., renovating small apartment buildings. The duo rehabbed apartment flats on the Near West Side and later in Old Town. The pair also constructed suburban apartment buildings, particularly federally subsidized projects for moderate-income and elderly individuals.

After selling Littlestone in 1971, Stein launched his namesake firm and led condominium conversion projects, including the Ludwig Mies van der Rohe-designed Gold Coast buildings at 900 and 910 N. Lake Shore Drive, the Lakeview building at 3900 N. Lake Shore, and conversions in Highland Park, Lombard and Willowbrook. With the condo craze cooling in the late 1970s, Stein constructed suburban office complexes, including the Lake Cook Office Centre and ArborLake complexes in Deerfield, and the Combined Centre complex in Northbrook.

Eyeing the Loop, Stein pursued larger commercial developments. He constructed the 27-story office building at 203 N. LaSalle St. on a long-stalled Loop property, along with an apartment tower and parking decks.

Mayor Harold Washington required Stein’s north Loop projects to steer 30% of all work to minority- or women-owned firms. Stein and Stasch supported the measure.

“Harold Washington’s greatest strength was his commitment to affirmative action,” Stein told the Tribune shortly after Washington’s death in 1987. “I tried to get across to him that a strong downtown provides jobs for the neighborhoods. He understood that.”

Stein built the 60-story AT&T Corporate Center — now known as Franklin Center — in the Loop, which was completed in 1989, and the adjoining 35-story USG building that finished in 1992. Stein also built the 27-story Metcalfe Federal Building, which opened in 1991, and the University of Chicago Graduate School of Business’ Gleacher Center and Loyola University Chicago’s Water Tower Campus building, which both opened in 1994.

Former Stein & Co. President Richard Hanson, hired in 1984 to help pursue commercial development, said Stein did “seemingly insane things that usually turned out great.”

“Richie led with action, not words,” Hanson said. “He expected you to do your best, as demonstrated by his own efforts, and instilled in you the desire to achieve the seemingly impossible. Richie’s spirit was contagious and everyone around him wanted to embrace it and be swept up in his enthusiasm.”

During the early-1990s economic slowdown, Stein adapted to greater public-sector and nonprofit construction. His firm was the developer arm for McCormick Place’s expansion and the owners’ representative for the United Center’s construction.

“It was clear that you couldn’t keep the pace of the ‘80s going forever,” he told the Tribune in 1992. “So about four or five years ago, we started a conscious effort to build up and do the things that (aligned) with our strengths.”

Stein also led renovations at the Chicago Board of Trade and the Civic Opera House.

In 1995, Glenview officials tapped Stein to oversee the mixed-use redevelopment of the massive former Glenview Naval Air Station, including 1,500 new residences. Stein’s firm advised Glenview and supplied a project manager.

Stein was also chosen to redevelop 110 acres of the shuttered lakefront Fort Sheridan military base in Highland Park and Highwood. The project was deeply personal for the Highland Park native, whose pitches to local officials invoked his lifelong connection to the area.

“I’m ecstatic, pleased, gratified and grateful,” he told the Tribune in 1996. “It’s very satisfying to be able to do something significant where your roots are. … It’s kind of humbling.”

Stein acknowledged that repurposing base buildings wasn’t easy.

“Mixing new and old residences and turning old military buildings into something that will sell in 1998 is a real challenge,” Stein told the Tribune in 1998.

In 1997, Stein’s firm was selected to redevelop UIC’s 45-acre South Campus, including the old Maxwell Street Market’s site, which was bulldozed in 1994.

“South Campus is as significant as anything we’ve ever tackled,” Stein told the Tribune in 2000. “The South Campus developments will unlock the value of the land and help UIC fulfill its mission.”

Along with the loss of Maxwell Street, opponents of the project have objected to how it displaced Near West Side communities, criticisms that extend back to the creation of the original campus in the 1960s.

In 1997, Mesirow Financial acquired Stein’s firm, forming Mesirow Stein Real Estate. Stein stepped back from daily operations while continuing to build relationships.

In 2014, Stein left Mesirow Stein to form RAS Development, a firm developing a 2.3 million-square-foot mixed-use project just north of Boston. He spent a decade-plus on that project.

“He was unique, he was creative (and) he was passionate about what he did,” said retired attorney Ted Novak, 85, who represented Stein for decades. “Richie was absolutely unique in terms of his passion, his character, his philanthropy and his care for people.”

Stein never retired.

In 1997, Landmarks Preservation Council of Illinois — now Landmarks Illinois — named Stein its “man of the year” for rehabbing Fort Sheridan’s century-old buildings.

Stein said personal initiative was what he liked most about real estate.

“If I don’t get out and hustle and call, and move, nothing happens,” he told the Tribune in 1980. “As you get older and bigger, more stuff comes your way but, still, the things I do I have to create myself.”

Outside of work, Stein enjoyed fly fishing. He traveled to Alaska to fly-fish for 30 years straight.

“He loved everything about fly-fishing — the beauty of the river and nature, the mental focus, the camaraderie of a group of people he loved participating in the sport he loved,” Hanson said. “Although we were business partners for almost 20 years, our most memorable times together were spent on a river. As time passed, he told me that other than family and friends, the thing he missed most was fishing.”

Stein was also involved with the Jewish United Fund, the Lambs Inc., the Anti-Defamation League and Ravinia Festival.

Two previous marriages ended in divorce. Stein is also survived by his wife of 24 years, Suzanne Lovell; another daughter, Barbara Stein; a stepdaughter, Alice Lewis; a stepson, William Rossiter; 11 grandchildren; and a sister, Joy Lodge.

Services were held.

Bob Goldsborough is a freelance reporter.

River AI, an AI startup founded by xAI co-founder Igor Babuschkin, has secured $1.1 billion in funding in a seed/Series A round led by General Catalyst and AMP PBC, with participation from Nvidia, AMD Ventures, Y Combinator, and Temasek.

(AMP PBC is an AI-focused investment firm founded in 2026 by former Andreessen Horowitz general partner Anjney Midha, backer of companies at a16z like Black Forest Labs, Mistral AI, LMArena and  OpenRouter.)

River came out of stealth in June with a fascinating mission. Babuschkin, whose resume includes AI roles at DeepMind and OpenAI, intends to reinvent AI from scratch, beginning with how models are trained. This is in order to turn agents into personally trainable assistants, rather than following the trajectory other AI labs are on: human worker replacements.

“To get there, we believe the stack has to be rebuilt end to end: training, models, the product layer, and new hardware that lets personal AI live close to you,” he wrote in his launch blog.

“Capable agents will be a normal part of everyday life. Less like the assistants you call on today when you need a task done, more like guardian angels: quietly present, on your side, helping with what actually matters to you. They will know you well, and they will be yours, not someone else’s,” he envisions.

River already offers an API, billed per 1 million tokens, with rates dependent on the open model used. The API allows developers to use both reinforcement learning (RL) and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on the models. This first product is intended to be an antidote to prompt engineering. “Prompting steers a model you don’t own and can’t improve. River lets you train open models into ones that are truly yours — and serve them like any other endpoint,” the product literature says.

While this round is an eye-popping-size investment for a nascent company, and perhaps another indication of the overheated AI atmosphere, River’s premise comes at a particularly auspicious time. Enterprises are waking up to wanting to control their AI model destiny by using a mix of models, including open weight. River is promising to solve the post-training expertise part of that problem with its neocloud offering.

“Any enterprise can complete a complex reinforcement learning run in 15 to 20 minutes with no infrastructure team required, at two to four times the cost savings relative to closed-source alternatives,” it wrote in its funding announcement.

The bigger vision of this company is that everyone will have their own agents, trained by themselves, and working on their behalf. We are already seeing this concept in action with the rise of personal, locally running agents in the form of OpenClaw and its derivatives. Plus, we are already seeing Nvidia partner with PC makers like Dell, Microsoft, and HP for AI-capable hardware.

How River’s tech will differ remains to be seen. But it’s starting out with a war chest full of cash to try.

Attorneys for Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk, asked a Utah district court judge to take the death penalty off the table over comments a prosecutor made to the media about a bullet fragment found during the autopsy.

Robinson’s attorney, Richard Novak, argued comments made to several media outlets by Christopher Ballard, a Utah County Attorney’s Office spokesperson who is also a prosecutor on the case, violated a pretrial publicity order.

The defense asked the judge to block prosecutors from seeking the death penalty if prosecutors are found in contempt for the comments.

﻿In several media interviews at the end of March and beginning of April, Ballard spoke about an inconclusive ballistics report referenced in a defense filing. Ballard later told the court he had included remarks indicating Robinson is presumed innocent in those interviews.

Novak called the comments “extremely reckless.”

“I find no credibility in Mr. Ballard’s sworn testimony that he only intended to communicate with the media generally about bullet fragment analysis,” Novak said.

Judge declines to boot cameras from courtroom for Charlie Kirk murder suspect’s trial

The public killing of the prominent conservative activist on a Utah university campus last September set off an avalanche of misinformation. Robinson’s attorneys have repeatedly raised concerns about news coverage of the high-profile case potentially harming their client’s right to a fair trial.

Ballard testified Friday he does not believe his comments violated the order, which prohibits the parties from making public statements about the case, except under certain circumstances. He said the defense misrepresented the results in a public filing, and his comments were made to clarify what the results meant.

“The goal of these interviews was to respond to the specific media inquiries that were being generated by the misinformation” in the filing, Ballard said.

The defense filing Ballard spoke to the media about – a motion to continue the preliminary hearing filed on March 27 – states the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives “was unable to identify the bullet recovered at autopsy to the rifle allegedly tied to Mr. Robinson.”

Prosecutors argued the defense’s statement in the filing omits an important piece of the report’s conclusion: the ATF was also unable to exclude the bullet as coming from the rifle, and say that is what Ballard was trying to clarify in the media.

Ballard and Utah County Attorney Jeffrey Gray, who also testified Friday, repeatedly pointed to a professional rule, referenced in the order, which allows attorneys to comment on public information when they believe there is a possibility of prejudicial pretrial publicity.

If the court does find Ballard in contempt, “the number one remedy should preclude the state from seeking death against Robinson,” Novak argued.

Other possible penalties include attending a continuing education program or referral to the state bar association, Novak added.

Prosecutors had announced in September last year they would seek the death penalty in the case against Robinson, who faces charges including aggravated murder, felony use of a firearm, obstruction of justice and witness tampering. He has not yet entered pleas.

During Friday’s hearing, Judge Tony Graf also heard arguments on whether hearsay evidence prosecutors plan to present would be allowed during the preliminary hearing beginning on July 6.

Defense attorney Michael Burt argued a video deposition of a key witness should not be admissible, as the witness could not be subject to cross-examination.

Ballard argued the defense is not entitled to cross-examine witnesses, as they are during other types of hearings, because the preliminary hearing has the limited purpose of establishing probable cause to bring charges to trial.

“If this court granted the defendant’s motion, it would be going where no other court has gone before,” Ballard said. “This court would be the first court to find that the Sixth Amendment right to confrontation applies at a preliminary hearing.”

The court is expected to issue its rulings on both matters on June 22.

As the government stalls on a response to key recommendations in the robodebt royal commission, it has legislated a huge expansion in the use of automated decision-making.

Legislation before parliament to reform the National Disability Insurance Scheme sets out an unprecedented expansion of automated government decision-making in reviewing support offered by the scheme. For what is believed to be the first time, it permits the automation of discretionary decisions rather than simply administrative calculations.

The bill explicitly allows for automation in cases where there is “(a) a discretion being exercised; (b) an evaluative judgement being made; (c) a state of mind being formed”.

“We haven’t come across this before,” says Ed Santow, a former Human Rights Commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute. “Generally, the advice that oversight bodies give to government is that discretion is something that is quintessentially a human task, and so automation should be more of those other sorts of non-evaluative judgements or calculations … Whereas discretion is something where a human is expected to exercise judgement.”

Santow says the power being proposed to automate decisions in the NDIS reform bill is incredibly broad. “Basically, it says that the government is able to decide which decisions are to be automated,” he says, “and those decisions may involve just that kind of calculation type question, as black and white questions, or they may involve discretion, or they may involve some combination of both.”

Santow, alongside colleagues Clare Brennan and Sarah Sacher, has raised these automation issues in a submission to the Senate inquiry into the NDIS reform bill. The inquiry has received more than 4000 submissions and hearings are set for the week ahead.

Santow says he has “grave” concerns about the legislation, which both allows for expansive use of automation and is scarce on safeguards.

“What this bill does is it creates what’s known as a facilitative power,” Santow says.

“It’s saying you can do this thing, you can kind of enable these automated decisions to take place. What we would also expect, and what’s not in the bill … are the safeguards that will make it much less likely that something will go wrong, and if something does go wrong, that the individual will be okay.”

According to the Australian Council of Social Service, the bill as it is currently drafted should not pass.

“Automation should not extend to discretionary decision-making,” says Jacqueline Phillips, the council’s executive director of policy and research. “These are extraordinary reforms in their scope and potential impact.”

Phillips says there should be human oversight in any decision where a person’s entitlements are reduced. “What’s quite extraordinary about the NDIS bill is it proposes very broad powers for the minister to delegate major areas of decision to automation but including discretionary decisions,” she says.

Labor is losing political skin on these reforms and associated savings measures, even as sustainability concerns about the scheme are widely shared. Over the next 10 years, a total of $184.9 billion will be taken out of the scheme, as its annual growth is restrained from more than 10 per cent to “5 to 6 per cent, or lower”. It is expected that 160,000 participants will be removed from the scheme.

The NDIS reforms are now at the forefront of growing concern about the expansion of automated decisions in government, as well as expansion in the use of artificial intelligence.

Twenty-three government agencies, from Services Australia and the Australian Tax Office to the Clean Energy Regulator and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, are authorised to use automated decision-making in their operations. A desktop review by the Australian Information Commissioner in January found only 17 per cent of the agencies disclosed that they used automated decision-making in their Information Publication Scheme, which they are required to do under the Freedom of Information Act.

The Commonwealth Ombudsman is investigating incorrect assessments under the aged home care Integrated Assessment Tool and there is a partial pause to the Targeted Compliance Framework for jobseekers receiving income support payments.

Officials from the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations indicated in Senate estimates this week that somewhere between 100,000 and more than 310,000 people have been affected by unlawful cancellation of social security payments, as brought to light by Economic Justice Australia.

There is a human override in the NDIS bill, but it is not expected to be widely used.

“It’s an unusual one,” Santow says. “The CEO of the NDIA [National Disability Insurance Agency] can override, but it’s a bit like the power that the immigration minister or home affairs minister exercises in our immigration and visa system, so it’s not like an internal review process, which would be a much more conventional thing.”

Adding to the anxiety within the disability community about cuts to participation is the lack of clarity and open-ended nature about where the automated discretion would apply, apart from the current trial of the I-CAN tool, an instrument designed to give holistic assessments of a person’s needs.

“Once AI starts coming into the way government’s running its services, that will explode, and we need to get the basics right now …”

“Our understanding is it could be applied overall,” says Megan Spindler-Smith, the acting chief executive of People With Disability Australia. “We currently have really deep concerns around the current I-CAN tool, because it’s only being tested on participants with non-complex or non-changing support needs. We don’t actually know if the decision-making that comes out of that, outside of non-complex spaces, is reasonable and actually meets the needs of the person with disability that it’s making decisions for.

“Other than the I-CAN tool, to the best of our understanding, and I’m saying to the best of our understanding, these systems have not been developed yet.”

The disability community wants to protect review rights. Currently disputed cases have access to the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART), but there is a request for clarity around automated decision-making.

“We have no guarantees that it is going to be an accessible process,” Spindler-Smith says. “If you are building an automated decision-making process and system on decisions that are currently being made by the NDIS, when the majority of NDIS cases that go to the ART are actually found in favour of the participants and against the decisions that are made by the NDIA, that shows that the NDIA actually gets it wrong, and that is why the safeguards are so essential.”

A government spokesperson told The Saturday Paper the bill has appropriate safeguards and that the use of automation is transparent and accountable. They also said NDIS participants will still have the right to seek a merits review through the ART.

“This bill will enable the NDIA to utilise a computer program to take certain administrative actions on behalf of a human where it is safe and responsible to do so,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “This will mean that our public servants can focus on more of the sophisticated tasks that require genuine human interaction and people can be supported in a more timely and consistent way.

“What we’ve set up in this bill is really an enabling power and we will step through this very carefully with the community how this will happen in practice.”

This new approach to automation comes as the Albanese government continues to deal with the fallout of the illegal robodebt scheme.

Last week, the social services minister outlined the government’s approach when questioned by the independent member for Curtin, Kate Chaney, about the legacy work of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme.

“Our approach is that in every case there needs to be human oversight of any of the use of AI,” Tanya Plibersek told parliament. “We don’t just hand over decision-making to abstract computer programs, as was the case under robodebt, which caused such great suffering for 430,000 Australians.”

While these issues with automated decision-making continue, there is also a major gap in the government’s response to the robodebt royal commission.

The Saturday Paper understands Attorney-General Michelle Rowland is still working on a consistent whole-of-government automated decision-making response to the royal commission, 16 months after a consultation period of eight roundtables and a small survey ended.

Some groups have complained that it has been 18 months since they were actively involved. There are four outstanding recommendations remaining from the royal commission, three of which require legislation.

“It certainly doesn’t look like it’s being approached with any sense of urgency at all,” Kate Chaney tells The Saturday Paper.

“We are seeing an increased use of automated decision-making in aged care, in NDIS, and the NDIS changes proposed will increase that again. Once AI starts coming into the way government’s running its services, that will explode, and we need to get the basics right now before there is that change in the future,” Chaney says.

It is argued the problems being experienced now across government are due to inconsistencies in how automated decision-making is applied and the absence of a clear set of guidelines for government departments.

“It’s stalled in the sense that it’s not complete yet,” Spindler-Smith says. “We still don’t have those clearer protections. We still don’t have an understanding from the learnings of the robodebt experience, especially around the needs for controls, including transparency, review rights and oversight.”

The recommendation that the government accepted to “consider opportunities” for a consistent legal pathway for automation is regarded as “ongoing”. The recommendation for establishing or expanding an existing body to monitor automated decision-making is also regarded as “ongoing”, although the government says it is ensuring there is appropriate oversight of automation and that it may consider an appropriate oversight body.

The Saturday Paper understands that after the public consultation period, the Attorney-General’s Department moved to consulting other Commonwealth agencies and other stakeholders.

“Responding to the Royal Commission with meaningful, durable reform is a priority for the government, particularly where it strengthens the integrity, lawfulness and transparency of Commonwealth decision making,” a spokesperson for Rowland said in a statement.

“The ADM (automated decision-making) framework will be designed to improve accuracy and consistency of administrative decisions, embed robust safeguards, including transparency obligations, and ensure that ADM is used lawfully, responsibly, and with appropriate human oversight. The ADM framework will also enable agencies to use ADM to lift productivity and deliver faster, more reliable services that are aligned with community expectations.”

The Albanese government’s whole approach to AI has been “under-resourced, too slow and too passive”, according to Chaney.

She says the potential benefits and harms are both enormous.  “I’m concerned that there’s another robodebt in the making somewhere in the system,” she says. “We have to be really careful that we’re not losing the human out of our human services.

“And automated decision-making can help with the efficiency of decisions – it can reduce the cost of delivering government services – but only if there’s really clear understanding of how it’s being used, and that a human can actually override those decisions if necessary. Because humans have common sense, and we need to actually make sure that we’re not losing the humanity when we’re trying to look after people.”

In addition to these concerns, there are ongoing issues with the Targeted Compliance Framework operated by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, the automated regulatory and tracking system that unlawfully cancelled welfare payments between April 2022 and July 2024. It has been paused, but is due to come back online after a revamp in 2027.

“We’ve just received legal advice, which has confirmed EJA [Economic Justice Australia] concerns, where people are getting their payments suspended automatically because they’re not meeting a mutual obligation requirement,” says Kate Allingham, the chief executive of EJA. “Under the legislation, there is a requirement of discretion and we have concerns that an automated process is not adequately applying that discretion in the way that it should do lawfully.”

Economic Justice Australia, the peak body for community legal centres, previously found the government unlawfully cancelled more than 300,000 welfare payments. It spotted a coding error in an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and applied it to the number of people it would have affected and came up with 310,000.

“It is unlawful because there were timeframes in regard to the amount of time they had to respond, and that timeframe was reduced because of the coding error, and so there was less time for them to respond, and so the timeframes are within the legislation, and that is of really significant concern,” Allingham says. “It’s pretty easy to figure out that if there is a coding error that’s impacted one person, it could potentially be impacting thousands more.”

When Greens Senator Barbara Pocock questioned the 310,000 figure at Senate estimates on Wednesday, a department official said the number of unlawful cancellations was in the “vicinity of that”.

There was, the official said, complexity because there were people who had found employment and did not need to “reconnect” to the system under mutual obligations, so it may be a “much smaller cohort”.

The Anti-Poverty Centre estimated the figure for unlawful cancellations would then sit around 100,000, which is about 10 times the number the department previously admitted to.

Also causing concern in estimates this week was an aged-care tool brought in last November, in part to speed up long waiting lists for assessments for home care. The algorithm has been criticised for repeatedly under-assessing levels of need.

Departmental officials conceded that the department had not consulted before removing the ability for human assessors to override incorrect outcomes.

Under the current settings for the automated Integrated Assessment Tool, humans collect clinical data that is entered into the tool where universal aged-care rules apply. A second human assessor can review the data, but they can’t override the decision.

“The rules have to apply to everybody equally,” Minister for Aged Care and Seniors Sam Rae told the ABC on Thursday. “There’s a component. There’s a mathematical component that’s the nature of a process. An algorithm is just a process. There is a process by which the aged-care rules are applied, that’s an automated process.

“After the decision … the person can seek a review of the decision and that then comes back into a separate process. Another human being, a third human being, is part of the review process.”

Despite that defence, the minister has requested the department conduct a rapid three-month review of the “prioritisations mechanism” of the tool.

The Commonwealth Ombudsman is already investigating.

Pope Leo XIV prays with Mayor Brandon Johnson and other members of Johnson’s delegation on Thursday at the Vatican.

Simone Risoluti / Vatican Media

Share

VATICAN CITY — The Chicago delegation led by Mayor Brandon Johnson that met with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican included a dozen leaders from various faith communities. They had a special request for the pope during their hour-long meeting with him on Thursday.

Bishop Horace E. Smith, senior pastor of the Apostolic Faith Church in Bronzeville, asked the pope if the group could pray for him. Flanked by Johnson, Roman Catholic and Protestant clergymen and two women — a rabbi and a Methodist pastor — standing at the center of the group, Leo received their blessing.

Johnson, who often cast the Vatican visit in spiritual terms, later said he felt the delegation’s audience with the Chicago-born pontiff had been profound, pastoral and comforting. He also called it “an affirmation.”

“The soul of Chicago is definitely in Rome and at the Vatican today — business leaders, labor leaders, community leaders, elected leaders, faith leaders, all coming together united in this moment to protect humanity,” he said in an interview Friday at a Caffé Portofino in Rome’s Prati neighborhood.

Many of the faith leaders who met with Leo used words such as “humbling” and “transformative” to describe the papal audience.

Rabbi Lizzi Heydemann, founder of Mishkan Chicago, was part of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s delegation that met with Pope Leo XIV.

Arthur Maiorella / Sun-Times

“I was moved in a way that surprised even myself,” said Rabbi Lizzi Heydemann of Mishkan Chicago, a progressive Jewish community in Ravenswood. “I found the whole visit to be an interesting cultural and religious experience up until the moment I sat in the room where we were all waiting, and there was his empty chair at the front of the room. Suddenly — and I’m getting weepy as I describe it to you — it suddenly hit me the number of people he stewards and carries as a religious leader. I don’t steward the spiritual lives of a billion Catholics. I run a progressive spiritual community in the city of Chicago with about 670 member families, but it’s been a rough couple of years as a Jewish religious leader.

“I felt — in that moment just seeing his empty chair, and then, when I had the opportunity to speak with him — just how he deeply understands that weight and models what I would say is an elegant and principled way of carrying it,” she said. “As an LGBTQ-friendly, inclusive community, as a female leader, as a Jew, we obviously have some major theological points of disagreement. But the areas where we share values were the reasons why we were there as a group from Chicago.”

When Smith gathered the group of faith leaders to bless and pray for Leo, it was a moment of “shared privilege,” the rabbi said. “It’s a privilege that comes with a weight that sits on our shoulders that actually felt a little bit lighter in his presence and in the presence of one another.”

Rev. Juan Vargas of Our Lady of the Rosary and Michael Okinczyc-Cruz, executive director of the Coalition for Spiritual and Public Leadership, at St. Peter’s Square in front of “Angels Unawares,” a bronze sculpture of immigrants on a boat.

Cathleen Falsani / Sun-Times

Praying for the pope with leaders of other spiritual communities, both Christian and non-Christian, was “a moment of unity, and that’s why we’re here, speaking with one voice,” said the Rev. Juan Vargas, associate pastor of Our Lady of the Rosary parish, which serves Dunning and Portage Park on the Northwest Side. “Pope Leo has resounded and highlighted for us what the Gospel is calling us to do and how to live it out.

“When we talked, I said, ‘I’m praying for you, we’re all praying for you because it’s not easy,’ ” Vargas said of his minute or two speaking directly with Leo.

He told the pope, “When I preach from the ambo at mass, to hear your voice proclaim and in a way shout, even though you’re not physically shouting, what the gospel’s inviting us to, it really encourages me to also continue to bring that to light.’ ”

He said Leo thanked him for his prayers and said he was praying for the priest and his parishioners.

“He’s listening to our cry, whatever cry it is all over the world,” Vargas said. “He’s very attentive, and he’s responding.”

A day after meeting Leo, Michael Okinczyc-Cruz, executive director of the Coalition for Spiritual and Public Leadership in Chicago, stood in St. Peter’s Square in front of “Angels Unawares,” the bronze sculpture by Timothy Schmalz that was installed by Pope Francis to mark the 105th World Migrant and Refugee Day. The weight of his encounter with Francis’ successor was fresh in his mind and reflected in his expression.

“In that moment, I was just overcome with emotion because of how difficult it’s been and how the work really has been led by our immigrant members,” said Okinczyc-Cruz, whose group recently reached a legal agreement after suing the federal Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to allow daily pastoral care at the Broadview ICE Detention Center. “They organized from the bottom up to make this happen. It wasn’t theoretical for them. This is their lived experience. These are their family members who’ve been detained and deported or moved around the country. And they took great risk to show up to Broadview in the midst of Operation Midway Blitz. All of that was in my mind and in my heart, speaking to the pope. And for him to be attentive to this struggle…was just so moving.”

When he spoke briefly with the pope, Okinczyc-Cruz, who also teaches theology at Loyola University’s Institute of Pastoral Studies, said he was shocked that Leo — who is a canon lawyer — had read about the legal agreement and was knowledgeable about the case.

“The gospel and Jesus’ message in Christianity, in general, has often been used and manipulated and wielded as a cudgel throughout history,” Okinczyc-Cruz said. “When the pope speaks about violence or genocide and hunger and poverty and exploitation, he’s not speaking on these matters from a partisan political perspective. He’s speaking from the perspective of being a pastor and a follower of Jesus Christ and the pope of the Catholic Church…. That’s what carries so much weight for those who are Catholic but also for those who are not Catholic. These values resonate deeply, and that also shines through.”

The Rev. Tanya Lozano Washington is pastor of Lincoln United Methodist Church in Pilsen and chief executive officer of the grassroots community organization Healthy Hood Chicago.

Provided

“We’re living through a spiritual crisis as much as it is a political one,” said the Rev. Tanya Lozano Washington, pastor of Lincoln United Methodist Church in Pilsen and chief executive officer of the grassroots community organization Healthy Hood Chicago, which works to improve health in some o the city’s most neglected communities. “This world, in general, has built systems that normalize cruelty and isolation and greed and violence…. I truly believe humanity is hungry for a different way forward.

“As a pastor, I’ll say that the church is at its best when it tells the truth about power,” she said. “Whenever fear and nationalism and militarism become more sacred than human life, the church has a responsibility to speak. What I really admire and appreciate both about Mayor Brandon Johnson and Pope Leo is their willingness to speak with moral clarity in a time where the many leaders are too afraid to.”

Lozano Washington is the daughter of the Rev. Walter “Slim” Coleman, the late liberation theologian, civil rights leader, Black Panther Party member and a co-founder of the Rainbow-PUSH Coalition. Her mother is Emma Lozano, a longtime Chicago civil and immigrant rights activist and leader of the group Pueblo Sin Fronteras. Her uncle was Rudy Lozano, a Chicago Chicano and labor rights activist who helped Harold Washington get elected as the city’s first Black mayor in April 1983. Two months later, Lozano was killed in his home in what many believe was a politically motivated assassination.

“What I really appreciate about Pope Leo is his willingness to recover the prophetic tradition of the church, the tradition that asks not only how people are saved but whether the poor are being crushed, whether peace is being pursued and whether human dignity is actually being practiced,” Lozano Washington said. “That’s what [Leo is] speaking to the church in this moment. As a Christian, as a United Methodist, I feel deeply aligned with [Leo’s] message. And I’m so grateful to the mayor and the mayor’s team that put together such a diverse delegation…of faith leaders, business leaders, political leaders, labor and union leaders. It was so representative of the soul of Chicago.”

Meeting Leo along with many other Chicago leaders “made me feel like we really have everything we need to shift the culture towards a place that prioritizes humanity,” Lozano Washington said. “This was such a monumental moment not just for Chicago but for the world.”

An editorial note re: The Journal and The 42’s reporting on the Uefa Nations League matches between Ireland and Israel is available to read here.

FOR THE SECOND successive Sunday, Ireland fans and otherwise curious viewers were treated to the bizarre spectacle of RTÉ’s compromise coverage of Ireland facing Israel in the Nations League.

The national broadcaster is curtailing how it covers the two games, and said last month that it would not be using its own employees on screen or studio punditry, with the commentary instead provided by Uefa’s global coverage.

RTÉ has said it is broadcasting the Uefa feed due to a decision to fulfil its “contractual obligations” while limiting commercial activity around the game. The broadcaster has been continuing to provide news coverage of the game and the events surrounding it.

No ads were broadcast before the match or at half-time.

As Ireland played their nominally home fixture against Israel in the north Serbian town of Bačka Topola tonight, things on TV looked much the same as they did last week.

The broadcast began with no introduction, continuity announcement, studio analysis or any of the other bells and whistles that would accompany an Ireland game aside from pictures and commentary from Uefa’s man on the ground.

The TV schedule said the game would start showing at 7.35pm, 10 minutes before kick-off, but the broadcaster so curtailed its coverage that it shaved another two minutes off the build-up and aired RTÉ 2′s staple Sunday evening nature documentary until 7.37pm.

After that belated introduction, much of the coverage from the Uefa feed was – like the notes in any good jazz standard – all about what the commentator didn’t say.

There has been no shortage of spikiness between the two sides in recent weeks, as well as questions about whether Ireland should play these games at all, whether the players would agree to do so, and why this game is happening 2,000km away from Dublin.

Tonight’s coverage did not allude to any of that, though there has been so much controversy around Ireland’s two fixtures against Israel that not even the Uefa guy could sanitise the elephant out of the room.

The pre-match patter began by referencing Israel’s game against Kosovo and Ireland’s 2-2 draw with Austria, with emphasis put on how a win here for either side would help them ahead of the final fixtures of the group.

It didn’t take long until the commentator made his first knowing reference to events off the pitch.

“Both these teams know the importance of a victory this evening in terms of…,” the commentator said, trailing off with a third-trimester pregnant pause before steering things back on course.

Print article

One Saturday afternoon in May 2026, families gathered on Poklonnaya Gora, a hilltop war memorial park in western Moscow. They came for a procession and a “moleben,” an Orthodox prayer service, for the well-being of Russian families. Church media billed it as the first Day of the Sanctity of the Family.

May 30 is the feast of St. Evdokia of Moscow, a 14th-century princess who took monastic vows late in life after being widowed. Her husband, St. Dmitry Donskoy, a prince who led a victory over the Mongols, is commemorated on June 1. The church joined the two into a single couple’s feast in 2015, with a decree stressing that they were “parents of twelve children.”

Just over five weeks later, Russians will celebrate another “holy couple.” July 8 honors Sts. Peter and Fevronia, a 13th-century prince and princess venerated as patrons of marriage and famed for their devotion to each other. First celebrated in 2008, the day became an official national holiday in 2022, though not a day off from work.

Both events serve a Russian government campaign to present itself as a defender of “traditional values,” a key part of my research as a scholar of marriage and sexuality in Russian Orthodoxy. The campaign is a partnership between church and state and is also meant to raise the birth rate. The Kremlin treats that goal as a matter of national survival, especially during the war in Ukraine.

Russia’s population has been shrinking for most of the past decade.

In recent years, deaths have outnumbered births by roughly 600,000 a year. As is true in many countries, fertility rates have fallen sharply. Russian women now average about 1.4 children each, far below the 2.1 needed to keep a population stable.

In the first quarter of 2026, demographer Alexei Raksha estimated there were about 272,000 births, the lowest for any quarter in roughly two centuries. Since then, the government has largely stopped publishing routine birth and death figures. Independent analysts, such as the U.S.-based Institute for the Study of War, offer two reasons for the blackout: the sheer scale of the decline and a wish to hide war casualties.

Those casualties are hard to count because Russia does not report them. Journalists at Mediazona and the BBC have confirmed the names of more than 230,000 Russian soldiers killed. A July 2026 analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated as many as 450,000 Russian deaths and 1.4 million total casualties. Emigration compounds the losses: As of 2024, at least 650,000 Russians who left after the invasion were still abroad, many of them young and educated.

Officials increasingly speak in emergency terms. The Kremlin’s spokesman has called the birth rate “catastrophic.” President Vladimir Putin declared 2024 a national “Year of the Family” and has made reversing the decline a priority.

Yet Russia also has one of the world’s highest divorce rates. Marriage has fallen to its lowest level in decades. The pro-family imagery runs well ahead of the reality it is meant to change.

The push for “traditional values” – and babies – depends on a close alliance between the Kremlin and the Russian Orthodox Church. The summer “couples” days are no exception.

July 8, in honor of Peter and Fevronia, grew from a 2006 campaign in the city of Murom, a few hours east of Moscow. Peter once ruled the small principality, and the saints’ relics rest there. Thousands of residents petitioned for a national family day, and Svetlana Medvedeva, the wife of then-President Dmitry Medvedev, took up the cause. Medvedeva designed a chamomile emblem for the day and created a medal for couples married 25 years or more.

Officials and clergy promoted July 8 as a Russian answer to Valentine’s Day. The church calls that holiday an alien import meant to destroy the Russian family, casting it as a celebration of fleeting passion rather than committed love. Government pollsters say the share of Russians marking Valentine’s Day fell from 51% in 2005 to 30% in 2025.

For the Kremlin’s purposes, though, there is a problem with July 8: “The Tale of Peter and Fevronia,” written in the mid-16th century, contains no children. In fact, their marriage ends with the couple taking monastic vows: an awkward fit for a holiday about childbearing.

I and other scholars have argued that this awkwardness likely pushed the church to create a second “family” day. While Peter and Fevronia were childless, Dmitry and Evdokia, the May honorees, raised 12 children.

Dmitry and Evdokia were venerated separately for centuries – her on May 30, him on June 1 – until the 2015 decree that combined them. As the decree noted, June 1 falls on International Children’s Day. The government often invokes that occasion in anti-abortion campaigns.

In 2026, church outlets reported that May 30 would be observed as the Day of the Sanctity of the Family, part of a church-run “family week.” Organizers launched it in 2024, during the Kremlin’s “Year of the Family,” and a tight alliance of church, state and civic groups runs it.

Russia’s broader “values” program portrays the country as a bastion against Western ideas about family and gender, such as support for LGBTQ+ rights. It rests on a 2022 presidential decree that centers “traditional spiritual-moral values,” such as family and patriotism.

Other measures have followed. A 2024 law penalizes “childfree propaganda,” meaning the promotion of a childless life. A demographic strategy running to 2036 sets birth-rate targets. In December 2024, a new presidential council took charge of family policy.

Church leaders have also repeatedly called for a national ban on abortions in private clinics and criminal penalties for “inducement”: pressuring a woman to end a pregnancy.

The government has resisted that demand. But many regions have implemented clinic restrictions and local “inducement” bans, making abortion harder to obtain across much of the country.

This push for “traditional” families plays out continuously and has intensified since the invasion of Ukraine.

For example, on June 22, 2026, the anniversary of the 1941 Nazi invasion, the Orthodox channel Spas opened a week of programming about the birth rate. It was titled “Gde vse?!,” or “Where is everybody?!”

The channel’s director, Boris Korchevnikov, called it a “special demographic operation.” The phrase echoes how the Kremlin describes its war on Ukraine: a “special military operation.” He gathered demographers, health officials and clergy for televised talks.

This spring, Russia’s legislature began debating a bill that would fund fertility treatment for veterans and their wives. It would also fund treatment for war widows who have not remarried, and allow them to conceive using their late husbands’ stored sperm, with the men’s prior notarized consent.

The church has not endorsed this bill, however, and Feodor Lukyanov, chairman of the Russian Orthodox Church’s Patriarchal Family Commission, has objected that the arrangement would create an “incomplete family.”

But on May 30 and July 8, Russia celebrates families the church does approve of: holy couples whose days have been carefully built to carry a message about marriage and childbearing.

The Rural Industry Adjustment and Development Fund has been in existence since 1985. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

A $28 million fund to assist farmers through industry changes has not been touched by the South Australian government for a decade.

The pool of money was established in the 1980s to provide loans and grants at the discretion of the primary industries and regions minister.

Liberal MLC leader Nicola Centofanti is calling for the money to be used to assist the struggling wine industry.

It has been revealed a South Australian government fund of more than $28 million to assist rural industries has sat unused for a decade.

The Rural Industry Adjustment and Development Fund was established in the 1980s to provide loans and grants at the discretion of the primary industries and regions minister.

The money can be used for farm development, changes in farming methods or to undertake a project or research for the benefit of farmers.

Growers in the state's Riverland said they were puzzled as to why the government had not used the funding to support the embattled region, which has hit crisis level after intense drought and poor wine market conditions.

The fund was established through the Rural Industry Adjustment and Development Act 1985. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

General manager of CCW Co-operative, a collective of independent Riverland growers, and Glossop wine grape grower Peter Szabo said he was shocked by the unspent funds.

"I was a little bit taken aback there was so much money just sitting around unspent and that this region is so in requirement of some financial assistance," he said.

"This sort of money injected into this region to help us keep our grape growers going and so forth would be just a change that would be fantastic for the entire region.

The fund has grown by $4 million since 2018, with about $1 million generated in interest in both 2024 and 2025, according to the auditor-general's reports.

Mr Szabo would like to see the funds help the region transform, including helping growers transition to other crops or out of the wine industry altogether.

"We need to find ways of transitioning to something else and that helps both our irrigation trusts and our local corner stores and retailers and tractor manufacturers and all the rest," he said.

"We've gotten to a point because we've received funding to employ a transformation officer … but it's very, very significant that there is a barrier of capital funds to allow people to transition to other commodities.

Peter Szabo says there is still a need for money to help grape growers through a hard time for the industry. (ABC Rural: Eliza Berlage)

"We are at a critical junction right now and probably 12 months [or] two years too late in seeking funding because a lot of people continue spending their own capital."

While some growers the ABC spoke to, who did not want to comment publicly, were not convinced more money would help due to global market pressures on wine, Loxton North wine grape and citrus grower Peter Hill would like to see it used to entice other industries to the region.

"I think that fund is certainly an opportunity for this region and obviously other agricultural regions in the state as well, but particularly the Riverland while it's suffering this downturn in the wine industry," he said.

Peter Hill says making the fund available would be a big opportunity for the region. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

"This region would be ideal for them to relocate to … whether it's a low-interest loan to relocate up here or there was new crops and that was incentivised.

"We need a more diversified region and then we've got less chance of this happening again.

Primary industries shadow minister Nicola Centofanti, who first highlighted the fund and questioned its lack of use in parliament, said she would like to see the unused money unlocked.

"The fund is sitting there, but at the same time we're not utilising it when growers are facing one of the most challenging periods in living memory," she said.

Nicola Centofanti wants the money to be made available to the state's wine industry. (ABC Riverland: Will Hunter)

The state government said the fund required interest on the loans to increase to commercial rates, which limited its effectiveness.

"If the Liberal Party was even aware the fund existed when they were in office, perhaps this limitation would explain why they did not utilise it at the time," a spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said primary industries minister Clare Scriven held two wine industry roundtables in the past 12 months and had reviewed recent funding for the industry and its future priorities.

South Australia's Premier has announced a $1 million reward for anyone who can provide critical information about the disappearance of Gus Lamont.

It has been almost a year since the four-year-old was reported missing from his home at Oak Park Station, a vast property near Yunta in South Australia's outback.

SA Police have said the investigation has been one of the largest and most intensive missing persons operations they have undertaken, with 11 ground searches conducted over 30 days as well as aerial efforts.
