ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Two children believed to have been abducted by a babysitter on Monday are safe and the suspect is in custody, according to the Atlanta Police Department.

Atlanta police say 11-month-old Norah Cooper and her sister 4-year-old Zola Cooper are safe and in good health, but taken to the hospital as a precaution.

The suspect’s name is Lakesha Brown, according to police. She has since been taken into custody after all three were found at the Gateway South Apartment Complex on Sylvan Road.

Brown is charged with kidnapping and will not receive bond.

Lt. Christapher Butler with Atlanta police said the suspect gained the mother’s trust over the course of a year before the abduction happened.

The girls’ mother, Elica Redding, said soon after having 11-month-old Norah, she’d befriended Brown online. She said Brown offered to come over and do Redding’s hair.

“She became a family friend from when I first met her on a mom group and she posted about giving free services for expecting moms. That’s how I met her, and after that we just started hanging,” said Redding.

Now, about a year later, Atlanta police said Redding let Brown babysit her children while she went out to eat Saturday around 6 p.m., but Brown and the children never came back. Redding reported the girls missing on Sunday.

“The mother thought she was leaving her children in the care of someone she could trust,” said Butler. “She’d gone out and there was some information that the suspect gave alluding to the fact that she was returning the children, which turned out not to be factual, so that’s what led to the delay of the 911 call.”

On Monday, Atlanta police said someone tipped them off in the Gateway South Apartment Complex. Officers arrived and heard a baby crying. That’s when they say they found Brown and the two girls in a trailer on the property.

An Amber Alert connected to the abduction was issued Monday morning. It included details about a white Ford F-350 truck with Alabama license plate number ICO87Y4.

Before the girls were found, Atlanta News First asked Redding what she wanted to do when she had her girls back in her arms.

“Hug them. I’m gonna hug them. I think they’re hungry, so I’m gonna feed them. I don’t know, I just want them back,” said Redding.

Police say this is not the first time Brown has been accused of doing something similar.

Atlanta police confirm Brown is the same woman arrested in Birmingham, Alabama, in 2021 for allegedly kidnapping a 4-day-old baby. Brown reportedly spent time getting close to the mother and plotting the kidnapping over several days.

She was charged with first-degree kidnapping. Butler said she has an outstanding warrant in Alabama for failing to appear in court.

Lynneice Washington, the Jefferson County district attorney in Alabama, told our sister station WBRC they will be filing a motion to revoke Brown’s bond after her arrest in Atlanta Monday.

“It’s sad. It’s scary and it’s sad. My heart goes out to the mother of those babies,” she said. “This is unacceptable, whether it’s in Georgia or Alabama. We have laws that are used to protect our children, and we also have laws that when they are violated, those adults have to be held accountable.”

Atlanta police thanked the Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) and the FBI for their assistance, and they credited cellphone data for getting them close to the suspect.

This is a developing story. Check back with Atlanta News First for updates.

ANALYSIS: As the US downgrades the nuclear submarines deal to second-hand vessels, Australia’s options to back out have narrowed to one possible shift in domestic politics.

Australia’s future Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines will all be second-hand – it’s about simplicity, according to Defence Minister Richard Marles. Previously, one of the boats was going to come fresh from the American production line but now all will be transferred from United States Navy service. Virginia-class submarines are built in versions or “blocks” so that new technology and design features can be incorporated over time. Australia will now get one block rather than two.

“What we will have here is a simpler pathway,” Marles told reporters at the International Institute for Strategic Studies Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore last week. “The Virginias we are acquiring will all be of the same type and I can’t overstate the significance of that.”

Of course, one easily could overstate the significance of this change, as the deputy prime minister went on to demonstrate by acknowledging it won’t make much difference to the price Australia pays for its submarines.

Still, Marles had a point. Before this latest announcement, Australia was effectively proposing to conduct four overlapping submarine projects: the upgrade of the navy’s existing Collins-class boats; introducing two versions of the Virginia-class; and the design and construction of an all-new submarine to be built in the United Kingdom and Adelaide. That’s now back to three, which, given Australia has never managed more than one submarine project at a time, still leaves plenty of room for risk.

Shadow defence minister Senator James Paterson had an uncomfortable question for the government: if getting only second-hand submarines is so clearly the right decision, why wasn’t it taken at the outset? Something else had clearly changed, but what?

The most plausible answer is that the US wants to keep the newest and most advanced version of the Virginia for itself. American shipyards are struggling to raise their productivity enough to fill the US Navy’s own order books, let alone meet the commitment to Australia. So the Pentagon is cutting its cloth, with Marles left to make the best of it.

The announcement reinforced a sense of scepticism about whether the Virginia-class submarines can be delivered at all. Up to this point, questioning of AUKUS has come predominantly from the progressive side of Australian politics. According to a report in The Australian newspaper this week, that now includes Labor Party backbencher Ed Husic and sections of the union movement.

Concerns about AUKUS now appear to be gaining purchase on the right, too. The Liberal Party had hitherto been loath to even consider the possibility of delays, but Senator Paterson gave a speech in April calling for the government to investigate alternative weapon systems that “may help fill any capability gaps that arise”.

If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities ... We may now have come too far to go back.

Former Abbott government treasurer Joe Hockey was more direct. Hockey is well briefed on this topic, as founding partner of the Washington, DC-based consultancy Bondi Partners, which says on its website: “With the evolution of AUKUS … Bondi Partners footprint continues to grow across the Pacific and the Atlantic.”

Hockey recently told the National Press Club that, for the first time, he was “a little nervous” about the delivery schedule for the Virginia-class submarines.

It raises a question that has seemed implausible until now: could the Albanese government step away from the AUKUS submarines? Is there a realistic pathway towards cancellation?

There are strong reasons to believe the government will maintain its commitment. For one thing, Marles is a powerful figure in the cabinet and appears to sincerely believe in the project.

If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities. It could have come to office in 2022 announcing an inquiry on the entirely justifiable basis that its endorsement of the project while in opposition was based on very little information released by the Morrison government.

Failing that, the Albanese government could have used the opportunity created by the Pentagon’s decision to review AUKUS, announced in June last year. That would have been the perfect moment to quietly communicate to the Trump administration that, if the review should happen to recommend against proceeding, Australia wouldn’t be too upset. This would have avoided any need for the government to take a “courageous” political stand against AUKUS. The prime minister could have told the nation this was America’s decision and, regretfully, Australia would have to move on from a flawed Morrison government initiative.

We may now have come too far to go back. Governments that invest significant political and financial capital in a major project are typically reluctant to admit a mistake, though it can happen. The last budget saw the cancellation of Inland Rail, which was expected to balloon to $45 billion. And, of course, Australia cancelled the French Attack-class project in 2021 to embark on AUKUS. But Australia had invested a mere $4 billion in the Attack-class before it was terminated; the sum for AUKUS is already more than twice that figure.

You might identify this as a textbook example of the sunk cost fallacy, a cognitive bias that sees people continue to pursue a project simply because they have already invested time, money and effort into it, even though it would be in their interest to stop. It’s not yet clear enough that AUKUS is failing for the government to think in these terms. AUKUS is inordinately risky, but we are still in the foothills of a project that will take 30 years or more, and it can’t be said that project is presently in crisis.

Another argument is that Australia has spent so long dithering over submarines that if we back out of AUKUS now, it will be too late to find submarines elsewhere before the Collins boats are retired. Australia, it is argued, cannot afford a submarine gap.

This elevates submarines to a status they don’t deserve. It is only mildly reductionist to say that a submarine is merely a transportation device, a way to move weapons (torpedoes and missiles) and the sensors that support them (sonars, infrared cameras and more) closer to their targets.

There are other ways to do that. If the mission is to sink enemy ships, you can use aircraft, surface ships and even missile-armed trucks. If the mission is to hit a target on the enemy’s territory, you can use bombers or long-range missiles. Granted, submarines can do things that these other platforms cannot and Australia is better off with submarines than without them – but not at any cost. If we must have a submarine gap, then we can compensate with other capabilities.

The government also has the alliance to consider. It is one thing to upset the French, but the Americans present altogether higher stakes. The entire AUKUS initiative has deep roots in Australia’s traditional fear of great-power abandonment. But we overstate the extent to which the purchase of American equipment will compel them to continue defending us and we exaggerate the damage that will be done by backing out. France, Germany and Türkiye caused far more offence to Washington in 2002-03 when they actively worked against the Bush administration’s plans to invade Iraq. All remain members of NATO to this day.

Should the Liberal Party’s doubts grow stronger, though, it will create “permission” for the government to move in the same direction. The whole reason the Labor government finds itself in this position is that when AUKUS was announced, less than a year before the 2022 federal election, the then opposition spotted a political trap – an unpopular Morrison government was baiting the Labor Party to oppose the initiative so the Liberals could revive their electoral fortunes by engineering a “khaki election”. Labor refused to take the bait, endorsing AUKUS immediately. If doubts on the Liberal side grow stronger and they even begin to see AUKUS as a stick with which to beat the government, the Labor Party’s incentives will change.

This is a slow drip, however. For a circuit breaker, a force that could disrupt AUKUS in a matter of days rather than months or years, it can only be US President Trump. The government recognised Trump’s unpopularity in Australia from the beginning and benefited from it electorally in 2025 when the Dutton opposition flirted with MAGA-ism and paid the price. The 2025 Lowy Institute Poll showed a 20-point drop in Australians’ trust in the US to act responsibly in the world.

We see this anxiety reflected also in Marles’s recent speech to the Lowy Institute, in which he implicitly distanced his government from Trump by arguing that Labor has always been the party committed to Australian independence. Quite how that squares with the embrace of AUKUS and the agreement to station US forces in Western Australia and the Northern Territory was not explained.

Australia has escaped lightly in its dealings with Trump so far. Indeed, last October’s Trump–Albanese White House meeting was a political triumph for the government. But so mercurial is this US administration that the relationship could change in an instant. Canada is the cautionary tale here and it is notable that Prime Minister Mark Carney has responded to Trump’s provocations by insisting that Canada should become less dependent on American weapons “so we are never hostage to the decisions of others when it comes to our security”.

In truth, that’s not a realistic ambition for Canada, which is bound to the US by geography. Australia faces no such physical constraints – only the psychological one of refusing to believe we can face a difficult regional security environment on our own.

Since the announcement of AUKUS in September 2021, I have been a frequent critic. I couldn’t see any rational explanation for its undertaking or any benefit that would make Australia more secure. In return for a vast expenditure of taxpayers’ dollars, Australia’s leaders decided to accept much greater risk to the nation – up to and including nuclear annihilation – without any tangible gain. They did so on the basis of the distant and possible non-arrival of promised nuclear-powered submarines.

Then I had a revelation. My approach until now had been to examine AUKUS through a national security lens. This was a mistake. I had wrongly assumed the government used the same methodology and in doing so I had failed to consider the cognitive limits of our political leaders. What I had not realised was that the government’s approach to national security has an overwhelming cultural bias, whose origins date to the establishment of the nation in 1901.

The enthusiasm of the Australian political class for AUKUS is founded on values that were codified at Federation and have underpinned national security decision-making ever since. AUKUS represents not so much a response to a security threat – Australia remains among the safest countries in the world – but rather the veneration of a longstanding cultural tradition.

This realisation does nothing to persuade me AUKUS is a good deal for the country, but at least I now understand how something so patently foolish came to be so easily accepted and vigorously defended by members of our political class. I now understand how the leaders of both the Labor and Coalition political parties have so easily wedded themselves to the same policy and have done so with minimal consultation, even with their backbenchers, let alone members of the public.

Australian national security culture is founded on the interaction of three factors: fear, self-delusion and status seeking. All date from the Federation of the nation in 1901 and have steered security decision-making for 125 years. I will take each one in turn.

Fear is Australia’s founding emotion. The nation’s history has witnessed numerous invasion scares in which a foreign power was supposedly poised to take over the country. Candidates for Australia’s potential overlord included France, Russia, Japan, China and even the United States. These scares all lacked any basis in reality. Our continent’s immutable geography has always made it among the safest places in the world. The only invasion it has known was the one that began in 1788 with the arrival of the First Fleet and its convict settlers.

Australian governments have always accepted as fact two unproven propositions – the possibility of invasion and the nation’s inability to defend itself. Consequently Australia has always relied on a great power protector for its security.

This fear of invasion masked an even greater terror that dominated the focus of the nation’s first leaders ­– the fear of the “yellow peril” from the north. Asia’s proximity caused many Australians to fear being overwhelmed by the mass arrival of migrants from there. In 1901, this fear was laid out in the most plain, direct and racist terms in the nation’s first parliament. Parliamentarians held nothing back as they debated and approved the Immigration Restriction Act, the foundational legislation of the White Australia policy.

Fear of Chinese and other Asian migrants taking over the country flowed into the second cultural factor that underpins Australia’s construction of national security, which is self-delusion. Australian governments have always accepted as fact two unproven propositions – the possibility of invasion, as noted above, and the nation’s inability to defend itself. Consequently Australia has always relied on a great power protector for its security. First it was the United Kingdom and now it is the US.

At Federation, Australia lacked the population, industrial development and wealth to defend itself against a major power, so handing national security to London was the best option. However, these weaknesses are no longer applicable. Australia is a modern, wealthy state with an educated population and has the enormous defensive benefit of possessing no land borders. Moreover, modern military technologies such as long-range precision missiles and drones, coupled with ubiquitous sensors, favour the defender.

So embedded has been this faith in a great power coming to Australia’s aid that even the failure of the Singapore Strategy in World War II has done nothing to deter subsequent government leaders from embracing it. All that happened was that we changed friends, not our beliefs or expectations.

The final factor is Australia’s continuing aspiration for a higher status in the ranking of the world’s nations than it would naturally deserve on its own. Australia claims to be a middle power, but the reality is that in the distribution of power only great states matter. Despite its vast natural resources, Australia lacks the population and industrial base to achieve great power status.

There is a substitute for power in our own right, however – the chance to bask in the reflected glory of more important friends. Clinton Fernandes, a professor of international and political studies at UNSW Canberra, hit the bullseye when he wrote of “sub-imperial power” to describe Australia’s ambition and place in the world.

Australia positions itself within the aura of a great power and thereby bestows upon itself the same place in the world, although this is not done without cost. When the protector was the UK, this positioning was a reflection of its place in the British Empire. As Britain’s status declined, Australia sought a new place to shelter and became an unofficial member of the American empire. When George W. Bush called John Howard his “sheriff” the term encompassed more than just a passing reference to Australia’s role in the region. It was a recognition of Australia’s position in the global order.

Australian leaders consider maintaining the relationship with the US to be their most vital defence responsibility. They pretend not to notice when the US starts an illegal war, threatens allies or implements a vindictive tariff policy. The equanimity with which Richard Marles received the US decision that Australia would only receive three second-hand submarines rather than two used and one new highlights the government’s inability to question Washington, despite being the victim of a bait and switch. The earlier desperation with which Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pursued a meeting with President Donald Trump and finally settled for a photo-op might be seen by many as an embarrassment. For the prime minister, it was policy.

The decisive role of this institutional mindset in Australian national security deliberations points to the challenge of making a change. There is a saying among those who think about strategy: culture eats strategy for breakfast. Australia demonstrates the insightfulness of those words.

Culture is always a factor in strategy-making, and it should be. How a people see themselves must play a part in a country’s deliberations on the way it approaches security. Yet entrenched culture must not be prioritised at the expense of other factors, as is being done in Australia. Geography, psychology and a realistic assessment of the threat environment must be accorded a high degree of influence.

Our perception of insecurity and our desire for global status dominate security decision-making. Moreover, these are cultural factors that were cemented in a bygone age. As the world has evolved and as Australia has changed, our political class has failed to keep pace and remains mired in an outdated mindset.

This can be read in government defence policy papers. Typically, they include a statement to the effect that the world is becoming more dangerous and unpredictable and is witnessing intense strategic competition. Invariably, the solution is to intensify the relationship with our protector, the US. Despite admitting to a changing security environment, the government’s solution is more of the same. AUKUS and a continued policy of dependence is the outcome.

Climate change, the growth of Chinese power, increasing irrationality in the US and the undermining of the global rules-based order all suggest the context for decision-making warrants something new. Yet the emergence of new problems is met with the same fear, self-delusion and desire to remain under the care of a protector.

After 125 years of this, the actions of our political leaders are testament to the difficulty of changing culture. However, Australia desperately needs to do so. It needs to accept the futility of remaining in a world shaped by the values of 1901.

AUKUS does make a perverse kind of sense, in that it is not an aberration but the extension of past practice. Any consideration of other and better options is simply not possible within the current cultural perspective. AUKUS’s validation rests on the founding ethos of an insecure nation. It is perpetuated by a present leadership that is unable to escape the limitations of the past.

Australia’s leaders could overcome the cultural bias that they bring to national security, but so far they have shown little interest in doing so. Leaders, by definition, are meant to lead. In this case, they are simply following a century of political predecessors.

Until this cultural baggage is dealt with, and governments begin making decisions based on contemporary realities and actual defence needs, AUKUS will stay.

Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

ANALYSIS: As the US downgrades the nuclear submarines deal to second-hand vessels, Australia’s options to back out have narrowed to one possible shift in domestic politics.

Australia’s future Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines will all be second-hand – it’s about simplicity, according to Defence Minister Richard Marles. Previously, one of the boats was going to come fresh from the American production line but now all will be transferred from United States Navy service. Virginia-class submarines are built in versions or “blocks” so that new technology and design features can be incorporated over time. Australia will now get one block rather than two.

“What we will have here is a simpler pathway,” Marles told reporters at the International Institute for Strategic Studies Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore last week. “The Virginias we are acquiring will all be of the same type and I can’t overstate the significance of that.”

Of course, one easily could overstate the significance of this change, as the deputy prime minister went on to demonstrate by acknowledging it won’t make much difference to the price Australia pays for its submarines.

Still, Marles had a point. Before this latest announcement, Australia was effectively proposing to conduct four overlapping submarine projects: the upgrade of the navy’s existing Collins-class boats; introducing two versions of the Virginia-class; and the design and construction of an all-new submarine to be built in the United Kingdom and Adelaide. That’s now back to three, which, given Australia has never managed more than one submarine project at a time, still leaves plenty of room for risk.

Shadow defence minister Senator James Paterson had an uncomfortable question for the government: if getting only second-hand submarines is so clearly the right decision, why wasn’t it taken at the outset? Something else had clearly changed, but what?

The most plausible answer is that the US wants to keep the newest and most advanced version of the Virginia for itself. American shipyards are struggling to raise their productivity enough to fill the US Navy’s own order books, let alone meet the commitment to Australia. So the Pentagon is cutting its cloth, with Marles left to make the best of it.

The announcement reinforced a sense of scepticism about whether the Virginia-class submarines can be delivered at all. Up to this point, questioning of AUKUS has come predominantly from the progressive side of Australian politics. According to a report in The Australian newspaper this week, that now includes Labor Party backbencher Ed Husic and sections of the union movement.

Concerns about AUKUS now appear to be gaining purchase on the right, too. The Liberal Party had hitherto been loath to even consider the possibility of delays, but Senator Paterson gave a speech in April calling for the government to investigate alternative weapon systems that “may help fill any capability gaps that arise”.

If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities ... We may now have come too far to go back.

Former Abbott government treasurer Joe Hockey was more direct. Hockey is well briefed on this topic, as founding partner of the Washington, DC-based consultancy Bondi Partners, which says on its website: “With the evolution of AUKUS … Bondi Partners footprint continues to grow across the Pacific and the Atlantic.”

Hockey recently told the National Press Club that, for the first time, he was “a little nervous” about the delivery schedule for the Virginia-class submarines.

It raises a question that has seemed implausible until now: could the Albanese government step away from the AUKUS submarines? Is there a realistic pathway towards cancellation?

There are strong reasons to believe the government will maintain its commitment. For one thing, Marles is a powerful figure in the cabinet and appears to sincerely believe in the project.

If Labor was ever minded to revise AUKUS, it has already passed up two golden opportunities. It could have come to office in 2022 announcing an inquiry on the entirely justifiable basis that its endorsement of the project while in opposition was based on very little information released by the Morrison government.

Failing that, the Albanese government could have used the opportunity created by the Pentagon’s decision to review AUKUS, announced in June last year. That would have been the perfect moment to quietly communicate to the Trump administration that, if the review should happen to recommend against proceeding, Australia wouldn’t be too upset. This would have avoided any need for the government to take a “courageous” political stand against AUKUS. The prime minister could have told the nation this was America’s decision and, regretfully, Australia would have to move on from a flawed Morrison government initiative.

We may now have come too far to go back. Governments that invest significant political and financial capital in a major project are typically reluctant to admit a mistake, though it can happen. The last budget saw the cancellation of Inland Rail, which was expected to balloon to $45 billion. And, of course, Australia cancelled the French Attack-class project in 2021 to embark on AUKUS. But Australia had invested a mere $4 billion in the Attack-class before it was terminated; the sum for AUKUS is already more than twice that figure.

You might identify this as a textbook example of the sunk cost fallacy, a cognitive bias that sees people continue to pursue a project simply because they have already invested time, money and effort into it, even though it would be in their interest to stop. It’s not yet clear enough that AUKUS is failing for the government to think in these terms. AUKUS is inordinately risky, but we are still in the foothills of a project that will take 30 years or more, and it can’t be said that project is presently in crisis.

Another argument is that Australia has spent so long dithering over submarines that if we back out of AUKUS now, it will be too late to find submarines elsewhere before the Collins boats are retired. Australia, it is argued, cannot afford a submarine gap.

This elevates submarines to a status they don’t deserve. It is only mildly reductionist to say that a submarine is merely a transportation device, a way to move weapons (torpedoes and missiles) and the sensors that support them (sonars, infrared cameras and more) closer to their targets.

There are other ways to do that. If the mission is to sink enemy ships, you can use aircraft, surface ships and even missile-armed trucks. If the mission is to hit a target on the enemy’s territory, you can use bombers or long-range missiles. Granted, submarines can do things that these other platforms cannot and Australia is better off with submarines than without them – but not at any cost. If we must have a submarine gap, then we can compensate with other capabilities.

The government also has the alliance to consider. It is one thing to upset the French, but the Americans present altogether higher stakes. The entire AUKUS initiative has deep roots in Australia’s traditional fear of great-power abandonment. But we overstate the extent to which the purchase of American equipment will compel them to continue defending us and we exaggerate the damage that will be done by backing out. France, Germany and Türkiye caused far more offence to Washington in 2002-03 when they actively worked against the Bush administration’s plans to invade Iraq. All remain members of NATO to this day.

Should the Liberal Party’s doubts grow stronger, though, it will create “permission” for the government to move in the same direction. The whole reason the Labor government finds itself in this position is that when AUKUS was announced, less than a year before the 2022 federal election, the then opposition spotted a political trap – an unpopular Morrison government was baiting the Labor Party to oppose the initiative so the Liberals could revive their electoral fortunes by engineering a “khaki election”. Labor refused to take the bait, endorsing AUKUS immediately. If doubts on the Liberal side grow stronger and they even begin to see AUKUS as a stick with which to beat the government, the Labor Party’s incentives will change.

This is a slow drip, however. For a circuit breaker, a force that could disrupt AUKUS in a matter of days rather than months or years, it can only be US President Trump. The government recognised Trump’s unpopularity in Australia from the beginning and benefited from it electorally in 2025 when the Dutton opposition flirted with MAGA-ism and paid the price. The 2025 Lowy Institute Poll showed a 20-point drop in Australians’ trust in the US to act responsibly in the world.

We see this anxiety reflected also in Marles’s recent speech to the Lowy Institute, in which he implicitly distanced his government from Trump by arguing that Labor has always been the party committed to Australian independence. Quite how that squares with the embrace of AUKUS and the agreement to station US forces in Western Australia and the Northern Territory was not explained.

Australia has escaped lightly in its dealings with Trump so far. Indeed, last October’s Trump–Albanese White House meeting was a political triumph for the government. But so mercurial is this US administration that the relationship could change in an instant. Canada is the cautionary tale here and it is notable that Prime Minister Mark Carney has responded to Trump’s provocations by insisting that Canada should become less dependent on American weapons “so we are never hostage to the decisions of others when it comes to our security”.

In truth, that’s not a realistic ambition for Canada, which is bound to the US by geography. Australia faces no such physical constraints – only the psychological one of refusing to believe we can face a difficult regional security environment on our own.

By NOAH SECOMB FOR AUSTRALIAN ASSOCIATED PRESS

Published:  16:13 AEST, 20 September 2026   |  Updated:  16:23 AEST, 20 September 2026

The average Australian will live to their mid-to-late 80s within a few generations, but the nation will have to get its health policies right to make the most of the added years.

Treasury's latest Intergenerational Report, to be published in full on Monday, will project the impact of government policies 40 years into the future.

An extract released on Sunday showed life expectancy at birth was forecast to reach almost 90 for women by 2065/66, up from about 86 years at present.

Life expectancy for men was predicted to rise to 86 years in the next four decades, up from 82 years.

The figures would retain Australia's record for one of the highest life expectancies in the world.

Australian Medical Association chief Danielle McMullen welcomed the rise as a sign of policy success, but warned of the challenge to ensure the extra years were worth living.

'Over the last few generations we're living longer, but we're also living more years in ill health with chronic disease or mental illness,' she told ABC News on Sunday.

'That's certainly something as doctors we would want to turn around and make sure people are staying healthy as well as living longer lives.'

Jim Chalmers (pictured) said the report was 'confronting' in some cases but not pessimistic

More focus should be put on preventative health, Dr McMullen said, noting regular interactions with doctors earlier in life could reduce chronic ailments later on.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the report laid out the case for further investments in Medicare and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, and the rollout of urgent care clinics.

But a growing and aging population would also be at the centre of long-term budget pressures, Chalmers told News24's Sunday Agenda program.

'There are elements of the intergenerational report which are confronting, but it's not a pessimistic report ... because Australians are genuinely better placed and better prepared for all of this accelerating change that we are seeing,' he said.

Australia's population is expected to be slightly lower by the mid-2060s than forecast in the 2023 Intergenerational Report.

Population growth was expected to slow to 0.9 per cent per year over the next four decades, down from 1.4 per cent annually in the previous 40 years, according to Treasury forecasts.

The nation's population was predicted to reach 39.3 million by 2065/66, 1.8 million lower than the 2023 forecast.

Much of the slowdown in population growth was tied to lower fertility rates as women continued to have fewer children.

Australia's population is set to be lower than first forecast in the 2023 Intergenerational Report. Pictured, commuters at Parramatta train station

'Almost half the decline in fertility rates is actually because fewer people are having three or more kids and what that reflects is mums having fewer kids later in life,' Chalmers said.

'Our job is to make it a little bit easier for people to make that choice if they want to,' he said, noting Labor's policies to subsidise child care, increase paid parental leave and lift mandatory superannuation contributions.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said young families should be able to have confidence they could afford to have children, but the Coalition had no plans to revive the Howard and Costello-era 'baby bonus' policy.

Future government debt is expected to be slashed by half a trillion dollars compared to forecasts in the 2023 report, but much of the economic progress relies on emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence.

'Overwhelmingly, the fiscal story is a little bit better; but still, lots, lots more work to do to manage some of these pressures and risks,' Chalmers said.

Previous Treasury advice suggested AI could provide significant productivity gains across the public and private sectors if the nation kept pace with the global shift towards the technology.

Mr Taylor said Labor would 'cook the books' and rely on rosy productivity assumptions to deliver better-than-expected budget forecasts.

An ICE officer shot a man in Austin, Texas, on Sunday, prompting a crowd of angry demonstrators to gather near the scene, hurl obscenities and clash with authorities.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) sources confirmed to Fox News that the man shot by the ICE officer is an illegal immigrant from Venezuela with a final order of removal.

The agency said the man "illegally entered the country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal during a law enforcement operation" in Austin, Texas Sunday.

"The illegal alien's condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal," DHS wrote on X.

'SQUAD' MEMBER CALLS DHS 'GREATEST THREAT TO OUR SAFETY' AFTER ICE-INVOLVED SHOOTING

The man was later identified by his lawyer as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez. His lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said her client entered the U.S. lawfully.

"We are actively working to obtain additional information and clarify the circumstances surrounding the matter. We do not want to speculate or provide information that has not yet been confirmed. What we do understand is that he previously held a valid work permit and that, based on the information available to us, he entered the United States lawfully," Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a statement to Fox News.

Video from the scene showed people holding up their phones and carrying flags as the commotion unfolded. Police said preliminary information indicated the man was shot once in the torso during a brief foot pursuit involving ICE. He was hospitalized in serious but stable condition.

Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis and Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz confirmed ICE was involved in the shooting and provided what they repeatedly stressed were preliminary details during a Sunday afternoon news conference.

Austin-Travis County EMS was notified of the shooting at approximately 12:56 p.m. and arrived in less than five minutes, Luckritz said.

The adult man was taken from the scene within nine minutes and transported to a local trauma center in serious but stable condition.

Davis said preliminary information indicated there was a brief foot pursuit before the shooting but cautioned that she had not yet been briefed by federal authorities.

ICE agents gather near the scene of a shooting in Austin, Texas. (KTBC)

"From what I'm hearing, there was a small foot pursuit," Davis said. "But again, this is all very preliminary."

Watson stressed that the information available was "extremely preliminary." He said city officials wanted to make themselves available as quickly as possible when they had information but warned against rushing to conclusions based on early claims circulating on TikTok, X and other social media platforms.

Watson added that the Austin Police Department was not involved in the shooting and only assisted with traffic control. APD's Special Investigations Unit and the Texas Rangers will work together to investigate the incident, Davis said.

"The city of Austin deserves answers," Davis said. "We're going to get all those questions answered, and we'll be as transparent as we can be."

DHS announced later Sunday that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), with assistance from the FBI, is taking the lead on the investigation.

A crowd of people gather near the scene of an ICE shooting in Austin, Texas. (KTBC)

Watson said he was "very angry" and "extremely unhappy" about the shooting, while accusing ICE of creating fear and chaos in Austin and other cities. He also questioned the agency's ability to investigate itself without local involvement.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client was released from the hospital and is believed to now be in ICE custody.

"Hospital attorneys at Dell Seton Medical Center have confirmed that Wilber Rafael Garces Perez has been released from the hospital into what we believe is ICE custody. After he was held for approximately six hours, officers declined to provide his wife with meaningful information about his status or circumstances," she said in her statement. "We are deeply concerned that his wife and family have not been permitted to see him and have not received a meaningful update regarding his current condition or whereabouts."

"Our immediate concern is ensuring that his family receives accurate and timely information and that appropriate access and communication are provided while the matter is being addressed," she continued.

ICE AGENTS IN FATAL HOUSTON SHOOTING WERE NOT WEARING BODY CAMERAS, SOURCES SAY

Rep. Greg Casar participates in a public forum on the use of force by Department of Homeland Security agents at the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 3. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

Lincoln-Goldfinch is scheduled to host a press conference in collaboration with the League of United Latin American Citizens at 1 p.m. Monday to address the incident.

Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, claimed in a post on X that "ICE has shot a person in Austin this morning" and called for a full, independent investigation and the immediate release of body-camera footage.

"Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened," Casar wrote. "We will demand truth, transparency and accountability."

During the news conference, Casar called the incident part of a "disturbing pattern" and said ICE's conduct "has got to stop."

The demand for Australian citrus in Korea was on display this season as consumers eagerly engaged with promotions run by the Australian industry.

Citrus Australia conducted the 2026 Australian Citrus Retail Promotion in August, delivered through the Australian Table Grapes Association (ATGA) consortium and supported by funding from the Accessing New Markets Initiative (ANMI).

”For industry members, it was a clear example of collaboration delivering practical outcomes by building relationships, strengthening market knowledge, and increasing understanding and appreciation of Australian citrus.”

Dane Richmond, Austrade trade and investment commissioner, said the promotion delivered exceptionally strong results.

“The campaign significantly increased awareness of Australian oranges among Korean consumers and helped position them as a premium seasonal fruit option during the summer months, complementing locally grown Korean produce,” he said.

The promotion generated strong commercial outcomes, with all 3 participating retailers reporting triple-digit growth in both sales and volume during the campaign period.

”Retailers were highly encouraged by the response from consumers,” Richmond said. “One retailer reported that strong sales momentum continued into the following weekend after the tasting event had concluded, while another expressed interest in extending the campaign due to its success.”

australian-national-security-culture-is-:
Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

Since the announcement of AUKUS in September 2021, I have been a frequent critic. I couldn’t see any rational explanation for its undertaking or any benefit that would make Australia more secure. In return for a vast expenditure of taxpayers’ dollars, Australia’s leaders decided to accept much greater risk to the nation – up to and including nuclear annihilation – without any tangible gain. They did so on the basis of the distant and possible non-arrival of promised nuclear-powered submarines.

Then I had a revelation. My approach until now had been to examine AUKUS through a national security lens. This was a mistake. I had wrongly assumed the government used the same methodology and in doing so I had failed to consider the cognitive limits of our political leaders. What I had not realised was that the government’s approach to national security has an overwhelming cultural bias, whose origins date to the establishment of the nation in 1901.

The enthusiasm of the Australian political class for AUKUS is founded on values that were codified at Federation and have underpinned national security decision-making ever since. AUKUS represents not so much a response to a security threat – Australia remains among the safest countries in the world – but rather the veneration of a longstanding cultural tradition.

This realisation does nothing to persuade me AUKUS is a good deal for the country, but at least I now understand how something so patently foolish came to be so easily accepted and vigorously defended by members of our political class. I now understand how the leaders of both the Labor and Coalition political parties have so easily wedded themselves to the same policy and have done so with minimal consultation, even with their backbenchers, let alone members of the public.

Australian national security culture is founded on the interaction of three factors: fear, self-delusion and status seeking. All date from the Federation of the nation in 1901 and have steered security decision-making for 125 years. I will take each one in turn.

Fear is Australia’s founding emotion. The nation’s history has witnessed numerous invasion scares in which a foreign power was supposedly poised to take over the country. Candidates for Australia’s potential overlord included France, Russia, Japan, China and even the United States. These scares all lacked any basis in reality. Our continent’s immutable geography has always made it among the safest places in the world. The only invasion it has known was the one that began in 1788 with the arrival of the First Fleet and its convict settlers.

Australian governments have always accepted as fact two unproven propositions – the possibility of invasion and the nation’s inability to defend itself. Consequently Australia has always relied on a great power protector for its security.

This fear of invasion masked an even greater terror that dominated the focus of the nation’s first leaders ­– the fear of the “yellow peril” from the north. Asia’s proximity caused many Australians to fear being overwhelmed by the mass arrival of migrants from there. In 1901, this fear was laid out in the most plain, direct and racist terms in the nation’s first parliament. Parliamentarians held nothing back as they debated and approved the Immigration Restriction Act, the foundational legislation of the White Australia policy.

Fear of Chinese and other Asian migrants taking over the country flowed into the second cultural factor that underpins Australia’s construction of national security, which is self-delusion. Australian governments have always accepted as fact two unproven propositions – the possibility of invasion, as noted above, and the nation’s inability to defend itself. Consequently Australia has always relied on a great power protector for its security. First it was the United Kingdom and now it is the US.

At Federation, Australia lacked the population, industrial development and wealth to defend itself against a major power, so handing national security to London was the best option. However, these weaknesses are no longer applicable. Australia is a modern, wealthy state with an educated population and has the enormous defensive benefit of possessing no land borders. Moreover, modern military technologies such as long-range precision missiles and drones, coupled with ubiquitous sensors, favour the defender.

So embedded has been this faith in a great power coming to Australia’s aid that even the failure of the Singapore Strategy in World War II has done nothing to deter subsequent government leaders from embracing it. All that happened was that we changed friends, not our beliefs or expectations.

The final factor is Australia’s continuing aspiration for a higher status in the ranking of the world’s nations than it would naturally deserve on its own. Australia claims to be a middle power, but the reality is that in the distribution of power only great states matter. Despite its vast natural resources, Australia lacks the population and industrial base to achieve great power status.

There is a substitute for power in our own right, however – the chance to bask in the reflected glory of more important friends. Clinton Fernandes, a professor of international and political studies at UNSW Canberra, hit the bullseye when he wrote of “sub-imperial power” to describe Australia’s ambition and place in the world.

Australia positions itself within the aura of a great power and thereby bestows upon itself the same place in the world, although this is not done without cost. When the protector was the UK, this positioning was a reflection of its place in the British Empire. As Britain’s status declined, Australia sought a new place to shelter and became an unofficial member of the American empire. When George W. Bush called John Howard his “sheriff” the term encompassed more than just a passing reference to Australia’s role in the region. It was a recognition of Australia’s position in the global order.

Australian leaders consider maintaining the relationship with the US to be their most vital defence responsibility. They pretend not to notice when the US starts an illegal war, threatens allies or implements a vindictive tariff policy. The equanimity with which Richard Marles received the US decision that Australia would only receive three second-hand submarines rather than two used and one new highlights the government’s inability to question Washington, despite being the victim of a bait and switch. The earlier desperation with which Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pursued a meeting with President Donald Trump and finally settled for a photo-op might be seen by many as an embarrassment. For the prime minister, it was policy.

The decisive role of this institutional mindset in Australian national security deliberations points to the challenge of making a change. There is a saying among those who think about strategy: culture eats strategy for breakfast. Australia demonstrates the insightfulness of those words.

Culture is always a factor in strategy-making, and it should be. How a people see themselves must play a part in a country’s deliberations on the way it approaches security. Yet entrenched culture must not be prioritised at the expense of other factors, as is being done in Australia. Geography, psychology and a realistic assessment of the threat environment must be accorded a high degree of influence.

Our perception of insecurity and our desire for global status dominate security decision-making. Moreover, these are cultural factors that were cemented in a bygone age. As the world has evolved and as Australia has changed, our political class has failed to keep pace and remains mired in an outdated mindset.

This can be read in government defence policy papers. Typically, they include a statement to the effect that the world is becoming more dangerous and unpredictable and is witnessing intense strategic competition. Invariably, the solution is to intensify the relationship with our protector, the US. Despite admitting to a changing security environment, the government’s solution is more of the same. AUKUS and a continued policy of dependence is the outcome.

Climate change, the growth of Chinese power, increasing irrationality in the US and the undermining of the global rules-based order all suggest the context for decision-making warrants something new. Yet the emergence of new problems is met with the same fear, self-delusion and desire to remain under the care of a protector.

After 125 years of this, the actions of our political leaders are testament to the difficulty of changing culture. However, Australia desperately needs to do so. It needs to accept the futility of remaining in a world shaped by the values of 1901.

AUKUS does make a perverse kind of sense, in that it is not an aberration but the extension of past practice. Any consideration of other and better options is simply not possible within the current cultural perspective. AUKUS’s validation rests on the founding ethos of an insecure nation. It is perpetuated by a present leadership that is unable to escape the limitations of the past.

Australia’s leaders could overcome the cultural bias that they bring to national security, but so far they have shown little interest in doing so. Leaders, by definition, are meant to lead. In this case, they are simply following a century of political predecessors.

Until this cultural baggage is dealt with, and governments begin making decisions based on contemporary realities and actual defence needs, AUKUS will stay.

Albert Palazzo is an adjunct professor at UNSW Canberra.

authenticity_pop_music:
Raw emotion, confessional lyrics and sharing everything in videos online.

In 2026, fans want their pop stars honest, raw and real.

Olivia Rodrigo, arguably the queen of the new, unfiltered breed of female singers, has dominated the UK charts this week with three top-five singles.

She's also landed a number one album which, in her words, chronicles a "love story that falls apart".

And Rodrigo's not the only one having similar success.

Lola Young and Olivia Dean are also among the singers whose perceived authenticity has won them millions of fans and multiple prestigious awards.

It seems to be the end result of a shift where the music industry has gone from a world run by record labels and managers to one where artists appear to control the narrative.

How real those stories are is something we may never know - even Olivia Rodrigo has previously admitted some of her songs aren't inspired by her own experiences.

But there's clearly a demand for the confessional style.

BBC Newsbeat's been speaking to artists and those who work behind-the-scenes on helping them to build their images about the opportunities it creates and the demands and challenges it presents.

British singer Alessi Rose, a BBC Radio 1 Sound of 2026 nominee, says pop music did not use to be seen as a place to process serious thoughts and emotions.

"Whereas now there are so many pop stars that speak about things that are so personal and so intricate and niche.

"It's so great that so many people relate to it," she tells Newsbeat.

The 23-year-old's poetic observations on heartbreak and self-doubt have led to her being dubbed by some as "Derbyshire's Olivia Rodrigo".

Rose's latest single, Skin, explores "feeling not quite myself and cycling through all these thoughts that the average teenager to 20-something is constantly going through".

Record label owner and artist coach Stevie Red McMinn feels fans want "more transparency" from artists and for "something to feel real and raw".

For a long time, he says, the music industry felt "curated and almost to a certain degree manufactured".

McMinn says even 10 years ago record labels were able to control the narrative more and decide how an artist would be presented to the world.

"It was sort of very gatekeepery as the only way that you could get your music or anything in front of fans was by going through specific channels, which were record labels and the media," he tells Newsbeat.

"Whereas with social media, you don't have to sign to a record label, you don't have to do press interviews, you can basically just speak to your fans."

Singer Rose says her honest outpourings aren't just limited to her songwriting, and she is "someone who's very myself online".

It can bring "excessive levels of both positivity, but also criticism," she says.

"But to be polarising is to be talked about and to be cared about, and I think I'd always rather that than be constantly treading on eggshells and trying to dictate how people perceive you."

Singer-songwriter Erin Le Count has capitalised on this shift by building a young, devoted fanbase through her alt-pop sound and selfie-style videos filmed in her bedroom.

When it comes to what posts she's putting out, the 23-year-old says she never worries about appearing authentic but focuses on being "creative" and "joyful".

"Everything on social media is really just me having a giggle, which is the truth of it. And that's all it should ever be, I think," she tells Newsbeat.

And while Le Count says she's not overthinking her content too much, McMinn observes she has still been able to curate a brand and an aesthetic by dressing her bedroom to reflect her gothic-pop style.

McMinn still thinks it feels "more human, more real" and "fans really, really resonate with it".

Deeply personal lyrics, hours of video and hundreds of social media posts can feel like a gift for devoted fans who want to pick through every morsel their favourite singer throws their way.

But some would argue it creates a parasocial dynamic where people feel like they have a relationship with a famous person they do not know.

London-born singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri says she feels it's important to show your authentic self, but also champions having boundaries.

"I feel like we live in a time where everyone feels like they're obligated to post everything about themselves, but actually you're allowed to keep things about yourself to yourself and you owe yourself that," she says.

"So be authentic, but you don't have to put everything online as well."

This desire for authenticity also comes as artificial intelligence has become more prevalent within online content and music.

McMinn believes fans have become "more sophisticated" and "knowledgeable" about the inner workings of the music industry as people are being more open about it.

"I just do think that the more unapologetic you are able to be, and the more honest you're able to be, I think it resonates," he says.

"If I'm ever working with an artist, I'm like: 'Only be authentic and vulnerable if that's what feels real to you'.

"Because at the end of the day, I don't think it's going to do you any favours to be performative anyway."

aws-billing-glitch:
A glitch with Amazon Web Services’ billing operation led some customers to believe they owed the world’s fifth most valuable company billions of dollars. Oops!

Bill Radjewski, who runs CollegeFootballData.com, was one of the affected customers. This morning, he woke up to a jarring email alert from AWS: He had racked up more than $1.5 billion in usage fees, and his August 1 bill was on track to be upwards of $3 billion.

“I've had this account for 6+ years and in that time my monthly spend has never exceeded $0.02,” Radjewski tells WIRED in an email. He shared screenshots of his three most recent monthly AWS invoices. They each came out to $0.01.

Based on replies to the AWS Support account on X, Radjewski is not alone. Others have received similarly shocking quotes: $22 billion; $75 billion; $110 billion. “Blud why did you hit me with a cost of 5 million USD what did I even do,” one user wrote. “Please explain man my heart will explode.”

When reached for comment, Amazon spokesperson Aisha Johnson referred WIRED to the AWS Service Health Dashboard. While it’s not clear exactly how many customers have been affected, the dashboard characterized the issue as “global.”

The dashboard also said that the billing console “began displaying incorrect estimated billing data” on Thursday, July 16, at 10:38 pm EDT.

The company began investigating the issue about six hours later, per the dashboard, and concluded that the “root cause” of the error was “an issue with unit pricing within the estimated billing computation subsystem.” It did not specify what the issue was.

In subsequent updates, AWS said it’s “rolling back a recent change to the billing computation subsystem” and that it was attempting to revert to its “last known good estimated bill computation.” It also said it had “paused estimated billing computations.”

The issue should be resolved by this weekend, and “there are no customer actions required at this time,” the company wrote.

Ultimately, some customers have decided to post through it.

One Reddit user posted a screenshot of their current "cost and usage overview" to the AWS subreddit, which showed that they had incurred $7.1 trillion in service fees since July 1—more than twice Amazon’s market cap.

aws_ai_investment_2026:
In this article

Amazon Web Services on Tuesday announced it is investing $1 billion in a new Forward Deployed Engineering unit that will help its customers build and roll out artificial intelligence systems.

A forward deployed engineer, or an FDE, is an employee who is embedded directly within a different business to try and accelerate a technical transformation. Defense contractor Palantir coined the term more than a decade ago, but it's seen a resurgence among software vendors looking to boost adoption by taking talent directly into clients' facilities.

Leading model developers, including OpenAI and Anthropic, announced their own FDE companies earlier this year, in partnership with banks, private equity and consulting firms. Now, AWS is looking to carve out its own piece of the market.

"We've had capabilities over the years, but structurally this is like getting everybody together in one business unit with a common rubric of deployment," Francessca Vasquez, AWS' vice president of frontier AI engineering and services, said in an interview. "It's the first time we're doing it in that way."

Amazon, which is the top cloud provider by revenue, is the first hyperscaler to announce this kind of initiative.

Vasquez said AWS' new unit will be seeded with "thousands" of FDEs. An initial pod of roughly five or six engineers will be embedded within an AWS customer at a time, and those employees will also work alongside AI agents, which are tools that can independently complete tasks on behalf of their users.

AWS said in a blog post that its FDE embeds will partner closely with customers' business, engineering and security staffers, and they'll look to leave behind self-sufficient teams with new solutions and capabilities in a matter of weeks.

"The currency that the customers are always talking about right now is speed," Vasquez said. "We do see FDE being a choice for customers who are looking for accelerated value back to their stakeholders, their customers, their executive teams."

In May, Anthropic announced it had formed a new "AI services company" with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs to help midsized businesses deploy its Claude AI models.

Days later, Anthropic's chief rival, OpenAI, announced the OpenAI Deployment Co. alongside TPG, Advent International, Bain Capital, Brookfield Asset Management and other firms. It said the new organization would expand OpenAI's ability to embed FDEs into companies that are working on "complex problems in demanding environments."

Amazon has poured billions of dollars into both Anthropic and OpenAI, but Amazon executives have not been shy about their ambitions to compete directly with the labs in some areas. A spokesperson for AWS said the company expects to have the opportunity to work with the FDE companies from OpenAI and Anthropic, and it will share more details about its partner programs in the near future.

Organizations including the Allen Institute, the National Basketball Association, Ricoh and the National Football League are already working with AWS FDEs, according to the company. Vasquez said companies in highly regulated industries with diverse datasets will be the next group of adopters.

"This is for customers that are really looking at ways to evolve their workflows," Vasquez said.

— CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed to this report.

baerbock_germany_team:
The president of the UN General Assembly, Annalena Baerbock, praises the diversity of Germany's football team as it plays in the World Cup.

Annalena Baerbock is a football fan and is often found cheering on Germany's national teams at major tournaments. Last year, she was on the edge of her seat rooting for the country's women's team at the Euros in Switzerland. And now, her fingers are crossed for the men's team at the 2026 World Cup in the United States, Canada and Mexico.

She's right in the thick of it because since 2025, Baerbock has been president of the United Nations General Assembly, which is based in New York.

Baerbock attended an award ceremony at the recently opened German House of Soccer, where former Bayern Munich forward Thomas Müller and goalkeeper Ann-Katrin Berger were awarded prizes. Müller, the most successful German player ever, currently plys his trade for the Vancouver Whitecaps in the MLS and received an honorary prize. The 36-year-old plays a key role in shaping the international image of German football beyond the field thanks to his easygoing, likable manner. Berger received the award in the player category because of the fighting spirit and determination the Gotham City keeper shows on the field.

Speaking at the event, Baerbock praised the Germany teams for the progress they have made in recent years, calling them role models.

"Today we have great diversity in the team, which symbolizes a new generation of German players," Baerbock told DW. "That wasn't always the case. When I had just graduated from high school, we had Gerald Asamoah, one of the first players born in Africa to play for the German national team." The 45-year-old recalled the discussions surrounding Asamoah at the time.

In 2001, the striker made his debut under then-Germany head coach Rudi Völler. His selection was met with approval by large segments of society, though there were also racist slurs directed at him. In addition, a debate arose over what constitutes a "true" German, since Asamoah was born in Ghana and moved to Germany at the age of 12.

Though Erwin Kostedde was the first Black player to represent the German national team, Asamoah's selection for the 2002 and 2006 World Cups, also paved the way for the modern era of players with African roots, such as Jerome Boateng, Jonathan Tah, Antonio Rüdiger and Felix Nmecha.

In the current World Cup squad, led by national team coach Julian Nagelsmann, 11 of the 26 players have an immigrant background — but this time around there was no debate like the one that arose when Asamoah was selected.

Nevertheless, some Alternative for Germany (AfD) politicians and supporters of the party refer to the Germany team as the "rainbow squad," criticizing the push for greater diversity and anti-discrimination. In the build-up to Euro 2024, a survey from German public broadcaster WDR revealed that 21% of the people polled voted "yes" when asked about wanting more white players on the team. The survey was criticized by Germany's head coach Julian Nagelsmann and team captain Joshua Kimmich.

"That shows how important anti-racism campaigns are," Baerbock said. "A team is also always a reflection of society."

She said the World Cup team underscores Germany's diversity, sends an important message to young people in Germany and shows: "You can make it anywhere. Sports—and football in particular—bring people together. On the pitch, everyone is equal, no matter where you are from, what your parents earn, or what language you speak. What matters is that you score and are a team player."

For this reason, too, Germany's former foreign minister hopes Germany will go far at this World Cup.

"We may not be the team most people have put their bets on, but we have a wonderful team spirit," Baerbock said. "Sometimes it's more important to have the best team rather than the most famous superstar."

banging-the-triangle:
…and we would get on a lot better if we admitted as much

Triangulation was about the only nearly plausible justification given at school for learning trigonometry. You can estimate the height of that tree without actually climbing the tree and dropping a tape measure, you just need the distance to the tree and the angle the top of the tree makes from where you’re standing.

Triangulation with satnavs (measuring your distance from three satellites) narrows your position down to two points, although the one you’re using probably uses more like 10 to increase accuracy and be robust against rogue measurements.

However, according to Verywellmind.com, triangulation in psychology means:

…a manipulation technique where one person involves a third party in a conflict to gain control or create division. This tactic is common in toxic relationships and among those with certain personality disorders, like narcissism and borderline personality disorder. Recognizing the signs and setting boundaries can help you protect yourself from its harmful effects.

Which is where it enters our political, business and personal lives of course. In politics, former US President Bill Clinton is most closely associated with triangulation. As Nesmith and Quirk have said in their book Inside the Presidency of Bill Clinton:

In this strategy, Clinton would stand firm on partisan Democratic positions when they were popular. On issues where Republican positions were more popular, however, Clinton would take advantage of the current Republican Congress’s tendency to overreach: he would make major concessions from conventional Democratic policies and adopt centrist positions that would have broader support than the Republicans’ offerings. By such systematic, instrumental positioning, Clinton hoped to win politically on most issues, no matter which party had the initial advantage in public opinion.

This approach was then adopted by Tony Blair with New Labour and has become pretty mainstream in politics ever since. Keir Starmer perhaps took it to new extremes with his Ming Vase strategy:

The Ming Vase strategy’s underlying premise was that, at least in matters of high political salience, policy-making should be above all driven by perceived electoral advantage. The metaphor was that Labour should treat its prospects as precarious and fragile, and that the utmost caution and prudence must be exercised in developing policy. As the term is used here, the Ming Vase strategy can be encapsulated in terms of two broad principle, opinion alignment and power accommodation. The former held that on issues which figure prominently on the public’s agenda (which of course excludes policy in many areas) policies must be adapted as closely as possible to voters’ perceptions and preferences as these can be culled from focus groups. The latter stipulated eschewing as far as possible policy options that were likely to antagonise or estrange the major constellations of power in society, those organised interests which had the capacity both to influence mass opinion and to affect the capacity of a government to deliver its policies—most notably the City and major corporations. The two arms of the strategy tended to be mutually reinforcing, in that both emphasised the need for circumspection, the avoidance of controversial and ambitious policies, and an accent on reassurance. We are not claiming that the Ming Vase strategy, as an operational code, was the sole determinant of decision-making behaviour, but rather that it was the weightiest.

And when opinion alignment and power accommodation (ie public opinion and the views of, say, powerful business lobbies) are in conflict? Well you have to pretend to be doing one thing while doing another. And there were a whole succession of examples of Starmer not acting as most of his backbenchers had been led to expect a Labour prime minister to act and putting it down to the fiscal rules they were operating under until Andy Burnham finally put him out of his misery. But the fiscal rules have remained.

These sorts of strategies ultimately tend to come unstuck because they underestimate the voters. Most people understand that our problems aren’t easy to solve, but if you make grand pronouncements about transforming politics while constraining your room for manoeuvre within fiscal rules set to appease particular interests which you don’t come clean about, then ultimately you will be regarded as untrustworthy. As you will also fail if you pin all of societies ills on desperate people taking their lives in their hands on small boats in the English Channel, and then find that none of those problems have disappeared but you now also have something resembling Trump’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) patrolling the seas.

The Grand High Triangle Lover from Sesame Street is always accompanied by Norman, who bangs a triangle to get the crowd’s attention for his boss. Think of Norman as a lobby journalist. The Grand High Triangle Lover likes to tell the story of how he became The Grand High Triangle Lover by managing to pull sticks from a stone and making them into a triangle. However Norman broke the big scoop that in fact his boss just found a hat with triangles on it one day.

It sounds like a normal day in our politics, but these are muppets. Recognise the signs and set boundaries. Let’s not let them assume the rest of us are.

In a horror scene right out of “Sweeney Todd,” a Yonkers barber gashed a customer’s artery during a wild attack with a straight razor — and  was then handed a paltry sentence by notoriously lenient judge.

Haircutter Jeury Fernandez Navarro, 38, flew into a rage because he suspected 27-year-old Carlos Santana Cordero had sex with his girlfriend, according to trial testimony.

Cordero was sitting in another barber’s chair at Escape Barber Shop on South Broadway on Aug. 4, 2025, when Navarro grabbed his hair and jerked his head back and held a gold-plated razor to his neck, according to a criminal complaint.

As the victim fought back, Navarro swung the razor toward his face, but instead struck his left arm, according to the complaint.

Navarro, who claimed the slashing was accidental, then picked the victim up by his hair a second time and held the razor to his neck while walking him out of the barbershop, as both slipped on the puddles of blood on the floor, according to the complaint and a video played in court.

Outside, the wannabe Sweeney Todd — the fictional “Demon Barber of Fleet Street’ who slit his victim’s throats with a razor and sent their bodies down a chute — continued his attack on Cordero until a Yonkers cop arrived at the scene and stopped him, officials said.

Cordero suffered a lacerated artery in his left forearm and had to undergo surgery at Westchester Medical Center, prosecutors said.

Crime scene photos obtained by The Post show blood staining the shop’s tile floor and the gold razor after the savage attack. Blood could also be seen on the sidewalk outside.

“The defendant in this case callously and intentionally grabbed a defenseless victim by the head and proceeded to viciously slash him, even as the victim attempted to protect himself,” Westchester County District Attorney Susan Cacace said.

After a jury found Navarro guilty of second-degree assault — a felony — and weapon possession, Cacace’s office asked Judge George Fufidio to sentence him to five years in state prison with five years of post-release supervision.

But the lenient judge let him off with 2 ½ years in prison and 1 and ½ years of post-release supervision.

“While we respect the court’s decision, my office firmly believes that a more substantial prison sentence was warranted given the severity and brutality of the defendant’s conduct,” Cacace said.

Last week, The Post wrote about Judge Fufidio setting a lower bail than the prosecutor requested for a man who beat up a Bronx bus driver in a Yonkers road-rage incident.

Cacace requested bail in the amount of $50,000 cash and $150,000 bond for Thywill Anasu, who allegedly “knocked out” BxM1 bus operator Johnny Rodriguez by slamming his head on the pavement and punching him repeatedly after a fender bender on April 4, a spokeswoman said.

But Fufidio ignored the request and set bail at $5,000 cash or $50,000 bond, which the accused attacker posted. Four months later, Anasu allegedly assaulted an FDNY fire marshal in uniform in the Bronx, according to a criminal complaint there — and another judge released him with supervision.

Rodriguez suffered two brain bleeds, a concussion and a torn ligament in his shoulder in the attack, he said.

“The judge made a mistake when he let him out,” Rodriguez said of Fufidio. “They need to look at what’s going on here.”
